US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a federal judge that President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch is a “generational national defense opportunity” in a legal briefing arguing the project is vital to protecting the nation’s capital. 

Originally proposed as a monument to celebrate the country’s 250th birthday, Trump last month debuted a new justification for building it, saying it would double as a tourist attraction and military complex where drones and ammunition could be stored and military snipers could be posted. 

The surprise proposal for this additional use of the 250-foot arch came as the project – a personal endeavor of the President that has become a key part of his Trump area  and his recent Executive Order  (Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again) and to support his legacy  which faces a slew of criticism and two lawsuits aimed at stopping its construction. 

In a written declaration submitted Wednesday, Hegseth defended Trump’s new rationale for the planned structure at Memorial Circle, a busy traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Tear your eyes away from the Trumps triumphal arch for a moment and consider the . new Tennessee Federal courthouse that is the real face of the President Trump-era future architectural legacy.

Just this last week in Tennessee, more than 500 miles away from Washington, DC, officials quietly unveiled a far more revealing illustration of the US President Trumps future architectural legacy.

Set to open in 2030, Chattanooga’s new courthouse will be a muscular Art Deco Greek temple. More than an imposing expression of judicial power, this state building also symbolizes something of national significance: It’s the first major new design announced by America’s federal building agency since Trump’s executive order, “Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again.” Its beauty is therefore now a matter of both architectural and political debate.

Almost a year has passed since President Trump formalized his disdain for modernism, postmodernism and brutalism by mandating that major federal buildings be designed in “classical and traditional” styles.

One further suggested way to celebrate President Trump’s magnificent presidency and his demonstrate his achievements to the American public, as well as delivering a significant gift to the America people would be to re-develop Camp David into a truly beautiful Abbey where President Trump and future Presidents can host visiting Kings and Queens and other Presidents when they visit the United States.

Many past presidents have proposed such developments at Camp David, but no one has succeeded to follow through and deliver such a wonderful facility.

Thus, a possible development by President Trump, to be considered as a further major legacy to the US people and future presidents, is the construction of a great architectural legacy (under his “Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again”) in President Trump’s name, similar to the White House complex ballroom and the Grand Trump Arch de Trump, celebrating the 250th year of the Great American Experiment

Camp David is a 125-acre (51-hectare) country retreat for the President of the United States. It lies in the wooded hills of Catocin Mountain Park In Frederik County, Maryland near the towns of Thurmont and Emmitsburg about 62 miles north-northwest of the national capital city, Washington DC.

However, what is really needed is a grand opulent castle or abbey that can accommodate and entertain very important visitors, visiting royalty and Presidents from across the world. Also, whilst it has a tiny golf course (one green and 4 Tees), plus a driving range, what it lacks is a tremendous golf course, fit for a President and his visitors plus an opulent Helipad

Thus as part of President Trump’s legacy, he should transform Camp David into something like the grand mansion of Downton Abbey in the United Kingdom, with the plan to re-name Camp David as Trump Abbey or Trump Castle.

The aim of this further Trump legacy would be to completely rebuild a magnificent  and opulent manor house or castle to replace the current rather dreary Camp David.

Downtown Abbey is of course based upon the Highclere Castle near Newbury in Hampshire, England .

Highclere Castle  (Downton Abbey) is a Grade 1 listed grand country house (or castle) built in 1679 and largely renovated during the 1840s, with a park designed by Capability Brown in the 18th century. The 5,000-acre (2,000-hectare) estate  in Highclere about five miles (eight kilometres) south of Newbury Berkshire, in England and 9+1⁄2 miles (15 kilometres) north of Andover in Hampshire.

The 19th-century renovation is in a Jacobean and Italianate style produced by architect Charles Barry. It is the country seat of the Hereditary British Earls of Carnarvon a branch of the Anglo-Welsh Herbert family

Going back to the Trump triumphal arch, the Secretary of War said that the location of the triumphal arch overlooks a number major national sites that are frequented by federal officials and its height will create elevation advantage and line-of-sight connectivity, while its central location will improve the ability to identify and assess potential threats, Hegseth argued. 

“It will be utilized as a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense,” he said. “The elevated position can also support authorized protective-overwatch and counter-sniper personnel by improving observational, situational awareness and coordination with other security elements.” 

In addition to Hegseth, Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, also defended the need for the arch’s dual purpose, saying the location “provides opportunities for increased capability for information -sharing and logistical coordination.” 

The full-throated endorsements for the arch’s potential national security uses from two cabinet members comes as the project is facing key tests to its progress. 

Hegseth’s and Mullin’s statements were part of the government’s submissions in a lawsuit being heard in the US District Court for the District of Columbia aimed at stopping the arch’s construction.

And next Thursday, the arch will be reviewed by the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), the last of two federal agencies overseeing architectural and design changes in Washington, D.C. that must approve the project. 
If approved by NCPC, the administration has already said they will start construction as early as that same day. 

However, final plans for the arch submitted to the NCPC for its November 5th meeting that were released last week included no mention of the military component. 
The plans excluded features such as the drones and snipers that Trump described in September, and the contours of the arch in the plans did not appear to reflect a national security purpose. Instead, they describe the project as a “ceremonial gateway” to the nation’s capital. 

Hegseth’s Wednesday filing stated that the military components would not require any structural modifications or alterations. “The security features will be fully integrated into the existing design,” he wrote. 

Trump has also claimed the need for national security enhancements as the primary justification for his project to build a White House ballroom where the East Wing once stood.

NewsXForge – the Global Breaking News network  that has fast facts and forging news into real facts has quoted that” This triumphal arch sounds less like a monument and more like an entirely new chapter for the capital. A triumphal arch doubling as a security and military facility would be an extraordinary departure from the original concept. 

The proposed 161-foot observation deck would also turn it into a major tourist attraction. And the idea of transforming Camp David into a grand presidential estate would be an equally dramatic architectural undertaking. Whether these visions become reality, they would leave a very visible and long-lasting mark on Washington and the Trump presidency.

In addition to Hegseth, Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, also defended the need for the arch’s dual purpose, saying the location “provides opportunities for increased capability for information -sharing and logistical coordination.” 

The full-throated endorsements for the arch’s potential national security uses from two cabinet members comes as the project is facing key tests to its progress. 

Hegseth’s and Mullin’s statements were part of the government’s submissions in a lawsuit being heard in the US District Court for the District of Columbia aimed at stopping the arch’s construction.

And next Thursday, the arch will be reviewed by the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), the last of two federal agencies overseeing architectural and design changes in Washington, D.C. that must approve the project. 
If approved by NCPC, the administration has already said they will start construction as early as that same day. 

However, final plans for the arch submitted to the NCPC for its November 5th meeting that were released last week included no mention of the military component. 
The plans excluded features such as the drones and snipers that Trump described in September, and the contours of the arch in the plans did not appear to reflect a national security purpose. Instead, they describe the project as a “ceremonial gateway” to the nation’s capital. 

Hegseth’s Wednesday filing stated that the military components would not require any structural modifications or alterations. “The security features will be fully integrated into the existing design,” he wrote. 

Trump has also claimed the need for national security enhancements as the primary justification for his project to build a White House ballroom where the East Wing once stood.

A triumphal arch doubling as a security and military facility would be an extraordinary departure from the original concept. 

The proposed 161-foot observation deck would also turn it into a major tourist attraction. And the idea of transforming Camp David into a grand presidential estate would be an equally dramatic architectural undertaking. text:
On October 30, 1994, a math professor in Virginia hit send on an email that would end up costing Intel $475 million.

Exactly 32 years later, to the day, Intel had its worst day on the stock market since 1974.

Let's start with the professor.

His name was Thomas Nicely. He taught at Lynchburg College, and he was running heavy math on prime numbers when he noticed something odd.

His brand-new Pentium was getting some division problems wrong.

Not often. One estimate put it at about 1 in 9 billion random divisions.

He reported it to Intel. Then he emailed colleagues and asked them to check their own machines.

Intel's answer was, roughly: it's not serious. If you can show us it affects you, we'll replace your chip.

That did not go well.

CNN ran the story. On December 12, IBM stopped shipping Pentium PCs. On December 20, Intel gave in and offered a replacement to anyone who asked.

In January 1995, Intel took a $475 million charge.

The chip was wrong once in about 9 billion divisions.

The message was wrong every time someone read it.

Andy Grove, Intel's CEO, ended up apologizing in public. Intel had tried to decide for its customers what they should worry about. Customers didn't agree.

Which brings me to this week.

On Friday, Intel's stock fell nearly 29%. Its worst day since 1974.

Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion. Analysts expected about $17 billion. The company pointed to two causes: an extended shutdown at its plant in Israel, where an explosion earlier this month killed two workers, and a PC slowdown it expects to last at least through the first half of next year.

This time, the causes were named plainly, on day one.

Here's the thing about deep tech.

Sooner or later, every company has a bad quarter, a slipped tape-out, a recall, a delay. The technology doesn't decide how that goes. The words do.

There's an old belief that when things go wrong, you say as little as possible and wait for it to blow over.

Grove learned the expensive way that people don't want to be managed. They want to be told the truth, early, in plain English.

The CEOs who earn trust on good days are the ones people believe on bad days.

Anyway, if you're a deep-tech CEO and you want your LinkedIn and X to build that kind of trust before you need it, that's what I write.

DM me the word TRUST.

It's not for everyone. If you never have a bad quarter, you're set.

P.S. Intel still came back from the Pentium bug and went on to dominate the PC era. Bad news rarely sinks a company. Hiding it can. DM me TRUST.

text:
The systems work. You don't wake up worrying about your next meal, how you're going to get from point A to point B, whether there will be electricity or whether basic services will function. Life is predictable, secure and considerably less stressful in many respects.

But there is another reality. Sometimes it feels like living in a beautifully maintained prison. Work, home, bills, obligations, repeat. Your life becomes a carefully choreographed routine, with very little room for spontaneity.

And if you have an entrepreneurial spirit, it can be suffocating. You want to think outside the box, take risks, explore unconventional opportunities and create something, but everything seems to pull you back into the same cycle.Zimbabwe, for all its dysfunction, offers an informal economy where resourcefulness, networking, calculated risk-taking and sheer ingenuity can create opportunities. Abroad, the systems are structured, but so are the barriers. Everything has a process, a regulation and a price. Sometimes you feel as though your entrepreneurial instincts are slowly being domesticated.

You have financial stability, but you sometimes wonder whether you've traded freedom, adventure and a sense of possibility for comfort and predictability.

My point is not that staying home is better than leaving. Migration can be life-changing, and I would encourage anyone with a genuine opportunity to take it. But let's not romanticise either side. Abroad, you may gain stability and financial security, but sometimes at the expense of spontaneity, community and the freedom to build something on your own terms.

You escape the struggle to survive, only to find yourself struggling to feel alive like me lol

Remember, God Loves You 
There will be days when the sunshine seems a little farther away, when the world feels hurried, and when kindness is harder to find than it ought to be.
But remember something wonderful: God's love does not disappear when the day grows difficult.
He knows the burdens we carry, the tears we never explain, and the quiet prayers that never reach another person's ears.
You may be overlooked by people, misunderstood by friends, or forgotten in the busyness of someone else's life. But you are never beyond the loving care of God.
His love is not measured by our popularity, our appearance, our possessions, or the attention others give us.
And sometimes, in the middle of an ordinary day, we need to remember one extraordinary truth:
You are not forgotten. You are not beyond His care. God loves you.
So carry a little kindness into the world today. Offer someone a smile, encourage a weary heart, and remember that the love God has shown us is worth sharing.
For even when the world seems short on affection, the Lord remains faithful.
 Jeremiah 31:3 — KJV
“The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.”
Remember, God loves you. And that is a truth worth carrying into every tomorrow.

text:
HOW DEMOCRACY GRADUALLY GROOMS ITS OWN SYCOPHANTS

When a political party remains in power for too long, something subtle but dangerous begins to happen within society.

People gradually adapt themselves to the system. Free benefits become expectations, personal favours become relationships, and a few familiar political faces begin to occupy permanent positions in people's lives.

Slowly, citizens start forgetting that they live in a democracy, not a monarchy.

An elected representative is supposed to be a public servant, accountable to the people every five years. Yet, somewhere along the way, the relationship gets reversed. The representative becomes the benefactor, and the voter becomes the grateful beneficiary.

Then comes the generational transformation.

Political loyalty gets inherited. People who have grown up around the same political establishment begin treating familiar politicians as family friends, well-wishers and eventually the sole messiahs of their communities.

Questioning these politicians becomes almost like questioning the community itself.

And thus, sycophants are born among otherwise capable people who gradually stop exercising independent judgement.

The political establishment soon discovers their usefulness. They become readymade PR agents, operating within villages, neighbourhoods and social circles.

A little recognition, occasional financial assistance, invitations to lunches, free meals, liquor parties, community feasts and small personal favours are sometimes enough to keep this informal machinery running.

Some amplify political narratives on social media. Others defend the leadership at public gatherings, manufacture goodwill and discourage uncomfortable questions.

The politician gets an army of unofficial promoters without having to appoint a single one of them.

And this is how an entire ecosystem of political sycophancy is groomed.

Look around us, particularly in Odisha. We have developed a strange social culture where the person who can spend money on liquor, arrange lavish meals, distribute favours and offer occasional privileges is often celebrated as the best friend, a great well-wisher or even a messiah.

But have we ever questioned what kind of friendship this really is?

Does arranging a feast make someone a good public representative? Does buying drinks make someone a well-wisher? And do occasional personal benefits compensate for years of compromised public governance?

We elect the same governments year after year, sometimes without even questioning ourselves about what we have gained as a society.

A few free lunches, selfies with influential people, personal favours and benefits to the family become sufficient reasons for lifelong political loyalty.

Meanwhile, education, healthcare, employment, infrastructure, industrial development and the larger interests of society quietly take a back seat.

This is how misrule can acquire the appearance of democratic permanence.

Elections continue, political speeches become louder, and the sycophants become the brand ambassadors and cheerleaders of the establishment.

They celebrate the rulers, defend their failures and convince everyone that questioning the leadership is almost an act of betrayal.

The greatest irony of democracy is that people can continue exercising their right to vote while gradually abandoning their responsibility to think.

An elected representative is not a monarch. A constituency is not an inherited kingdom. Public money is not personal generosity.

We are citizens, not subjects.

Our votes are mandates, not lifetime loyalty cards. #Democracy

text:
According to the 1860 United States Census, there were 488,070 free Antebellum-Black Americans in the United States of America just before the Civil War began in 1861 (roughly 488,000 to 500,000 people, making up about 11% of the total Black population). These individuals already had first, middle, and last names. Many were landowners and business owners, some owned slaves themselves, some were citizens and fewer had the right to vote in the Northern or non-slave states.

Regional Distribution
Total Free Black Population: 488,070
Free States (North): 226,152 (approx. 46.3%)
Slave States (South & Border States): 261,918 (approx. 53.7%), with a large majority of Southern free Black residents living in the Upper South (such as Virginia and Maryland) rather than the Lower South.

When the 13th Amendment abolished slavery in 1865, approximately four million formerly enslaved individuals gained the legal right to choose their own surnames. Prior to the 1870 US Census, the first federal census to record formerly enslaved or Antebellum-Black Americans by name rather than as unnamed property statistics, naming practices were incredibly fluid.

A common historical misconception is that most freed people automatically adopted the last name of their final enslaver. In reality, historians and genealogists note that roughly 80% of Antebellum-Black Americans chose or "made up" new surnames to intentionally break ties with their most recent oppressors, protect themselves, or freely declare their new identities.

During the Antebellum Era, the enslaved generally did not have official, legally recognized surnames. They were typically known only by a first name.
Freed Black individuals and families, whether they gained freedom through manumission or escape between the 1600s & the American Civil War, chose or inherited surnames through a variety of personal, familial, and practical methods rather than simply adopting the names of their former enslavers.
Surnames only became a widespread necessity after emancipation (the end of the Civil War and the 13th Amendment), when newly freed Antebellum-Black Americans (Antebellum-Moor Americans) registered for marriages, land, employment and the 1870 US Census.

How Surnames Were Chosen
-Patronymics and Ancestral Names: Many Antebellum-Black Americans adopted the first name of a father, grandfather, or respected family elder as a surname to honor family ties and signal lineage such as John, James, Henry, Roberts, Thomas.
Johnson (Literally "Son of John", widely adopted to cement family lineages)
-Williams (Derived from "Son of William")
-Brown (Simple English surname widely used to denote family branches)
-Jones (Derived from John or Jonas, highly utilized across the South)
-Thomas (Elevating a paternal given name to a last name)
-Harris (Derived from Harry or Harrison)
-Robinson (Derived from Robert or Robin)
-Robert/Robertson (Derived from Robert)
-Davis (Derived from David, sometimes used to adapt secret family lines)
-Henry (Reclaiming a common ancestral first name)
-James (Reclaiming a common ancestral first name)
-Lewis (Reclaiming a common ancestral first name)
-Allen (Adopted as a family identifier)
-Walker (Often tied to ancestral lines or symbolic of moving away from bondage)
-Scott (Frequently used as a traditional family name passed down orally during slavery)
-Young (Used to distinguish younger generations establishing new lines)

-Declarations of Status: Freed people frequently "made up" surnames based on local landscapes, regions, or words associated with royalty & personal dignity to replace the humiliating classical names (like Caesar or Jupiter), Names like: 
Freeman (Literally declaring a "free man")
Freedman (Marking the transition from enslavement to liberty)
Liberty (Chosen to celebrate emancipation)
Justice (Reflecting the hope for a fair society)
Hope (Chosen as a forward-looking family marker)
Independence (Adopted to assert self-reliance)
King or Queen (A status name chosen to assert dignity, honor, and self-worth)
Prince (Selected to project high regard
White (Sometimes chosen adaptively to blend into records or camouflage identity for protection)

-Aspirational and Historical Figures: 
Many Antebellum-Black Americans selected names of foundational figures, military leaders, or prominent abolitionists to align their new families with national ideals or symbols of freedom, prestige and dignity.
-Washington (The absolute most common surname chosen by freed people, chosen to honor the country's ideals or mark survival)
-Lincoln (In honor of Abraham Lincoln and the Emancipation Proclamation)
-Jackson (Often associated with Andrew Jackson or adopted from Southern prominence)
-Jefferson (Highly concentrated among Black Americans, linked to Thomas Jefferson)
-Grant (To honor Union General and President Ulysses S. Grant)
-Douglass (Deliberately taken to honor the legendary abolitionist Frederick Douglass)
-Franklin (Inspired by Benjamin Franklin or chosen for its linguistic association with being a "free landholder")
-Madison (Inspired by James Madison)
-Monroe (Inspired by James Monroe)
-Clay (Often selected due to political prominence)
-Lee (Widespread in the South, frequently adopted or adapted)

-Occupational and Craft Names: Antebellum-Black Americans who possessed highly specialized skills used their trade to create their new family identity. During slavery, their labor belonged to someone else; in freedom, they chose to own the title of their expertise.
Names tied to trades & skills, such as 
-Smith (Commonly adopted by plantation blacksmiths who held high communal value)
-Miller  (Operators of grain and lumber mills)
-Farmer (Emphasizing a family's new connection to working their own crops)
-Green (Often occupational for groundskeepers or symbolic of new growth)
-Gardener (Cultivators of land and botanical skills)
-Parker  (Keeper or warden of a park)
-Carter (Derived from cart drivers or transporters)
-Cooper (Barrel makers, a vital skilled trade in the Antebellum era)
-Mason (Stonemasons and builders)
-Carpenter (Woodworkers & structural builders)
-Cook (Reflecting culinary mastery)
-Turner (Lathe operators or wood-turners, also associated with Nat Turner's rebellion)
-Taylor / Tailor (Adopted by skilled clothes makers and seamstresses)
-Shepherd / Sheperd (Livestock handlers & caretakers)
-Wright (Craftsman or woodworker)
-Barber (Haircutter, surgeon, or tooth-puller)
-Tanner (Leather tanner)
-Fuller (Scourer & thickener of raw cloth)
-Dyer (Dyeing cloth specialist)
-Collier (Coal or charcoal burner/seller)
-Silver (Silver smith or worker)
-Weaver (Cloth weaver)
-Baxter (Female or traditional baker)
-Webster Female cloth weaver (later general weaver)
Chapman, Chandler, Coach  Author, Butcher, Baker, Fisher, Hunter, Sailor, Cutter, Hammer, Page, Bishop, Elder, Potter, Goldsmith, Barker, Waller, Chamberlin, Butler, Fletcher, were adopted to reflect a person's competence, livelihood, and standing in the community.

-Geographical and Land-Based Names: Individuals selected names based on local geography, towns, counties, rivers, or agricultural life (such as Banks, Hill, Marsh, Clay, Fields, Woods, Brook, Ford, Bridge, Stone, Lane, Shore, Camp, Rivers, Lake, Lee / Leigh, Holmes, Hall, Grove, Underwood, Forest, Moore, Heath, Dike, Ash, Bailey, Cross, Burton, Cliff or specific place names) to anchor their identity to a physical place rather than a master.
-Ordinary or Blend-in Names: Common English or Anglo-American surnames like Pearce, Johnson, Williams, Brown, and Jones were chosen to integrate smoothly into the broader community and offer a degree of everyday safety or anonymity. 
-Former Enslaver Surnames (Selective): While some freed individuals did keep the surname of a past or current enslaver for continuity or to help locate scattered family members from the same plantation, historian research (such as that by Herbert Gutman) shows this was often linked to an older plantation where the family unit was last intact, or rejected entirely once true legal autonomy arrived.
-Colonial and Creole Heritages: In regions like Louisiana, free people of color (gens de couleur libres) often carried French (Dubois, Dumas, Duvall, Fontaine or Spanish (Rios, Silva, Bettencourt) surnames dating back to the 1700s, documented extensively through church and notarial records.
-While many people assume that Antebellum-Black Americans exclusively hold English last names, surnames of Irish ( Bryant, Carroll, Lynch, or Sullivan) , German and Dutch (  Schumacher/Shoemaker, Van Buren, Schuyler, Meyers, Hoffman, or Linker), Welsh and Scottish (Campbell, Mcintosh, Pierce, Piers, Gordon, Grant, Scott, Jones, Williams, and Evans) are highly prevalent.
-Paternal Ancestry and Coercion
DNA and genealogical evidence show a significant divergence between chosen surnames & biological ancestry, heavily rooted in the exploitation of enslaved women (Antebellum-Moorena). White overseers, plantation owners, and neighboring laborers of Irish, Scottish, or German descent frequently fathered children with enslaved women through coercion and rape. In the Reconstruction period, some individuals chose to take the surname of their biological father, even if he was white and had never legally recognized them.
-Integration: In urban areas during both the antebellum era (for free Antebellum-Black populations) and Reconstruction/Postbellum eras 1865 - 1945, Antebellum-Black Americans lived & worked alongside working-class Irish and German immigrants. Surnames were occasionally adopted through close social ties, community integration, or intermarriage within these working-class neighborhoods.
-Institutional and Bureaucratic Assignment
During the antebellum period, if an enslaved person was manumitted (freed), or during the Reconstruction era when registering to vote, signing labor contracts, or applying for Civil War pensions, the federal government or local courts required a full legal name. If an individual did not have a surname, or if a census taker or Freedman's Bureau officer couldn't understand or spell their preferred name, a European surname common to the local area (such as a local German or Irish name) was often assigned to them on official paperwork.

How Surnames Were Chosen World Wide

-Surnames developed across these cultures & regions through a mix of medieval administration, religious edicts, tax registries, and 19th-to-20th-century state modernization laws.

China
Ancient Origins: Chinese surnames date back thousands of years & originally had two components: Xing (姓), which were ancient matrilineal clan names, and Shi (氏), which were patrilineal branch or status names.
Patrilineal Shift: Over time, Xing and Shi merged, and surnames became strictly patrilineal, passed down from father to child to emphasize lineage and imperial organization.
Common Names: Most surnames are monosyllabic (Wang, Li, Zhang) and often trace back to ancient feudal states, professions, or aristocratic titles. Women traditionally kept their maiden names after marriage.

Italy
Northern Beginnings: Hereditary surnames first appeared around the 9th & 10th centuries in trading hubs like Venice and northern Italy, driven by urban growth and commerce.
Spread South: The practice moved southwards over the next 500 years, standardizing completely after the 16th century. Common patterns include patronymics, pluralized endings (-i, Rossi), and regional occupational or nickname roots.

Spain
Patronymic Endings: Many Spanish surnames originated as patronymics marked by the suffix -ez (meaning "son of"), such as Rodríguez (son of Rodrigo) or González (son of Gonzalo).
Consolidation: Emerging during the Middle Ages, surnames spread from nobility to commoners for tax and property tracking, eventually becoming fixed hereditary multi-part surnames (combining paternal and maternal lines)

England
Norman Conquest (1066): The ruling Norman elite introduced hereditary surnames to track feudal landholdings and tax obligations.
Diffusion: Surnames trickled down to the general population through the 13th–15th centuries. They generally fall into four buckets: topographic (Hill), locative (Atwood), occupational (Smith), and patronymic (Johnson, prefixed with Mac- or Fitz-)

Germany
Urban & Regional Growth: German family names (Familiennamen) began emerging around the 12th century in southern & urban centers, solidifying northward through the 16th century. 
Four Main Types: Berufsnamen (Occupational, Müller [miller] or Schneider [tailor])
Übernamen (Nicknames/physical traits, Klein, Schwarz)
Herkunfts-/Wohnstättenamen (Geographic or landscape origins, Bergmann, Bauer)
Vatersnamen (Patronymics like Peters or Albrecht)

France
Aristocracy to Commoners: Noble families adopted "de + place name" starting in the 11th century to mark land ownership.
State Registration: The practice trickled down to commoners over the next few centuries and became legally anchored when the Council of Trent (1563) and royal decrees by King Francis I mandated parish baptismal and civil records.

Jews
Early Origins: Scholars and prominent individuals in North Africa, Spain, France, and Italy used non-hereditary patronymics, occupational, or toponymic names as early as the 10th and 11th centuries.
Sephardic Tradition: Exiles from Spain and Portugal (1492/1496) carried fixed Iberian surnames ( Toledano, Alves, Abravanel) across North Africa, the Ottoman Empire, and Europe.
Ashkenazi Mandate: In Central and Eastern Europe, most families did not have permanent surnames until government decrees forced them to adopt German-style names, such as Austria’s Patent über die Judennamen issued by Joseph II in 1787 and similar laws in the Russian Empire. Common endings include -berg, -stein, and -witz. 

Arabs
The Nasab System: Traditional Arabic naming uses a chain of patronymics (ibn or bin meaning "son of"; bint meaning "daughter of"), alongside a kunya (honorific "father/mother of") and a nisba (denoting tribe, region, or craft).
Hereditary Surnames: Fixed family names (ism al-usra) expanded significantly under late Ottoman administration, Western colonial influences, and 19th-to-20th-century national civil registries. Many start with the definite article Al- (Al-Masri, Al-Husseini). 

Scandinavia: 
Many Scandinavian regions did not adopt fixed hereditary surnames until the 18th and 19th centuries.

Korea
Aristocratic Privilege: Historically, surnames were restricted to the royalty and nobility (Yangban), while the general population (commoners and slaves) did not have formal family names.
Dynastic Continuity: Unlike many other regions where shifting dynasties wiped out old ruling families, Korea’s peaceful dynastic transitions (Silla, Goryeo, Joseon) allowed core ruling lineages like Kim, Lee (Yi), and Park to maintain and spread their names.
Universal Adoption: Surnames became universal for all citizens during the Gabo Reforms in 1894, allowing commoners to adopt names (often purchasing them or taking the names of local patrons/clans), leading to a heavy concentration of a few major surnames. Each surname is tied to an ancestral seat.

Japan
Samurai vs. Commoners: For most of Japanese history, hereditary family surnames were reserved for the samurai, nobility, and upper classes. Commoners typically used only personal names or identified themselves by their village, occupation, or house.
The 1875 Mandate: Following the Meiji Restoration, the government made surnames mandatory for all citizens in 1875 (Hisei Shinbutsu / Family Name Decree) to modernize taxation, conscription, and census tracking.
Nature and Geography: Because ordinary citizens had to scramble to pick or register a surname, many chose names derived from local geography, nature, or farming landscapes (Yamamoto meaning "base of the mountain", Sato). Japan now boasts hundreds of thousands of distinct surnames.

Philippines
Pre-Colonial Naming: Before Spanish colonization, Filipinos used indigenous naming systems (often single personal names or descriptive monikers), sometimes influenced by trade connections with China and Southeast Asian neighbors.
The Claveria Decree (1849): Spanish Governor-General Narciso Claveria issued a decree in 1849 requiring native families to select surnames from a vast Spanish-language catalog (Catálogo Alfabético de Apellidos) to improve tax collection & Catholic parish registries.
Modern Hybridity: As a result, Filipino surnames are predominantly Spanish (Dela Cruz, Santos), alongside indigenous and Chinese-derived surnames. Western naming order (first name, middle name/mother's maiden name, and last name) is standard.

Thailand
Mononym Tradition: For most of Siam's history, the general population used only a single given name (mononym), supplemented by nicknames, parental references, or hometowns.
The Surname Act of 1913: King Rama VI (Maha Vajiravudh), influenced by his education in Britain, introduced the Surname Act in 1913 to modernize state bureaucracy, census records, and military tracking.
Unique Uniqueness Rule: A unique feature of the 1913 law was that no two families could register the exact same surname. Because common words were quickly taken, families invented long, virtuous, or poetic compound words. Consequently, sharing a traditional Thai surname almost always implies a direct blood relation.

Indonesia
Absence of a Universal Surname Culture: Indonesia is a vast archipelago with over 300 ethnic groups, and most ethnic groups (such as the Javanese) traditionally do not use hereditary family surnames. Instead, many individuals go by a single given name (mononym, like Sukarno or Suharto) or multi-word personal names without a fixed family-name component.
Regional Exceptions: Certain ethnic groups do practice patrilineal or clan-based surnames, such as the Batak people in Sumatra (Sitorus, Nababan), Minangkabau matrilineal lineages, or Christian/Eastern Indonesian communities influenced by European or local clan traditions.
The Chinese-Indonesian Experience: During the Suharto regime (starting in the late 1960s), anti-Chinese assimilation policies forced ethnic Chinese Indonesians to drop traditional Chinese surnames & adopt Indonesian-sounding mononyms or names. After 1998, restrictions were lifted, though many families kept their adopted Indonesian names. Official Indonesian documents treat a person's entire name sequence as a single personal identifier rather than dividing it into first, middle, and last names

Turkey
Ottoman Era: Turks traditionally used given names followed by father's names, religious titles (such as Effendi or Pasha), or geographic/tribal tags rather than permanent European-style family names.
The 1934 Surname Law: Modern Turkey transformed its naming conventions when the Turkish Surname Law was enacted on June 21, 1934 (effective 1935), requiring every citizen to adopt a fixed, hereditary Turkish surname

Nigerian
Traditional Naming: Various ethnic groups (Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Fulani) historically relied on single given names, patronymics, clan lineages, or praise-names that reflected birth day circumstances or ancestral deities.
Colonial & Religious Shift: Fixed, hereditary Western and Islamic surnames became widespread during British colonial administration after the 1900s, Christian missionary schooling, and the deeper integration of Islam in northern regions.

Ghana
Origin & Structure: A distinctive feature of Ghanaian (particularly Akan) culture is the day-name system, where children are given a first name or surname based on the day of the week they were born, carrying deep symbolic meaning (e.g., Mensah for third-born children, or Cudjoe for a child born on Monday). Surnames also reflect ancestral clans, occupational trades, or spiritual beliefs (Quansah - "God is watching you").
Common Examples: Mensah, Nkrumah, Adu, Quansah.

Senegal
Origin & Structure: Senegalese surnames are deeply rooted in West African ethnic groups like the Wolof, Serer, and Fula/Pulaar. Many surnames trace back to ancient royal clans (such as Diop, a Wolof royal clan name), occupational castes, or Islamic lineage spread via trade and scholarship across the Sahel.

Ethiopia
Origin & Structure: Ethiopia traditionally does not use European-style hereditary family surnames. Instead, an individual’s second name is their father’s first name (patronymic), and sometimes followed by the grandfather’s first name. Names frequently carry Amharic or Ge'ez meanings tied to religious faith, gratitude, or virtues (Tadesse, Tesfaye - "hope").
Common Examples: Tadesse, Tesfaye

Kenya
Origin & Structure: Kenyan surnames vary by community (such as Kikuyu, Luo, or Kalenjin). Among the Kikuyu, names frequently honor ancestors or reflect cultural milestones (Mwangi). British colonization also introduced partial anglicization or record formalization, though traditional patronymic and clan-based naming structures remain culturally prominent.
Common Examples: Mwangi, Kenyatta, Otieno.

Morocco
Origin & Structure: Moroccan surnames are shaped by Amazigh (Berber) indigenous roots combined with centuries of Arab-Islamic history & Andalusian migration. Many surnames are patronymics (using Ibn meaning "son of"), tribal/geographic attributions (describing a region or city of origin), or honorific/royal lineage claims such as Alaoui (linked to the reigning Alaouite dynasty).

No, recognizing the historical origins of surnames does not sound like slavery. It is a factual description of how naming worked under the USA system during the Antebellum era and what happened afterwards.

What English or Western surnames Means
It refers to surnames of European linguistic origin English, Scottish, Irish, Welsh, German French, Dutch, etc. that became the norm in the USA and other Western societies. For Antebellum-Black / Anglo-Black / Anglo-Moor Americans in the USA the great majority of common surnames ( Washington, Williams, Johnson, Smith, James, Brown, Jackson and many others are of this type. As I documented earlier they are not automatically "slaveholders  names" though many are. After emancipation, Antebellum-Black Americans had the right to choose their own surnames, and the surnames they choose were for a variety of reasons. The process was more varied than the simple " everyone took the master's name" stereotype, but American, English, Western surnames became the standard or rule.
The Comparison to Other Groups
Globally, mononyms (single names) were historically the norm in most cultures. Aside from the Chinese, Europeans were among the first to adopt surnames during the Medieval period. However, between the 1500s and 1700s, surnames remained a privilege of the few, largely reserved for royalty, rulers, wealthy individuals, and landowners. The widespread adoption of family names by commoners, peasants, serfs, slave populations, and the landless occurred much later, often imposed by government decrees, for collecting taxes & tracking ownership of property.
Similarly, single given names were the standard across most traditional African cultures. Surnames were not widely adopted in Africa until the era of European colonialism in the 1900s. At that time, people began adopting family names derived from Islamic traditions, improvised terms, birthdates, religious rituals, occupations, environmental features, or descriptive phrases. Consequently, traditional African surnames as we understand them today did not exist prior to the 1900s. Individuals can honor and celebrate their broader African heritage while still deeply respecting the distinct lineage of their Antebellum-Black / Antebellum-Moor American ancestors, however taken on African or Islamic surnames is absolutely absurd, Islam is not a native African religion, it is Arabic, and it caused havoc across the African continent, isolating Western and Central Africa from non-Arabic middle-eastern and European cultures, the Arabs became middle-men between Europe, the middle-east, Asia and West Africa, in my opinion Africa would have been better-off practicing Coptic Christianity, a religion that was well establish in Africa by the Egyptians, Nubians, Libyans and Ethiopians in the first, second and third centuries, before they were invaded and conquered by the Arab-Muslim in the 7th & 8th century.
I lived worked and traveled through several African countries between 1994 - 1996, I nearly married a Cape-Malay Muslim girl in Cape Town. I wasn't impress with African culture, African food or Ancient African history. While regions like Egypt, Sudan, and Ethiopia possess extensively documented histories, physical artifacts, and ancient texts, finding non-Arabic written records, non-Arabic or pre-colonial physical artifacts, monuments, religious temples, architectural ruins, palaces and non-Islamic historical narratives on Western and Central Africa, specifically the Ghana, Mali, Songhai and Kanem-Bornu empires presented a considerable historical challenge.

text:
@seanhannity A generational defense opportunity: 

Hegseth offers full-throated endorsement of Trump’s arch amid legal battle 

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a federal judge that President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch is a “generational national defense opportunity” in a legal briefing arguing the project is vital to protecting the nation’s capital. 

Originally proposed as a monument to celebrate the country’s 250th birthday, Trump last month debuted a new justification for building it, saying it would double as a tourist attraction and military complex where drones and ammunition could be stored and military snipers could be posted. 

The surprise proposal for this additional use of the 250-foot arch came as the project – a personal endeavor of the President that has become a key part of his Trump area  and his recent Executive Order  (Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again) and to support his legacy  which faces a slew of criticism and two lawsuits aimed at stopping its construction. 

In a written declaration submitted Wednesday, Hegseth defended Trump’s new rationale for the planned structure at Memorial Circle, a busy traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Tear your eyes away from the Trumps triumphal arch for a moment and consider the . new Tennessee Federal courthouse that is the real face of the President Trump-era future architectural legacy.

Just this last week in Tennessee, more than 500 miles away from Washington, DC, officials quietly unveiled a far more revealing illustration of the US President Trumps future architectural legacy.

Set to open in 2030, Chattanooga’s new courthouse will be a muscular Art Deco Greek temple. More than an imposing expression of judicial power, this state building also symbolizes something of national significance: It’s the first major new design announced by America’s federal building agency since Trump’s executive order, “Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again.” Its beauty is therefore now a matter of both architectural and political debate.

Almost a year has passed since President Trump formalized his disdain for modernism, postmodernism and brutalism by mandating that major federal buildings be designed in “classical and traditional” styles.

One further suggested way to celebrate President Trump’s magnificent presidency and his demonstrate his achievements to the American public, as well as delivering a significant gift to the America people would be to re-develop Camp David into a truly beautiful Abbey where President Trump and future Presidents can host visiting Kings and Queens and other Presidents when they visit the United States.

Many past presidents have proposed such developments at Camp David, but no one has succeeded to follow through and deliver such a wonderful facility.

Thus, a possible development by President Trump, to be considered as a further major legacy to the US people and future presidents, is the construction of a great architectural legacy (under his “Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again”) in President Trump’s name, similar to the White House complex ballroom and the Grand Trump Arch de Trump, celebrating the 250th year of the Great American Experiment

Camp David is a 125-acre (51-hectare) country retreat for the President of the United States. It lies in the wooded hills of Catocin Mountain Park In Frederik County, Maryland near the towns of Thurmont and Emmitsburg about 62 miles north-northwest of the national capital city, Washington DC.

However, what is really needed is a grand opulent castle or abbey that can accommodate and entertain very important visitors, visiting royalty and Presidents from across the world. Also, whilst it has a tiny golf course (one green and 4 Tees), plus a driving range, what it lacks is a tremendous golf course, fit for a President and his visitors plus an opulent Helipad

Thus as part of President Trump’s legacy, he should transform Camp David into something like the grand mansion of Downton Abbey in the United Kingdom, with the plan to re-name Camp David as Trump Abbey or Trump Castle.

The aim of this further Trump legacy would be to completely rebuild a magnificent  and opulent manor house or castle to replace the current rather dreary Camp David.

Downtown Abbey is of course based upon the Highclere Castle near Newbury in Hampshire, England .

Highclere Castle  (Downton Abbey) is a Grade 1 listed grand country house (or castle) built in 1679 and largely renovated during the 1840s, with a park designed by Capability Brown in the 18th century. The 5,000-acre (2,000-hectare) estate  in Highclere about five miles (eight kilometres) south of Newbury Berkshire, in England and 9+1⁄2 miles (15 kilometres) north of Andover in Hampshire.

The 19th-century renovation is in a Jacobean and Italianate style produced by architect Charles Barry. It is the country seat of the Hereditary British Earls of Carnarvon a branch of the Anglo-Welsh Herbert family

Going back to the Trump triumphal arch, the Secretary of War said that the location of the triumphal arch overlooks a number major national sites that are frequented by federal officials and its height will create elevation advantage and line-of-sight connectivity, while its central location will improve the ability to identify and assess potential threats, Hegseth argued. 

“It will be utilized as a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense,” he said. “The elevated position can also support authorized protective-overwatch and counter-sniper personnel by improving observational, situational awareness and coordination with other security elements.” 

In addition to Hegseth, Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, also defended the need for the arch’s dual purpose, saying the location “provides opportunities for increased capability for information -sharing and logistical coordination.” 

The full-throated endorsements for the arch’s potential national security uses from two cabinet members comes as the project is facing key tests to its progress. 

Hegseth’s and Mullin’s statements were part of the government’s submissions in a lawsuit being heard in the US District Court for the District of Columbia aimed at stopping the arch’s construction.

And next Thursday, the arch will be reviewed by the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), the last of two federal agencies overseeing architectural and design changes in Washington, D.C. that must approve the project. 
If approved by NCPC, the administration has already said they will start construction as early as that same day. 

However, final plans for the arch submitted to the NCPC for its November 5th meeting that were released last week included no mention of the military component. 
The plans excluded features such as the drones and snipers that Trump described in September, and the contours of the arch in the plans did not appear to reflect a national security purpose. Instead, they describe the project as a “ceremonial gateway” to the nation’s capital. 

Hegseth’s Wednesday filing stated that the military components would not require any structural modifications or alterations. “The security features will be fully integrated into the existing design,” he wrote. 

Trump has also claimed the need for national security enhancements as the primary justification for his project to build a White House ballroom where the East Wing once stood.

NewsXForge – the Global Breaking News network  that has fast facts and forging news into real facts has quoted that” This triumphal arch sounds less like a monument and more like an entirely new chapter for the capital. A triumphal arch doubling as a security and military facility would be an extraordinary departure from the original concept. 

The proposed 161-foot observation deck would also turn it into a major tourist attraction. And the idea of transforming Camp David into a grand presidential estate would be an equally dramatic architectural undertaking. Whether these visions become reality, they would leave a very visible and long-lasting mark on Washington and the Trump presidency.

Trump has also claimed the need for national security enhancements as the primary justification for his project to build a White House ballroom where the East Wing once stood.

NewsXForge – the Global Breaking News network  that has fast facts and forging news into real facts has quoted that” This triumphal arch sounds less like a monument and more like an entirely new chapter for the capital. A triumphal arch doubling as a security and military facility would be an extraordinary departure from the original concept. 

The proposed 161-foot observation deck would also turn it into a major tourist attraction. And the idea of transforming Camp David into a grand presidential estate would be an equally dramatic architectural undertaking. text:
#AvaraachanAndSons - Review

#AvaraachanAndSons Is A Malayalam Family Comedy-Drama That Revolves Around #Avaraachan, A Carefree Widower Whose Irresponsible Lifestyle And Drinking Habits Create Constant Problems For His Two Grown-Up Sons, #Jaison And #Jaimon. Unlike Typical Family Dramas, The Story Focuses On A Father Whose Behaviour Becomes A Burden For His Children. After Another Incident Creates Trouble In His Hometown Of Chellanam, Avaraachan Moves To His Sister's House In The Hill Regions. His Journey Gradually Introduces New Relationships, Unexpected Situations And An Opportunity To Understand His Own Mistakes. The Film Explores Family Relationships, Loneliness, Alcoholism, Responsibility And Personal Transformation With A Blend Of Humour And Emotion❤️. #BijuMenon❤️ Is The Biggest Strength Of The Film, Delivering A Natural And Enjoyable Performance As Avaraachan. His Comedy Timing, Expressions And Emotional Performance Make The Character Both Irritating And Likeable At The Same Time👏. #SreenathBhasi Delivers A Restrained Performance As Jaison, Portraying A Responsible Son Who Constantly Deals With His Father's Problems. #Ganapathi Is Convincing As Jaimon, Bringing A Refreshing Naturalness To His Character. #VinayForrt Makes A Strong Impression As Ani, Adding A Different Energy To The Later Portions. #GraceAntony, #AkhilaBhargavan, #PaulyValsan, #ParvathyBabu And #JohnyAntony Provide Good Support To The Narrative. Director #Thamby🎬 Chooses A Simple And Realistic Approach Rather Than Depending On Overdramatic Family Sentiment. The Coastal Village Atmosphere Of Chellanam And The Hill-Station Setting Give The Film A Natural Identity🌴. The Relationship Between Avaraachan And His Sister, His Interactions With His Sons And The Different Characters He Encounters Provide Several Interesting Situations. #SajithPurushan's Cinematography🎥 Captures The Locations And Everyday Atmosphere Beautifully, While #AkashJosephVarghese's Editing Maintains A Mostly Smooth Narrative Flow. #SanalDev's Music Supports The Film's Emotional And Entertaining Moments. One Of The Biggest Positives🔥 Is #BijuMenon's Performance And The Film's Natural Characterisation. His Chemistry With #PaulyValsan Is Particularly Enjoyable, While The Father-Son Relationship Provides Several Relatable Moments❤️. The Film Also Handles Loneliness, Alcoholism And The Need For Personal Change Without Depending Too Much On Melodrama. #VinayForrt's Entry Brings Fresh Energy To The Later Portions And Makes The Narrative More Interesting. However😕, The Screenplay Loses Its Focus On The Family In Certain Sections. Some Subplots Continue For Too Long, And The Central Conflicts Do Not Always Receive Enough Dramatic Depth. The Overall Narration Also Feels Uneven In Parts, Preventing Some Emotional Moments From Reaching Their Full Potential. The Major Highlights🔥 Are #BijuMenon's Excellent Performance, #SreenathBhasi's Natural Acting, #Ganapathi's Convincing Contribution, #VinayForrt's Memorable Character, The Family Relationships, The Humour, The Coastal Atmosphere🌴 And The Emotional Moments. The Main Drawbacks Are The Uneven Screenplay, Underdeveloped Family Conflicts And Certain Extended Subplots That Affect The Narrative Flow. Overall #AvaraachanAndSons Is A Pleasant And Relatable Malayalam Family Drama That Works Mainly Because Of #BijuMenon's Outstanding Screen Presence👌. The Film Offers Natural Performances, Light-Hearted Humour And Meaningful Emotional Moments Without Depending On Excessive Commercial Elements. Although The Screenplay Could Have Explored The Father-Son Relationships More Deeply And Maintained Better Narrative Focus, The Characters And Performances Make It An Enjoyable Watch. A Good One-Time Watch For Viewers Who Appreciate Realistic Family Dramas And Feel-Good Malayalam Cinema❤️.

RATING : 2.75/5

text:
I’m 31, and until recently, I was earning about $57,000 a year as an operations supervisor at a hotel in Pennsylvania. The work was demanding, the pay was average, and every time a management position opened up, someone with more experience seemed to get it.

So when I applied for a resort operations director position and made it through three rounds of interviews, I was already surprised.

Then the offer came.

$98,000 a year, free accommodation on the property, and a title that would finally put me on the management track I had been chasing.

I nearly accepted on the spot.

During the final interview, however, the owner explained something the job listing had barely mentioned.

The resort operated beside a large lake in a remote part of northern Michigan. It welcomed guests from spring through autumn, but closed completely for four months during winter.

During that period, I would be expected to remain on the property to monitor the buildings, oversee maintenance, inspect storm damage, and coordinate contractors whenever problems arose.

There would be no regular staff living there with me.

I asked whether I could leave on weekends.

The owner hesitated before answering.

“You can, technically. But if a major storm hits or a pipe bursts, you're the person responsible for responding.”

He explained that the previous manager had resigned halfway through the winter season. Apparently, the isolation had affected him more than he expected.

I drove home thinking about the money, the title, and the possibility of finally getting ahead financially.

Then I told my family.

My mother immediately called it a terrible idea. My older brother laughed and said I was about to become a caretaker with an executive salary.

I thought they were being dramatic.

After all, I would still have electricity, internet, a furnished apartment, and a job that could transform my career.

At least, that was what I believed before I visited the property.

@RepChipRoy A generational defense opportunity: 

Hegseth offers full-throated endorsement of Trump’s arch amid legal battle 

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a federal judge that President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch is a “generational national defense opportunity” in a legal briefing arguing the project is vital to protecting the nation’s capital. 

Originally proposed as a monument to celebrate the country’s 250th birthday, Trump last month debuted a new justification for building it, saying it would double as a tourist attraction and military complex where drones and ammunition could be stored and military snipers could be posted. 

The surprise proposal for this additional use of the 250-foot arch came as the project – a personal endeavor of the President that has become a key part of his Trump area  and his recent Executive Order  (Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again) and to support his legacy  which faces a slew of criticism and two lawsuits aimed at stopping its construction. 

In a written declaration submitted Wednesday, Hegseth defended Trump’s new rationale for the planned structure at Memorial Circle, a busy traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Tear your eyes away from the Trumps triumphal arch for a moment and consider the . new Tennessee Federal courthouse that is the real face of the President Trump-era future architectural legacy.

Just this last week in Tennessee, more than 500 miles away from Washington, DC, officials quietly unveiled a far more revealing illustration of the US President Trumps future architectural legacy.

Set to open in 2030, Chattanooga’s new courthouse will be a muscular Art Deco Greek temple. More than an imposing expression of judicial power, this state building also symbolizes something of national significance: It’s the first major new design announced by America’s federal building agency since Trump’s executive order, “Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again.” Its beauty is therefore now a matter of both architectural and political debate.

Almost a year has passed since President Trump formalized his disdain for modernism, postmodernism and brutalism by mandating that major federal buildings be designed in “classical and traditional” styles.

One further suggested way to celebrate President Trump’s magnificent presidency and his demonstrate his achievements to the American public, as well as delivering a significant gift to the America people would be to re-develop Camp David into a truly beautiful Abbey where President Trump and future Presidents can host visiting Kings and Queens and other Presidents when they visit the United States.

Many past presidents have proposed such developments at Camp David, but no one has succeeded to follow through and deliver such a wonderful facility.

Thus, a possible development by President Trump, to be considered as a further major legacy to the US people and future presidents, is the construction of a great architectural legacy (under his “Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again”) in President Trump’s name, similar to the White House complex ballroom and the Grand Trump Arch de Trump, celebrating the 250th year of the Great American Experiment

Camp David is a 125-acre (51-hectare) country retreat for the President of the United States. It lies in the wooded hills of Catocin Mountain Park In Frederik County, Maryland near the towns of Thurmont and Emmitsburg about 62 miles north-northwest of the national capital city, Washington DC.

However, what is really needed is a grand opulent castle or abbey that can accommodate and entertain very important visitors, visiting royalty and Presidents from across the world. Also, whilst it has a tiny golf course (one green and 4 Tees), plus a driving range, what it lacks is a tremendous golf course, fit for a President and his visitors plus an opulent Helipad

Thus as part of President Trump’s legacy, he should transform Camp David into something like the grand mansion of Downton Abbey in the United Kingdom, with the plan to re-name Camp David as Trump Abbey or Trump Castle.

The aim of this further Trump legacy would be to completely rebuild a magnificent  and opulent manor house or castle to replace the current rather dreary Camp David.

Downtown Abbey is of course based upon the Highclere Castle near Newbury in Hampshire, England .

Highclere Castle  (Downton Abbey) is a Grade 1 listed grand country house (or castle) built in 1679 and largely renovated during the 1840s, with a park designed by Capability Brown in the 18th century. The 5,000-acre (2,000-hectare) estate  in Highclere about five miles (eight kilometres) south of Newbury Berkshire, in England and 9+1⁄2 miles (15 kilometres) north of Andover in Hampshire.

The 19th-century renovation is in a Jacobean and Italianate style produced by architect Charles Barry. It is the country seat of the Hereditary British Earls of Carnarvon a branch of the Anglo-Welsh Herbert family

Going back to the Trump triumphal arch, the Secretary of War said that the location of the triumphal arch overlooks a number major national sites that are frequented by federal officials and its height will create elevation advantage and line-of-sight connectivity, while its central location will improve the ability to identify and assess potential threats, Hegseth argued. 

“It will be utilized as a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense,” he said. “The elevated position can also support authorized protective-overwatch and counter-sniper personnel by improving observational, situational awareness and coordination with other security elements.” 

In addition to Hegseth, Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, also defended the need for the arch’s dual purpose, saying the location “provides opportunities for increased capability for information -sharing and logistical coordination.” 

The full-throated endorsements for the arch’s potential national security uses from two cabinet members comes as the project is facing key tests to its progress. 

Hegseth’s and Mullin’s statements were part of the government’s submissions in a lawsuit being heard in the US District Court for the District of Columbia aimed at stopping the arch’s construction.

And next Thursday, the arch will be reviewed by the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), the last of two federal agencies overseeing architectural and design changes in Washington, D.C. that must approve the project. 
If approved by NCPC, the administration has already said they will start construction as early as that same day. 

However, final plans for the arch submitted to the NCPC for its November 5th meeting that were released last week included no mention of the military component. 
The plans excluded features such as the drones and snipers that Trump described in September, and the contours of the arch in the plans did not appear to reflect a national security purpose. Instead, they describe the project as a “ceremonial gateway” to the nation’s capital. 

Hegseth’s Wednesday filing stated that the military components would not require any structural modifications or alterations. “The security features will be fully integrated into the existing design,” he wrote. 

Trump has also claimed the need for national security enhancements as the primary justification for his project to build a White House ballroom where the East Wing once stood.

NewsXForge – the Global Breaking News network  that has fast facts and forging news into real facts has quoted that” This triumphal arch sounds less like a monument and more like an entirely new chapter for the capital. A triumphal arch doubling as a security and military facility would be an extraordinary departure from the original concept. 

The proposed 161-foot observation deck would also turn it into a major tourist attraction. And the idea of transforming Camp David into a grand presidential estate would be an equally dramatic architectural undertaking. Whether these visions become reality, they would leave a very visible and long-lasting mark on Washington and the Trump presidency.

The proposed 161-foot observation deck would also turn it into a major tourist attraction. And the idea of transforming Camp David into a grand presidential estate would be an equally dramatic architectural undertaking. I now have FIRSTHAND evidence of the fact that there are many individuals in this State who have REPEATEDLY SET ASIDE ANY LAW OR POLICY THAT WOULD BENEFIT ME IN ANY WAY.
