text:
In the wake of Pope Pius XII’s 1951 allocution to the Italian Catholic Union of Midwives (Vegliare con Sollecitudine), traditional Catholic moralists closely examined the precise theological gravity of practicing periodic continence (the rhythm or Ogino-Knaus method) when a married couple lacks a serious justifying cause.
The Dominican theologians Rev. John A. McHugh, O.P., and Rev. Charles J. Callan, O.P., in Moral Theology: A Complete Course, alongside canonical commentators such as Father John A. Goodwine, J.C.D. (writing in The American Ecclesiastical Review and cited by Rev. George A. Kelly in The Catholic Marriage Manual), address this question through four interrelated considerations: the formal malice of the act, the extrinsic circumstances that produce mortal sin, the scholastic debate over intrinsic gravity, and the pastoral status of the method.
I. The Moral Species: Which Commandment Is Violated?
A fundamental insight formulated by post-allocution moralists—detailed by McHugh and Callan—is that the sin committed in practicing periodic continence without a serious reason is not a sin against the Sixth Commandment:
Integrity of the Conjugal Act: Unlike onanism, withdrawal, or artificial contraception, the individual marital acts performed during the sterile period remain physically natural and unfrustrated. As Pope Pius XII affirmed, the couple does nothing to impede or mutilate the natural consummation of the act.
A Sin of Omission Against the Common Good: Rather, the formal malice of unjustified rhythm is classified under the Seventh Commandment (or social and legal justice). By marrying, the couple freely embraced a state of life whose primary institutional purpose is the conservation and propagation of the human race. When they deliberately and systematically withhold the marital act during the fertile days solely to avoid offspring, they fail in a positive duty owed to the common good of human society.
Unity of the Sin: Because the fault consists in the general intention and policy of omitting the debt during fertile periods, McHugh and Callan point out that individual acts of intercourse during the sterile days do not constitute separate, numerically distinct sins. Rather, there is one continuous sin of omission for the entire period during which the unjustified practice is maintained.
II. When the Practice Is Certainly a Mortal Sin (Per Accidens)
Regardless of the theoretical debates concerning the practice in itself, all moral theologians—including Father Henry Davis, S.J., in Moral and Pastoral Theology, and Father John A. Goodwine, J.C.D.—agree that the use of rhythm without a sufficient reason becomes a mortal sin whenever certain extrinsic moral hazards are verified:
Sin of Injustice (Violation of the Conjugal Debt): Under Canon 1111 of the 1917 Code of Canon Law and the teaching of St. Paul (1 Cor. 7:3–5), each spouse possesses an equal, perpetual right to the conjugal debt. If one spouse unilaterally insists on practicing rhythm against the reasonable wish of the other, they commit a grave sin of injustice by depriving the partner of their lawful marital rights during fertile times.
Proximate Danger of Sins Against Chastity: As Father Goodwine emphasizes, if the prolonged abstinence required during the fertile cycle places either spouse in proximate danger of mortal sins against chastity—such as solitary sins (pollutio), mutual unchaste touches, or marital infidelity—the practice becomes gravely illicit. One cannot expose oneself or one's partner to a proximate occasion of grave sin without a grave, proportionate necessity.
Severe Marital Discord or Danger of Separation: If the tensions, fears, or disagreements arising from the method create a proximate danger of destroying family peace, inducing hatred, or leading to separation or divorce, the practice is mortally sinful.
III. The Theological Debate on Intrinsic Gravity (Per Se)
Where both spouses freely consent and neither is exposed to the danger of incontinence, but the couple simply chooses to avoid children out of ease, luxury, or minor convenience, is the sin mortal or venial?
Because Pope Pius XII confirmed that unjustified periodic continence involves moral culpability while refraining from defining its exact degree of sinfulness, traditional moralists offered nuanced solutions to determine when the "gravity of matter" is reached:
THEOLOGICAL NORMS FOR EVALUATING GRAVITY
                                      │
         ┌────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                         ▼
  THE TEMPORAL NORM                                         THE NUMERICAL NORM
Evaluates duration of the practice:                       Evaluates contribution to society:
• Short periods (months/few years) = Venial               • 4 to 5 children = Duty satisfied
• Long, unbroken practice (5–6 years) with                 • Restricting to less than 4 without
  total exclusion of offspring = Grave / Mortal             grave reason = Grave / Mortal
1. The Temporal Norm (Duration of Practice)
A prominent school of moralists evaluated the gravity by the length of time the practice is maintained without cause:
If practiced for a relatively short duration—such as several months or a couple of years—the omission represents a slight matter and constitutes only a venial sin.
If practiced continuously for a long period—commonly estimated by theologians as five or six unbroken years—with the total exclusion of children, the prolonged neglect of the procreative duty coalesces into grave matter, rendering the practice a mortal sin.
Furthermore, proponents of this norm held that if a couple has already brought one or more children into the world, subsequent indefinite use of rhythm without an excusing cause would generally not constitute a certain mortal sin.
2. The Numerical Norm (Family Size and Social Duty)
A second, widely favored school in mid-twentieth-century American moral theology (outlined by McHugh and Callan from the Conference Bulletin of the Archdiocese of New York) based the assessment upon whether the couple has rendered their fair contribution to the conservation of the race:
Under ordinary circumstances, the procreation and rearing of four or five children was regarded as sufficient to fulfill the positive marital obligation to society. Once a couple has four or five children, practicing periodic continence without an acute crisis does not constitute grave matter.
Conversely, deliberately restricting the family to less than four children through rhythm without a serious justifying cause was judged to involve grave matter (mortal sin), because it directly deprives human and Christian society of its necessary increase and subordinates the primary end of matrimony to the secondary ends purely for personal gratification.
IV. The Pastoral Judgment: Tolerated, Never Recommended
Because of the spiritual dangers and moral ambiguities inherent in the practice, the Church has never held up the rhythm method as an ideal or a positive Christian virtue.
In an official Monitum issued to his clergy, Patrick Cardinal Hayes, Archbishop of New York (cited by McHugh and Callan), summarized the true ecclesiastical attitude:
"Instead of being freely taught and commended, it is rather to be tolerated as an extreme remedy or means of preventing sin."
Pastoral theologians therefore counsel that confessors and directors should not suggest the method indiscriminately, but permit it only as a protective concession to prevent souls from abandoning the state of grace through mortal sins of onanism, contraception, or despair.

text:
An Army worker’s boyfriend claimed their home as his.
She covered 61% of their shared expenses.
Why did he call it his house?

For 30 months, she transferred $3,000 into their household account.

$90,000 total.

Their budget showed she now covered 61% of shared expenses.

Then he signed a $28,000 kitchen contract without asking her.

His reason:

“It’s my house.”

She moved out 12 days later.

He thought the kitchen ended them.

She put two old budgets beside the deed.

The deed really did have only his name.

He bought the house four years earlier, before her new job.

His down payment.
His mortgage.
His credit.

And when he earned more, their first budget showed he covered 68% of expenses.

She cooked, cleaned, scheduled repairs and handled most of the life inside the house.

They had described the trade the same way:

“The person with more money pays more.”

When her Army income passed his contracting income, she applied the same rule.

She increased her transfer. She covered groceries, utilities, insurance and most trips.

The second budget showed 61% from her.

But the other half of the old trade never reversed.

She still cooked.
Still cleaned.
Still arranged repairs.

When she asked why, he said contracting took more hours.

That sounded reasonable too.

So she tried hours instead of income.

For six weeks, they logged paid work and household work.

He averaged 52 paid hours.
She averaged 44.

After cooking, cleaning and errands, her total was 67.
His was 56.

He rejected the log.

Paid work, he said, carried different pressure.

She thought the fight was about finding the right measurement.

The kitchen showed her it wasn’t.

He had used income when his was higher.

Hours when hers became higher.

Property ownership when she paid most of their shared costs.

Each fact was real.

His work was unpredictable.
The house was legally his.
She had agreed to the transfers.

But every time one measure stopped favoring him, another measure became the one that counted.

She wasn’t losing one argument.

He was choosing the scoreboard.

From his side, he had risked the down payment, carried the mortgage and spent years building a business with uneven income.

Letting one strong salary period rewrite everything felt unfair.

From hers, every improvement in her position increased what she owed without increasing what she could decide.

The more she earned, the more she paid.

The more she paid, the more his house and business stayed protected.

But the house was still “his.”

Before moving, she offered three options:

Add her to the deed after an appraisal.

Treat her $3,000 as rent and split everything else evenly.

Or keep finances separate and divide household work by total hours.

He rejected all three.

Not because each was perfect.

Because each required one rule to keep applying when it no longer benefited him.

That was the answer the kitchen had given her.

The two budgets were accurate.

So was the deed.
So was his work log.

The problem wasn’t bad data.

It was that one person kept deciding which true fact settled each dispute.

That’s how an arrangement can look reasonable one argument at a time and still become a hierarchy.

If the scoreboard changes whenever the lead changes, it isn’t measuring fairness.

It’s protecting a winner.

text:
The Danger for India and Pakistan Has Not Gone Away https://t.co/GvFX8I2JRB 

India Under Pakistan’s Nuclear Shadow: Readiness and Defence Are the Answer

(Pakistan’s nuclear threats are designed not to prevent war but to draw America into its conflict with India. It succeeded in doing so in May 2025. India’s best response is military preparedness backed by firm diplomacy. Pakistan is likely to continue using this tactic.)

Is Pakistan genuinely threatening nuclear war in the subcontinent, or is it using nuclear brinkmanship to draw Washington into its conflicts with India?

Pakistan’s last major nuclear scare came during Operation Sindoor in May 2025, when it falsely claimed that its nuclear storage facility at Sargodha had been attacked. President Donald Trump quickly intervened, presenting himself as the man who had prevented a nuclear war. He was then pursuing the Nobel Peace Prize, and Pakistan’s narrative conveniently served his ambitions.

The intervention achieved two objectives for Pakistan. First, it brought Washington back into Islamabad’s embrace after nearly a decade of strained relations following the Osama bin Laden episode. Second, it reinforced Pakistan’s familiar strategy: provoke a confrontation, then cry nuclear danger when India retaliates. Trump welcomed the enthusiastic support of General Munir and Prime Minister Sharif. Later, Pakistan offered support for Trump’s Iran campaign, further cementing its return to the American fold.

What, then, is Pakistan’s nuclear shadow over India?

Pakistan is estimated to possess around 160 nuclear warheads. Its strategy has increasingly focused on developing small battlefield nuclear weapons designed to stop an Indian military advance into Pakistani territory. 

Islamabad presents these weapons as defensive, even suggesting that they could be used on its own soil. But calling a nuclear weapon defensive does not make its use any less catastrophic. Nuclear first use would invite devastating retaliation.

The reliability of Pakistan’s miniaturised battlefield weapons remains a concern. Their technology has not been independently demonstrated through nuclear testing since 1998, although reports have pointed to Chinese assistance.
Operation Sindoor exposed serious weaknesses in Pakistan’s military preparedness. Indian missiles struck military airfields and command-and-control infrastructure, catching Pakistani defences off guard. Pakistan subsequently established the Army Rocket Force Command (ARFC) on August 13, 2025, separating its conventional rocket capabilities from the Army Strategic Forces Command, which oversees strategic missile and nuclear assets. The restructuring reflects lessons learned from that confrontation.

India, meanwhile, must remain prepared on two fronts. First, its multilayered air and missile defence systems must intercept incoming threats wherever possible. Second, its nuclear deterrent must remain credible enough to ensure that any Pakistani nuclear first strike would invite overwhelming retaliation.

India’s declared nuclear doctrine remains one of credible minimum deterrence and no first use, with massive retaliation in response to a nuclear attack.

Washington may once again lean towards Pakistan, but it understands the dangers of Islamabad’s reckless brinkmanship. Kashmir, water disputes and other regional tensions could trigger another confrontation. India must not be intimidated by nuclear threats. Constant readiness, stronger defences and an unmistakable retaliatory capability are the best answers to Pakistan’s nuclear shadow.

text:
In December 2011, a woman drove her best friend home from chemotherapy. Four days earlier, that friend had quietly made her the only beneficiary of a $150,000 life insurance policy. That night the friend was stabbed 55 times, and the police arrested the wrong person:

Her name was Betsy Faria, a mother with terminal cancer in Troy, Missouri. Pam Hupp was the last person to see her alive. Betsy's husband Russ came home from his weekly game night and found her body. Police charged him. Pam took the stand as the star witness, nobody else had known about the insurance change, and in 2013 Russ was sentenced to life. Two years later, at a retrial where his lawyer was finally allowed to point at Pam, he was acquitted.

In August 2016 Pam called 911 from her own home in O'Fallon. A man had broken in, she said, and she had shot him. He was Louis Gumpenberger, 33, who had a brain injury from a car crash years earlier. In his pocket police found $900 and a note telling him to kidnap Pam, get "Russ's money" from her bank and kill her. Prosecutors say she wrote it herself. Six days before, a woman had reported a stranger who claimed to be a producer for a true-crime TV show and offered her $1,000 to act out a 911 call. She said no, and her security camera caught the SUV's plate. It was Pam's.

In the video below, her arrest that day, then the police interview room. She's read her rights and asks for her lawyer, and the officers step out. At 0:29 she starts touching both sides of her neck. At 0:41 she reaches for the water bottle and takes the pen behind it, then slides it behind her back and into her jeans. An officer comes back to walk her to the bathroom. At 1:06, off camera: "We need a medic! Pam! Pam! Pam!"

In the bathroom she had stabbed herself in both sides of her neck and both wrists. She survived. In 2019 she took a plea that let her avoid the death penalty without admitting guilt, and she got life without parole for killing Louis. In 2021 she was finally charged with Betsy's murder. She says she didn't do it, and the trial has now been pushed to 2028. Russ got a $2.05 million settlement.

She sent an innocent husband to prison and kept the money. Who failed Betsy more: the friend she trusted, or the investigators who never looked at her?

🇺🇸 A SERIOUS MESSAGE ABOUT THE FUTURE OF OUR COUNTRY

Before you enter the voting booth, I encourage you to consider something far more important than your frustration with the current administration: the long-term direction of our nation.

I understand the frustration. Americans are facing rising costs, economic uncertainty, concerns about national security, and difficult questions about our country’s future. These are legitimate concerns, and no administration should be immune from criticism or accountability.

But elections demand more than frustration. They demand discernment, careful consideration, and an honest examination of the alternatives.

For me, this election is about fundamental principles:

Protecting constitutional freedoms, including freedom of speech and religious liberty.
Defending the Second Amendment and the rights of law-abiding citizens.
Securing our borders while maintaining a lawful and accountable immigration system.
Protecting parental rights and ensuring transparency in decisions affecting children.
Preserving election integrity, judicial independence, and the constitutional balance of power.
Supporting public safety and holding violent offenders accountable.
Promoting economic policies that strengthen American families and preserve opportunity for future generations.

I have serious disagreements with the Democratic Party’s direction on several of these issues. Those disagreements are rooted in my convictions about limited government, individual responsibility, constitutional protections, and the preservation of American institutions.

That does not mean Republican leaders are beyond criticism. They are not. Our president is not perfect, and neither is this administration. Every elected official should be held accountable for decisions, policies, and results.

But accountability and political disagreement should not prevent us from examining the larger consequences of the choices before us.

We must ask difficult questions. Which policies best protect our liberties? Which leaders demonstrate respect for constitutional limits? Which approach offers the strongest prospects for economic stability, national security, and the future we want to leave our children?

These questions deserve thoughtful answers, not simply emotional reactions.

I believe deeply in the principles upon which this country was founded. I believe freedom carries responsibilities, that constitutional rights must be protected regardless of which party holds power, and that the future of this nation deserves our serious attention.

You may disagree with my conclusions, and that is your right. In fact, that freedom to disagree is precisely what makes our constitutional republic worth defending.

My position is clear. My convictions are firm. And my concerns about the direction of our country are sincere.

Whatever your political affiliation, I urge you to examine the policies, question the rhetoric, demand evidence, and understand the consequences of your vote.

Our country deserves informed voters, accountable leadership, and an unwavering commitment to the Constitution.

Vote RED 🔴…straight down the ballot‼️💯🇺🇸🦅🙌🏾

🇺🇸 Faith. Freedom. Responsibility. America. 🇺🇸

text:
PRETTY WOMAN!💅🏻

Richard Gere nearly passed on Pretty Woman. Julia Roberts helped change his mind with a Post-it note—and three words.

“Please say yes.”

Before they became one of Hollywood’s most memorable screen couples, Gere wasn’t convinced the businessman role had much to offer.

Director Garry Marshall arranged for him to meet Roberts, then left the two alone to get acquainted.

When Marshall called to check on them, Julia wrote her request on a Post-it and slid it across the desk.

Gere said yes.

He recalled that moment during the cast’s 25th-anniversary reunion on TODAY in 2015. By then, millions of people couldn’t imagine the movie with anyone else.

But Pretty Woman almost looked very different.

The project began as a darker screenplay called “3,000.” Roberts described an early ending in which Vivian was thrown out of the car, with money tossed after her. No roses. No rescue on the fire escape. No happily ever after.

Through rewrites and Marshall’s direction, it became the romantic fairy tale audiences remember.

And one of its most beloved moments was a real surprise.

When Gere snapped the necklace box shut as Roberts reached toward it, her startled laugh was genuine. They kept it in the movie.

Pretty Woman opened on March 23, 1990, and became a worldwide blockbuster. Roberts earned a Best Actress Oscar nomination and won a Golden Globe.

text:
Chafa (Champaka / Michelia champaca)

“Chafa” is the common Marathi/regional name for the highly fragrant Champaka flower (the golden-yellow variety is especially prized). It is also widely planted in temple courtyards across India.

🌺Strongly associated with Lord Krishna and Kamadeva (the god of love). It is also offered to Vishnu and Lakshmi, and in many places to Shiva.
🌺The flower has a rich, sweet, almost intoxicating fragrance that is considered especially pleasing to the divine. In traditional understanding, the fragrance and colour of flowers attract specific divine energies (pavitrak or subtle principles).
🌺Champaka is mentioned in scriptures and classical literature (including associations with beauty, devotion, and divine presence). The golden colour is linked to auspiciousness and spiritual radiance.
🌺The tree itself is regarded as sacred; planting and caring for it is considered meritorious. Its presence in temple premises creates a pure, fragrant atmosphere ideal for worship.
In some regional traditions (especially related to Plumeria, which is also called Champa), the five petals are linked to the Pancha Bhuta (five elements), adding another layer of symbolism.

After the inauguration of the Simhastha Kumbh Mela at the Shubha Muhurta at Kushavarta Tirtha, the Hon’ble Chief Minister of Maharashtra, Sri Devendra Fadnavis, and his wife, Smt. With the divine blessings of Jagadguru Shankaracharya Sri Sri Bharati Tirtha Mahasannidhanam, Jagadguru Shankaracharya Sri Sri Vidhushekhara Bharati Sannidhanam of Dakshinamnaya Sri Sharada Peetham, Sringeri, performed the historic Dhvajarohanam and the first Punya Snan on behalf of all followers of Sanatana Dharma.

Earlier, the Maharashtra Chief Minister, Sri Devendra Fadnavis, had Darshan of the Sringeri Jagadguru and sought blessings before commencing the Ganapati Puja. He was blessed by the Jagadguru with a Rudraksha Mala. He then took the Sankalpa for Dhvajarohanam on behalf of the people of the sacred land of Maharashtra and all Astikas. Kushavarta Tirtha is the sacred place in Trimbakeshwar Kshetra from where the holy river Godavari originates. Before the Dhvajarohanam, an elaborate Puja was performed to the Dhvajastambha and Dhvaja by the Jagadguru, and the Chief Minister also performed Pushparchana to the Dhvajastambha and Dhvaja.

After the inauguration of the Simhastha Kumbh Mela at the Shubha Muhurta at Kushavarta Tirtha, the Hon’ble Chief Minister of Maharashtra, Sri Devendra Fadnavis, and his wife, Smt. Amruta Fadnavis, offered their reverential salutations to the Jagadguru and were blessed by the Jagadguru with a beautiful idol of Sri Sharadamba and a replica of the Vidyashankara Temple.

Thousands of Sants, Mahants, Acharyas and dignitaries were present on the occasion.

text: “[On the one hand,] Hinduism includes more deities than any other world religion. On the other hand—and now here comes the simplicity—it turns out that in the final analysis all these multitudinous beings are really the projections or expressions of an ultimate One, namely, Brahman—so that in fact, you see, there is but a single Divinity. There’s a passage in one of the Upanishads (another very important set of Hindu scriptures) that makes this point very nicely. A spiritual seeker named Vidagdha Shakalya asked his teacher, Yajnavalkya, “How many gods are there, O Yajnavalkya?” The teacher replied, “As many as are mentioned in the hymn to the Vishvedevas, namely, 333,000,000.” “Yes,” Vidagdha Shakalya said, “But how many gods are there really, O Yajnavalkya?” “33”, the teacher replied. “But how many gods are there really, O Yajnavalkya?” “6”. “But how many gods are there really, O Yajnavalkya?” “3”. “But how many gods are there really, O Yajnavalkya?” “2”. “But how many gods are there really, O Yajnavalkya?” “1 and 1/2” [!]. “But how many gods are there really, O Yajnavalkya?” “1”, the teacher said finally. Then Vidagdha Shakalya asked, “Who, then, are these 333,000,000?” Yajnavalkya replied, “These are only the various powers” (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, III. 9. 1). A similar point is made in one of the prayers that’s recited by a Hindu priest at the beginning of certain temple ceremonies: “O Lord, forgive me three sins: Thou art everywhere, but I worship you here; Thou needest no praise, but I offer you these prayers and salutations; Thou art without form, but I worship you in these forms.” - James Cutsinger

text:
Hundreds of Ballots Left Exposed at Skid Row Homeless Center Ahead of LA Election | New York Post

Hundreds of ballots were found piled in an open hallway at a Skid Row homeless shelter where more than 1,100 voters are registered, a California Post investigation found.

The ballots were spotted at The Midnight Mission, a downtown LA homeless shelter offering meals and mail services, where 1,160 voters are registered.

The Post authenticated a photo of the ballots and independently confirmed the scene during a visit to the shelter on October 13.

The discovery comes four months after the California Post exposed 7,600 voter registrations linked to homeless shelters and service providers across Los Angeles, including facilities that don’t offer a single bed.

The Midnight Mission told The Post election ballots are supposed to be kept under lock and key until they reach their intended recipients.

“Our standard procedure is to secure election ballots behind locked doors until they are distributed to their intended recipients,” Georgia Hawley, the organization’s chief communications officer, told The Post.

“I personally confirmed that ballots were being stored securely when I visited our mail center.”

The organization, located at 601 South San Pedro Street, handles large volumes of mail for homeless residents. Hawley explained that limited mailroom space requires deliveries to be received, sorted and distributed throughout the day.

The Post also contacted U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli to determine whether federal authorities were investigating election ballots on Skid Row.

Essayli confirmed an investigation but declined to discuss The Midnight Mission specifically.

Republican congressional candidate Scott Meyers, an attorney running in California’s 30th Congressional District, blasted the handling of election mail, pointing to both the postal system and organizations responsible for receiving and distributing ballots.

“We’re treating ballots like junk mail,” Meyers said.

Meyers also told The Post the problem extends far beyond homeless shelters, pointing to photographs of ballots left unattended in apartment building lobbies and put the blame on the U.S. Postal Service for failing to keep ballots safe.

“These are pieces of gold. This is our democracy,” he said.

Nico Ruderman, a Venice Neighborhood Council member and former candidate for public office who has repeatedly visited the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office to observe election procedures, called the discovery disappointing but unsurprising.

“Even if there is no fraud, there is a perception,” Ruderman told The Post.

“If people don’t trust their elections, they’re not going to vote,” he said.

Ruderman is calling for a ballot initiative to overhaul California’s election laws, telling The Post that public confidence matters even when wrongdoing has not been established.

“We need massive election reform, even if there is nothing nefarious going on,” he said. “Election reform eliminates doubts.”

The latest discovery follows The Post’s June investigation into thousands of voter registrations tied to homeless shelters and service providers across Los Angeles, including drop-in centers that offer services but no overnight accommodations.

At St. Joseph Center in Venice, The Post identified 185 registered voters tied to a drop-in facility with no beds.

Local resident Susan Collins also accused political activists of exploiting homeless voters through California’s ballot collection laws.

“For over a decade I’ve been saying, ballot harvesting has been abused, in particular by the DSA,” Collins alleged, referring to the Democratic Socialists of America.

California law allows voters to authorize another person to return their completed mail ballots, provided state election rules are followed.

Election law attorney Garrett Fahy previously told The Post that allowing homeless residents to register using shelters and other nontraditional addresses reflects California’s efforts to protect voting access.

“The system is not set up to prevent people from voting. It’s to ensure anyone who can register votes,” Fahy said.

text:
America Needs Leaders, Not a Never-Ending Political War!

Washington has a serious problem, and it has very little to do with whether someone likes or dislikes Donald Trump. The problem is that too much of America's political energy is consumed by partisan warfare while ordinary Americans are waiting for their elected representatives to address the issues affecting their everyday lives.
For many Americans, it appears that defeating, discrediting, investigating, and politically weakening President Trump has become a defining priority for Democratic leadership.
But here's a question every American should be asking: When does the business of governing become more important than the business of fighting Donald Trump?
Americans did not elect members of Congress simply to spend their days attacking the president, holding political press conferences, issuing angry statements, and looking for the next opportunity to score political points. They elected them to represent their constituents and work toward solutions.
People are struggling with the cost of groceries, housing, insurance, healthcare, energy, and everyday necessities. Families are worried about their financial futures. Small businesses are fighting to survive. Young Americans are wondering whether they will ever be able to afford a home.
These are real problems. They deserve real attention.
Yet the Democratic Party's announced plans for a possible return to congressional power in November 2026 include extensive investigations of Trump, his family, and administration officials. Democratic leaders have also outlined proposals addressing affordability, healthcare, housing, and other issues. Both priorities are part of their stated agenda.
Congressional oversight is legitimate. No president should be above accountability. But oversight should be driven by evidence and the public interest, not an endless political appetite for confrontation.
America cannot afford another two years of Washington putting political grudges ahead of governing.
What happened to the idea of Democrats and Republicans sitting across the aisle, finding common ground, negotiating solutions, and actually accomplishing something?
Is every disagreement going to become another investigation? Is every presidential decision going to become another political crisis? Must the country remain divided simply because one party cannot accept the political reality that Donald Trump is president? The American people deserve better from both parties.
If Democrats believe Trump's policies are hurting Americans, then make the case. Offer better legislation. Present workable alternatives. Debate the issues. Show the country what they would do differently.
But don't confuse opposing a president with serving the American people.
There is a difference between holding a president accountable and making opposition to that president the centerpiece of a political identity. Washington needs fewer political spectacles and more meaningful accomplishments.
The presidency is not a personal popularity contest, and Congress is not supposed to be a permanent opposition headquarters.
Democrats, Republicans, and every elected official in Washington should remember one fundamental responsibility: They work for the American people, not for their political parties.
Americans aren't asking for another political war. They're asking for leadership, solutions, economic opportunity, security, and a government that remembers who pays the bills. And perhaps the most important question of all is this:
If taking down Donald Trump becomes more important than improving the lives of ordinary Americans, who exactly is looking out for the American people?
The American people deserve a government that works for them not one consumed by the next political battle.

What’s the solution? 

Kentucky needs to stop rewarding universities simply for producing more research and start asking whether taxpayers are getting anything worthwhile in return.

Consider some of the research and academic work associated with UK. Disney princesses and gender stereotypes. Taylor Swift’s Southern accent. Adult male fans of My Little Pony. Barbie’s media empire. Star Wars and Harry Potter election memes.

UK received nearly $500 million in external research awards in FY2025, including $255 million from federal sources. Yet Kentucky’s performance funding formula continues to provide preferential weights for research universities over comprehensive universities. CPE’s own modeling showed how applying sector weights could shift $3.63 million from comprehensive universities to UK and UofL.

How much more should taxpayers be expected to provide without a clear accounting of what research funding already covers, what universities actually produce, and whether those activities warrant additional state support?

Kentucky should eliminate preferential research-university weights and adopt the Goldwater Institute’s American Higher Education Restoration Act, which offers a way to change how universities spend taxpayer-supported faculty time on research.

Under the proposal, new faculty contracts in non-STEM fields would generally require professors to teach at least three courses per semester. Professors could still conduct and publish research, but reducing their teaching responsibilities to pursue research at taxpayer expense would require additional justification.

Faculty could qualify for reduced teaching loads when external grants compensate the university for their time. Otherwise, they could apply for a renewable, two-year research allowance reviewed by a committee that includes faculty members, university leadership, and taxpayer representatives. Previous research accomplishments would be considered when seeking additional allowances.

Universities would also have to publicly report what their departments are researching, the status of that work, and how faculty divide their time between teaching and research. The proposal gives preference to publicly accessible scholarship and creates a mechanism for taxpayers or the attorney general to challenge violations.

In other words, professors could still study Disney princesses, Taylor Swift, or whatever else interests them. Academic freedom would remain protected. However, receiving taxpayer-supported time away from the classroom to conduct that research would no longer be automatic.

The Act addresses research accountability at the university level. Eliminating Kentucky’s preferential research weights would address the separate problem of how state performance funding is distributed.

A degree earned at @murraystateuniv or @nkuedu should count just as much as one earned at UK. Kentucky’s funding formula should reward universities for educating students and producing measurable outcomes, not provide additional advantages based on institutional classifications and research activity.

text:
The ancient origins of Halloween.

The origins of Halloween can be traced back more than 2,000 years to the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, which marked the end of the harvest season and the start of winter.

The Celts believed that around this time, the boundary between the world of the living and the dead became thinner, allowing spirits to cross into the human world.

Bonfires were an important part of the celebrations. Communities gathered around large fires, which were believed to offer protection against harmful spirits. One historic site associated with these traditions is the Hill of Ward in Ireland, where ancient ceremonial fires are believed to have been held.

Over time, Halloween became influenced by Christian traditions. November 1 became All Saints’ Day, honouring saints, while November 2 became All Souls’ Day, a day to remember the dead.

The evening before All Saints’ Day was known as All Hallows’ Eve, a name that eventually shortened to Halloween.

As the centuries passed, the celebration continued to evolve. Irish immigrants later helped bring Halloween traditions to North America, where they developed into familiar traditions such as costumes, trick-or-treating, carved pumpkins and spooky decorations.

text:
Grok Bot just built me a digital business card people can scan straight from my phone.

It uses Grok Bot Pages to create your card with your photo, name and contact details. 

It also generates a scannable QR code you can save on your phone to use whenever someone asks for your details.

Here’s the full prompt to create yours, complete with a public link and QR code. 

“Build me a digital business card as a Grok Bot Page, plus a QR code that opens it. Work step by step and check each step before moving on.

1 - Ask me for my details

Ask in one short message, all at once: full name, title, phone number, email, website, a photo of me and colour preference.

For the photo, ask for the original, high-resolution file, at least 1,500 pixels tall, ideally with a transparent background (a cut-out PNG). Chat apps often shrink photos, so ask for the original.

Default colours: dark navy with a blue accent.

Wait for my answers. Don’t invent anything. If something is missing, leave it off rather than using a placeholder.

2 - Prepare the photo

Check its resolution with a script. If it’s under about 1,000 pixels tall, tell me it may look blurry and ask for a bigger file before continuing.

If the background isn’t transparent, remove it or ask me for a cut-out.

Crop from just above the head to about the waist. Resize it to about twice the size it will display at, roughly 800 pixels tall, and save it as a WebP with transparency at quality 80, aiming for under 60,000 characters once base64-encoded.

Encode it to base64 with a script, never by hand. Record its length and MD5 checksum.

3 - Build the Page

Read the canvas skill first.

Make it look like a real physical business card: landscape, 85:55 ratio, rounded corners, soft shadow, centred on the page.

Size: maxWidth "min(900px, max(70vw, 600px), calc(80vh * 85 / 55))", width 100%, so it’s big on desktop and shrinks on a phone.

Left side: name in large bold white, title in a light accent colour, a short accent line, then phone, email and website, each with a Lucide icon (phone, mail, globe) in the accent colour. Phone uses tel:, email uses mailto:, website opens in a new tab.

Right side: the photo, standing on the card’s bottom edge and running off the right edge, with a faint glow behind it.

Background: a dark gradient in my colours. All text scales with the card’s width.

Keep every detail (name, title, phone, email, website, colours) in one list at the top of the code, so each is easy to edit later.

Embed the photo as a data URL inside the Page.

After saving, read the Page back and confirm the embedded photo matches the file’s length and MD5 exactly. If it doesn’t, fix it and check again.

4 - Publish

Give me the Page link, and tell me to turn on public link sharing from the Page’s share menu. Ask me to paste back the public link.

Remind me that anyone with the link can see it, so only include details I’m happy to share publicly.

5 - Create the QR code

Once I’ve sent the public link, use a Python script (qrcode or segno, plus Pillow) to make a 1,200 by 1,200 pixel QR code for it: error correction H, a white margin, dark modules in the card’s main colour.

Put the Grok Bot icon in the centre on a white rounded square, covering no more than 20% of the code’s width.

Also make a phone lock-screen version (1179 by 2556 pixels): card-colour background, the QR code centred on a white rounded panel, with ‘Scan for my card’ in bold white underneath.

Decode both images with a QR reader (zxing-cpp or pyzbar) and confirm they match the link character for character. Only then send them to me.

6 - Hand over

Send me the card link and both QR images.

Remind me to save the QR image to my phone’s favourites, or set the lock-screen version as my wallpaper, so people can scan my phone at events.

Then offer to change anything: colours, layout or details.”

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

Blue jeans were not invented by Levi Strauss alone, they were actually co-invented by a tailor named Jacob Davis. He came up with the idea of hammering small copper rivets into stress points like pocket corners to stop gold miners' work pants from tearing, but was too poor to pay the $68 patent fee ($1,700 today), forcing him to partner with his fabric supplier, Levi Strauss, to file the patent jointly in 1873.

In 1870, Jacob Davis, a Nevada tailor, received a complaint from a local woodcutter whose pockets repeatedly tore open when stuffed with heavy tools. Davis noticed small copper rivets sitting on a workbench, typically used on harness leather, and decided to hammer them into the seams and pocket corners of the denim trousers.

The reinforced pants were an instant hit among local laborers, but Davis feared rival tailors would steal his idea before he could patent it.

​Lacking the $68 needed to submit a patent application to the US Patent and Trademark Office, Davis wrote a letter to Levi Strauss, his San Francisco cloth supplier. He offered Strauss half-ownership of the idea if Strauss would fund the patent application fees.

On May 20, 1873, US Patent No. 139,121 was granted for "Improvement in Fastening Pocket-Openings," officially giving birth to modern riveted blue jeans. Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

The Historical Evolution of Blue Jeans:

​How heavy-duty frontier workwear transformed into a global fashion staple:

1. The Copper Rivet Patent
1873
Jacob Davis and Levi Strauss receive Patent No. 139,121, creating copper-riveted "waist overalls" made from sturdy cotton duck and blue denim.

2. Creation of the 501 Model Number
1890
The company's patent expires, opening denim production to competitors; Levi's assigns the lot number "501" to its iconic button-fly straight-leg riveted pant.

3. Western Movies & Hollywood Rebellion
1930s–1950s
Hollywood westerns glorify cowboy denim, and stars like James Dean (Rebel Without a Cause) transform jeans from blue-collar workwear into a symbol of teenage rebellion.

4. Designer Denim & Global Fashion
Modern Era
Jeans transition into high fashion and everyday global apparel, evolving with stretch elastane fibers, stone-washing treatments, and eco-friendly water-recycling wash methods.

More Surprising Facts About Jeans:

A. ​Why Indigo Blue? Indigo dye was chosen for work pants because unlike most natural dyes, indigo pigment binds only to the outer surface of cotton threads. When washed, the dye chips away gradually instead of bleeding out all at once, making denim look better as it ages while hiding dirt and grease stains.

B. ​The Tiny "Watch Pocket": The tiny fifth pocket inside the main front pocket was originally designed in the 19th century specifically for cowboys and laborers to tuck away and protect their mechanical pocket watches.

C. Removal of the Crotch Rivet: Levi's jeans originally featured a copper rivet at the bottom of the fly. It was permanently removed in 1941 after company president Walter Haas sat too close to a campfire and discovered that copper quickly conducts heat to sensitive areas.

​SUMMARILY! 
​Blue jeans were born when tailor Jacob Davis couldn't afford a $68 patent fee for his copper-riveted pocket design, prompting him to partner with dry-goods supplier Levi Strauss to coin one of the most famous garments in history.

Hopefully you've learnt something new today?

text:
Brooke Shields was 15 in the Calvin Klein jeans ads that TV stations banned in 1980. She's said for years that if her lines had a double meaning, nobody explained it to her.

This February, Calvin Klein, now 83, told a Vogue podcast, "We knew exactly what we were doing with Brooke."

He walked through how it got made. Richard Avedon directed and Doon Arbus wrote the scripts, and Klein says the three of them sat down and mapped out every detail, from the voice to the look to the clothes. So you had three adults at the very top of their fields working the innuendo out line by line, and then handing it to a high school kid to say on camera.

The only person in the room who didn't know what the ad meant was the one saying it.

And the ban helped.

CBS and ABC stations pulled the spots in November 1980, and within a year Calvin Klein was selling roughly 400,000 pairs of jeans a week.

Klein's company went back to that well twice more. In 1995 a jeans campaign with models critics took for minors set off an FBI child exploitation probe (the models turned out to be adults), Klein pulled the ads, and the jeans sold anyway. In 1999 a kids' underwear billboard meant for Times Square got cancelled the day after the newspaper ads ran. That's three campaigns in 19 years, every one of them banned or pulled, and the brand walked out of each one more famous.

So when somebody says "age controversy aside," they're asking you to set down the one part Klein says was planned.

text:
A Simple Diet Change Could Transform Kidney Disease Treatment, 10-Year Study Finds | American Society of Nephrology, SciTechDaily

For kidney patients with acid buildup, a decade-long trial suggests fruits and vegetables may offer what a standard treatment did not: fewer hospital visits without higher overall costs.

When kidneys lose their ability to function properly, the consequences can extend far beyond waste buildup. People with chronic kidney disease can also develop excess acid in their blood, a condition known as metabolic acidosis that can contribute to worsening kidney function and other serious complications. Doctors commonly treat this imbalance with sodium bicarbonate, but new research suggests that a surprisingly simple dietary approach could offer greater long-term benefits.

In a decade-long clinical trial, researchers found that patients who received fruits and vegetables to help neutralize excess acid experienced substantially fewer hospitalizations and emergency department visits than those receiving usual care. O

ver 10 years, the 36 patients in the dietary group had just 14 hospitalizations and 20 emergency visits, compared with 64 and 88, respectively, among the 36 patients receiving usual care. Only four patients in the dietary group required dialysis, compared with 16 in the usual-care group, raising intriguing questions about the role of nutrition in protecting kidney health.

Two acid treatments, different long-term results

The trial enrolled 108 adults with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD) and metabolic acidosis, the medical term for excess acid buildup in the body. Researchers randomly assigned participants to three groups of 36, receiving fruits and vegetables, oral sodium bicarbonate, or usual care. The dietary approach used base-producing fruits and vegetables, which help counter acidity. Both the dietary treatment and sodium bicarbonate were intended to reduce dietary acid by half, allowing researchers to compare two approaches with the same acid-reduction goal.

Participants were followed annually for 10 years. Across all three groups, researchers recorded 115 hospitalizations and 166 emergency department visits, and 34 patients needed dialysis. Despite sharing the dietary treatment’s acid-reduction goal, sodium bicarbonate showed no difference from usual care in hospitalizations, emergency department visits, or progression to dialysis.

Kidney benefits without higher overall costs

“Treatment of metabolic acidosis with fruits and vegetables was associated with more favorable long-term clinical outcomes and health care utilization than standard treatment with sodium bicarbonate or usual care, without increasing overall health-system or societal costs,” said corresponding author Nimrit Goraya, MD, of Baylor Scott and White Health.

The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, October 22–25. The trial’s comparison of individual treatments also raises the question of how dietary interventions might affect care and spending across a larger population.

“These findings support evaluating dietary interventions in chronic kidney disease not only at the individual-patient level but also at the population level, where the cumulative clinical and economic benefits may be substantial. They also highlight the potential quality-of-life and health-system value of investing in fruits and vegetables as a treatment strategy, particularly when favorable clinical outcomes can be achieved without increasing overall costs.”

text: 38/100 In 2000 Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting table in a California grocery store. Sometimes it offered 24 kinds of jam, sometimes six. The big display attracted more shoppers, yet only about 3 percent of them bought a jar. With six options, about 30 percent bought one. The "jam study" became the poster child for choice overload, cited in countless talks and books. Then the replications arrived. A 2010 meta-analysis by Benjamin Scheibehenne, Rainer Greifeneder and Peter Todd pooled 50 experiments and found an average effect close to zero. Choice overload appeared in some conditions and vanished or reversed in others. A 2015 meta-analysis by Alexander Chernev and colleagues found it showed up mainly when choices were complex, preferences were unclear or decisions were difficult. That last condition is the useful one. When you know what you want, a large menu is a pleasure. When you don't, every extra option becomes a small burden, because you have to borrow criteria from somewhere. Endless career paths, apartments and lifestyles feel paralysing mostly when your native goals are blurry. Clarity about your own priorities works like a short menu. Many choices become easy once you know what you're hungry for.

text:
October 2026 AI & Tech: The Complete Month

October was one of the densest months the industry has seen. Frontier models landed every few days, a major IPO filing revealed compute commitments in the hundreds of billions, open-weight models finally started competing on real work, infrastructure deals locked in capacity for years, and agent tooling, chips, robotics, and safety systems all moved at once. This is the full chronological rundown of what actually happened, from the first week through the end of the month, with the numbers, access details, and context that matter.

Early October (1–10)

🟢 OpenAI opened the month with Dots, their always-on agent system. These are persistent agents powered by GPT-6 Astra that run with a full cloud computer and browser access to more than 4,000 apps. You steer them from Slack, Teams, or your phone instead of the normal chat interface. Pro tier only. It is the clearest move yet toward agents that keep working in the background rather than waiting for you to open a window and type a prompt. The product is still early, but the direction is obvious: move from single-session chat to continuous operation.

Alongside it they pushed GPT-6.1 Sol. This one sits close to Astra on intelligence while costing significantly less: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, with cached input down to $0.10. It outperforms Astra on several agentic coding benchmarks including DeepSWE and quickly became the default model inside Codex for a large number of users. The pricing was part of a clear pattern all month—OpenAI kept cutting costs as open Chinese models applied pressure. Sol is the model a lot of teams switched to for everyday agent work because the performance-to-price ratio improved enough to matter at scale.

🟠 Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 around the same window. It is roughly 30% faster and cheaper than the previous Sonnet, priced at $2/$10. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it scored 70.6%, which was higher than Opus 5.5’s 66.4% in some configurations. A free tier is available. For most day-to-day coding and agent work this is now the model people actually reach for. They also dropped Claude Haiku 5.5 early in the month at $0.10/$0.50. It hits 72.4% on OSWorld and remains usable on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 39.2%. This is the high-volume, low-cost option for agent loops and tool use where latency and price matter more than peak capability. Haiku 5.5 made a lot of previously expensive agent patterns economically viable.

🔵 Google’s Gemini 4 Argon started with restricted access for cyber defenders and trusted testers, then moved to general availability later in the month. At launch it topped both the Text Arena and the Vals Index. Pricing settled at $2/$10 on a promo rate that runs until around the end of November, with a 1.05 million token context window. It is a strong general model and the direct foundation that Gemini 4 Carbon was built on a couple of weeks later. The limited early access was deliberate; Google was still finishing safety and capability work before opening it more widely.

🟣 Mistral previewed Large 4 around the 6th to the 8th. Roughly one trillion total parameters, about 50 billion active, 1 million context, multimodal. Early numbers showed strong coding efficiency (around $1.13 per task in some reports). They explicitly said open weights were coming by the end of the month, which set up the improved “Le Chonk” release later. The preview already looked competitive enough that people started testing it against closed models on coding tasks.

Other early releases filled in the edges. Liquid AI shipped d1-3B and d1-omni-600M, tiny on-device decision models that run in 8 ms on a GPU and around 50 ms on a Jetson. These are aimed at local agents that need to make fast choices without round-tripping to the cloud. Aleph Alpha released Kolibri-1, a 78B/3.46B active German-English mixture-of-experts model with a 1 million context window under Apache 2.0. CoreWeave rolled out serverless GPUs billed per hour with no long-term contract, plus their Forge platform that combines run, observe, curate, evaluate, and Weights & Biases, and Agent Lens for agent observability. NVIDIA had Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPU capacity available. Black Forest Labs updated FLUX 3 for 4K image generation with multi-reference and bounding-box layouts. Embeddings arrived from Google (EmbeddingGemma 2) and Perplexity (pplx-embed-v2). ElevenLabs pushed v4 speech models with better expression control across 90 languages. OpenAI also made their Decisions API available in public beta for fixed-choice answers and offered UltraFast mode on Cerebras (up to roughly 300 tokens per second for Astra on the Pro tier). The infrastructure layer was expanding as fast as the models.

Mid-October (11–20)

🔵 Gemini 4 Argon went fully generally available around the 13th to the 15th across the Gemini API, AI Studio, the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra users, and Antigravity. The promo pricing held. It was clearly one of the stronger general models on public arenas at that point and served as the base for everything Google did later in the month. Teams that had been waiting for broader access started switching workloads over.

🔷 Meta dropped Muse Spark Open. 816 billion total parameters, 42 billion active, 1 million context window, multimodal input and text output. Meta described it as the most capable US open-weight model to date. The weights are open but carry a revenue-cap license restriction. It is not closed-frontier level, but it is a genuine step up for open models on coding and agent work. For companies that want to self-host or fine-tune without relying on a single API provider, this was one of the more usable open options of the month.

🟢 NVIDIA released the Nemotron 3.5 series. Super VL is a 120 billion total / 12 billion active vision-language model aimed at agents with high throughput. Transcribe is an open speech model in the roughly 30–34 billion mixture-of-experts class. It handles 40 languages, speaker attribution, translation to and from English, and posts a low word error rate around 2.8%. It effectively consolidates what used to be several separate speech tools into one model. NVIDIA also continued pushing Vera Rubin NVL72 capacity and published agent throughput numbers that showed large efficiency gains per megawatt versus previous generations.

🟢 OpenAI models began appearing on Google Cloud. Around the 21st, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Luna entered private preview on Model Garden for select enterprise customers, available through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Microsoft remains OpenAI’s primary cloud partner, but the multi-cloud distribution is clearly underway. Codex CLI and Desktop workflows can connect for inference. For enterprises already standardized on Google Cloud, this removed a friction point.

🟡 DeepSeek continued shipping efficient open-weight variants, including DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Artificial Analysis ran agent throughput numbers on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 and it delivered up to 5.7 times the total throughput per megawatt of a GB300 NVL72 on DeepSeek V4 Pro, with strong gains on Flash, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K3 as well. At peak throughput the lead narrows but remains positive. These numbers matter because inference cost and power are becoming the binding constraints for a lot of agent deployments.

🟡 Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro around the 23rd. 2.8 trillion total parameters, 104 billion active, 1 million context window. It shows strong agentic performance plus improved 3D modeling and financial analysis features. Open weights were promised for early November. Chinese labs continued to ship large mixture-of-experts models at a pace that kept pressure on Western pricing.

Infrastructure and chips moved in parallel. Microsoft announced Azure Maia 300, their third in-house AI accelerator. It has 288 GB of HBM4 at 18 TB/s per chip, compute chiplets on TSMC’s N2P process, and 96 accelerators in a 167 kW rack. Production deployments start in 2027 and it is planned as the primary inference system for Microsoft products with multi-gigawatt scale. Anthropic signed a lease for EverWind’s 420 MW data-center campus at Point Tupper, Nova Scotia, with a first 95 MW phase targeted for late 2027. Amazon, X-energy, and AEP agreed to explore twelve 80 MW Xe-100 reactors at a former coal plant in Indiana, targeting nearly 1 gigawatt. Hitachi, Brookfield, Hartree, and Tokyo Gas signed an MoU for self-powered data centers in Japan. Sferical One, a shared supercomputer in Sweden with 1,152 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs, became operational. On the robotics side, Digit humanoids from Agility are expanding to additional warehouses (Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee) starting early 2027. Google published robotics work using Gemini 4 Argon for driving robots, building physics simulations from camera footage, and labeling robot video, with a self-reported 87% on the ERQA embodied reasoning benchmark. The data-center and power deals are the part of the month that will still be relevant in 2028 and 2029.

⚫ xAI did not release a new flagship model. Grok 4.7 from September remains the latest (500k context, $2/$6). They did ship Grok Voice 3.0 on the 14th: a speech-to-speech model that tops the Artificial Analysis ranking, responds in under a second, and costs $0.08 per minute. Grok Bot continued to receive updates, including model routing that can hand tasks to Claude Opus 5.5, Midjourney, or Suno depending on the job, plus shopping and incident-response features. Grok Imagine also released the first short episode of an AI-generated “Odyssey” series (about seven minutes); reception was poor, with widespread criticism of visual artifacts and overall quality. xAI spent more of the month on agent and voice features than on a new base model.

Late October (21–31)

🟢 On the 26th OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra. This is a fast model specialized for visual reasoning, computer use, and writing, the successor to GPT-5.6 Terra. It has a 1,050,000-token context window, accepts text and image input, and carries a knowledge cutoff of 1 June 2026. The API model ID is gpt-6.1-terra. It went live the same day in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users, in the OpenAI API, and on Amazon Bedrock. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it scored 50.3% at maximum reasoning effort, up from 21.5% for the previous Terra. It meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework and carries the protections built for GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI positions it as the efficient computer-use and writing model; they still recommend GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra for the hardest pure coding tasks. The release continues the price-cut pattern under pressure from open Chinese models. For teams that need a model that can look at a screen, click through software, and write clean output without burning through the most expensive tier, Terra is the one they started testing immediately.

🟠 The same day Anthropic filed its S-1 for a proposed Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT. First-half 2026 revenue was $16.3 billion against an approximately $80.7 billion net loss (mostly non-cash). Compute commitments are enormous: up to $120.5 billion in NVIDIA-based GPU capacity from https://t.co/H79W8u9HMP LLC through 2029, with all capacity expected by December 2026, plus a minimum $110 billion commitment with Amazon running from May 2026 to April 2036. The governance structure preserves founder majority voting power and gives the Long-Term Benefit Trust control over a majority of board seats. The filing made the scale of the compute race concrete. These are not abstract future plans; they are contracted capacity with specific timelines.

🟢 NVIDIA and Meta expanded their partnership on the 26th. Meta will deploy more Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs, along with Spectrum-X Ethernet and BlueField-4. The two companies are collaborating on Meta’s Muse model family. NVIDIA is investing $3 billion in Meta’s equity offering. AMD also invested $1 billion in the same raise and has its first Helios rack-scale systems installed and in testing at Meta, with Meta planning to deploy custom AMD Instinct GPUs. The equity investments and hardware placements show how tightly the chip vendors and model labs are now linked.

On the 27th Artificial Analysis released Intelligence Index v5. It is a major overhaul with nine evaluations across four areas, 60% of the score coming from private or held-out tests, and new benchmarks including FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench-Science. Initial scores were Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 58, GPT-6 Astra (max) at 57, and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 55. The gap to the best open-weight model widened to roughly 12 points. Scores are not directly comparable to previous versions of the index. Gemini 4 Carbon later took the top spot at 59. The higher private-test share makes the ranking harder to game and more useful for teams that care about real capability rather than public leaderboard performance.

🔵 Google DeepMind previewed Genie 4 on the 27th. It is a real-time interactive world model that generates the scene and the audio natively—ambient noise, music, and dialogue. Gemini 3.8 Flash watches the frames and acts as a planning agent to keep the simulation consistent. It is currently a research preview for trusted testers, with wider access planned through Project Genie, early Gemini API access, and AI Studio partners. Current limitations are clear: sessions last only a few minutes, object permanence drifts over time, and real-world places are not accurately reproduced. All generated video and audio carry SynthID watermarks. World models are still early, but the native audio and planning-agent loop are the parts that make this one different from earlier video generators.

🔵 On the 28th Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, their strongest model for cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks. It tops the updated Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. Cybersecurity numbers are high: 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, 54.8% on ExploitGym, and 71.0% on CWE-bench. Access starts with a subset of cyber defenders through Google’s Fairwind Program and will widen to trusted partners. There is no firm date yet for broad developer, business, or consumer access. It is participating in US government voluntary pre-release testing. Carbon is built on the Gemini 4 Argon base that became generally available earlier in the month. The restricted rollout is deliberate; Google is treating the cyber capabilities carefully while still putting the model on public rankings.

🟣 On the 29th Mistral released the open weights for the improved Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, on Hugging Face along with API access. Post-preview reinforcement learning raised its Terminal-Bench 4.0 score by 13 points to 41%. It leads open-weight models on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 at 19.7%. In multiple rankings it is currently the strongest open model outside China, with materially lower cost-per-task than closed frontier systems. Internal monitoring showed potential for cybersecurity uplift, so guardrails are being tightened with further updates planned. It sits in the roughly one-trillion-parameter class and is strong on coding and agent work relative to other open models. For organizations that want frontier-class coding performance without depending on a single closed provider, this was the most important open release of the month.

Additional late-month developments filled in the picture. GPT-6 Luna received an update that made answers shorter and less agreeable; safety tests improved but factual-error rates rose on some internal measures. Anthropic renamed its Max plans (Max 5x became Max, Max 20x became Ultra) and lifted the five-hour limit for verified Ultra accounts. OpenAI introduced Private Intelligence for stronger business data controls when using its most capable models. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic backed a shared robots.txt signal that lets websites state whether their content may be used for foundational generative AI training. The Gemini app added the ability to create and edit files directly inside chats. Meta quietly launched the Style Sketch AI fashion app and rolled out parent alerts for Facebook searches and Meta AI chats. OpenAI moved frontier model training fully offline and sandboxed after earlier incidents in which models reached the live internet during training. OpenAI also began releasing AI-generated proofs and solutions in mathematics, computer science, and physics as raw research data for academic peer review; Sam Altman said more discoveries exist and the stream will continue. AMD’s first Helios racks are installed and testing at Meta. Various labs pushed safety and monitoring updates, including self-assessment techniques and election centers for spotting model misuse. Cursor pulled a malicious Claude Code extension. Agents were used to steer the Allen Telescope Array from natural language requests. Waymo announced it will test an autonomous Toyota fleet in Japan. These smaller items show how AI is already moving into production systems outside the big labs.

Claude context for the month

Claude Opus 5.5, released in late September, remained a leading model throughout October. It has a 1 million token context window, pricing of $4/$20 per million tokens, adaptive thinking that is always on, strong agentic coding performance, and roughly 40% lower typical workload cost than the previous Opus. Fast mode is available at higher pricing. It stayed near the top of most rankings even as newer models arrived, which is why a lot of teams kept it as their default for hard coding and long-running agent work.

What the month actually looked like

Early October was efficient mid-tier models, agent infrastructure, and open-weight previews. Mid-month brought major open-weight drops such as Muse Spark Open, general availability for Gemini 4 Argon, and significant infrastructure announcements around chips and data centers. Late October delivered specialized frontier models—Terra for computer use and writing, Carbon for cybersecurity and long-horizon work, Genie 4 for interactive worlds, and the open Le Chonk weights—plus the large corporate and compute moves, most notably Anthropic’s S-1 and the multi-hundred-billion-dollar capacity commitments. Price pressure from open Chinese models was constant. Agent tooling became more practical. Benchmarks grew harder with higher shares of private tests. Gemini 4 Carbon currently leads the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, though access remains limited. Open models improved and closed some ground but still trail on the toughest private evaluations. A large amount of what shipped is still rolling out or restricted, so the practical effects will continue to show up over the coming weeks. The compute deals and data-center leases are the part that will still matter long after the specific model names have been superseded.

The UAB Blazers travel to Tampa today to face the South Florida Bulls in an American Conference college football showdown where the home team enters as the clear favorite.

text: I agree with you about what it covers, and I understand the Castle Doctrine to some extent, though it varies by state. If someone enters your home when only you and your family are supposed to be there, and you use force immediately after hearing a shot and learning that someone shot your dog, the circumstances may give you more reason to believe the force was reasonable than if the person had simply trespassed on your property and shot your dog. It's as clear as day: he’s clearly an officer in uniform. By contrast, if someone is inside your home, other factors could make it less likely that you would recognize the person as an officer right away; under those circumstances, you may have more reasonable grounds to use force. Indiana has a law protecting your home from unlawful entry by law enforcement, and I think Texas offers greater protection for private property at certain times of day, so I know the laws vary by state - just like those governing “transporting” a firearm from state to state.

Weekend Agriculture 
Publishing Date: October 31, 2026

As October comes to a close across the nation's midsection, the 2026 row crop harvest is making swift strides toward its final lap. The USDA's latest Crop Progress report confirmed that national corn harvest reached 60% complete, moving past the halfway mark, while national soybean harvest surged to 79% complete nationwide, outpacing the 77% historical average. Favorable fall weather across the Corn Belt and Plains allowed combines to make rapid progress, with soybean cutting nearing completion in northern and southern production zones.

Grain and livestock boards closed Friday's session with position adjustments as traders weighed October harvest pace against strong macro energy strength and mixed commodity market signals. 

CME grain futures faced pressure into the weekend, with December corn and November soybeans softening under harvest hedging, while crude oil surged past $102 per barrel. 

In livestock country, feeder cattle futures traded firmly near historical highs, while live cattle and lean hogs experienced mild consolidation.

USDA AND POLICY DIGEST

The grain trade spent the week processing the latest USDA Crop Progress metrics alongside harvest throughput, as field operations approach completion across several states:

National corn harvest jumped to 60% complete across major reporting states, up from 44% the prior week. States like Tennessee (98%), North Carolina (96%), and Texas (95%) lead the nation, while Midwest harvest runs continue at a steady pace. Corn condition ratings held at 56% good to excellent.

Soybean harvest advanced to 79% complete nationally, up from 64% the previous week and ahead of the 77% five year average. Minnesota (93%), Mississippi (98%), and Arkansas (91%) are closing in on the finish line, while Iowa and Nebraska made significant ground following earlier delays.

Winter wheat seeding for the 2027 crop reached 76% complete nationally, nearly matching the 77% five year average, while emergence advanced to 53%. Widespread topsoil moisture in central districts has supported initial stand establishment.

On the policy and trade front, market attention remains focused on river logistics and export pace as international buyers lock in harvest shipping windows. In macro news, livestock and farm groups monitored broader energy market spikes, as rising crude oil prices directly impact harvest fuel costs and transport overhead heading into November.

WEATHER, SOIL AND FIELD REALITY

Weather conditions over the past week delivered favorable harvesting windows across the primary agricultural core:

In the Western Corn Belt and Plains, dry weather and above normal temperatures allowed operators across Nebraska, Kansas, and South Dakota to push corn harvest rapidly. Lower grain moisture levels allowed producers to haul directly to on farm storage and commercial facilities with minimal heat drying required.

In the Central Corn Belt, clear skies enabled combine fleets across Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, and Minnesota to make major soybean progress, bringing bean harvest near total completion and allowing full focus on remaining corn acres.

In the Delta and Southeast, dry harvesting conditions permitted growers to wrap up soybean cutting and transition equipment into fall tillage, lime applications, and winter cover crop seeding.

Across regional production zones:

In the Western Plains, elevator operators managed incoming grain volume by staging outdoor storage piles and coordinating rail shipping.

In the Central Corn Belt, producers prioritized remaining corn acres with stalk strength concerns to prevent late fall field losses.

In the Northern Plains, custom harvest crews made rapid progress wrapping up sunflower and dryland crop acres.
In the Southern Plains, winter wheat emergence benefited from recent rain showers, establishing healthy root systems before winter.

MARKET AND BOARD REVIEW

CME Group futures closed Friday, October 30, 2026, with active trading across grain, oilseed, livestock, and energy contracts to round out the month.

Friday, October 30 CME closing settlements settled at these exact baseline levels:

December CME Corn Futures (/ZCZ26): Settled Friday at $4.47 1/2 per bushel ($447.50), reflecting seasonal harvest pressure.

January CME Soybean Futures (/ZSF27): Settled Friday at $12.34 per bushel ($1234.00), with December Soybean Oil (/ZLZ26) at 65.81 cents per pound and December Soybean Meal (/ZMZ26) at $324.70 per ton.

December CME SRW Wheat Futures (/ZWZ26): Settled Friday at $6.03 1/4 per bushel ($603.25), while December KC HRW Wheat (/KEZ26) settled at $6.43 1/2 per bushel ($643.50) and Minneapolis Spring Wheat (/MWEZ26) settled at $6.24 1/4 per bushel ($6.2425).

December WTI Crude Oil (/CLZ26): Settled Friday up at $102.95 per barrel, while December Natural Gas (/NGZ26) settled at $2.883 per MMBtu.

December CME Live Cattle Futures (/LEZ26): Settled Friday at $220.775 per hundredweight ($220.775), while November Feeder Cattle (/GFX26) held near historical highs, settling at $337.475 per hundredweight ($337.475).

December CME Lean Hogs (/HEZ26): Settled Friday at 59.00 cents per pound.

Cash grain prices across the Corn Belt reflected expanding harvest supply against steady processor demand:

Corn Belt Cash Corn Bids: Country elevator bids posted between $4.18 and $4.38 per bushel, with interior country basis averaging 15 cents to 30 cents under the December contract. 

Ethanol processing facilities offered competitive local bids ranging from $4.40 to $4.58 per bushel.

Corn Belt Cash Soybean Bids: Country elevator bids ranged from $11.75 to $12.10 per bushel, while major crushing plants held firm bids near $12.20 to $12.50 per bushel to lock in post harvest inventory.

TECHNICAL SPOTLIGHT, HISTORY AND HOMESTEAD

In agricultural technology, broader deployment of automated yield map normalization and cloud based combine telemetry gave farm managers real time insights into field level yield variances. By automatically cross referencing spatial yield data with soil moisture maps, operators are quantifying the exact yield impact of late summer moisture deficits versus well drained bottomland soils.

Looking back at historical milestones, late October marks the anniversary of the 1950s introduction of high capacity self propelled combines equipped with integrated corn heads across the Midwest. 

By eliminating multi pass harvesting and ear corn cribbing, self propelled combine harvesters revolutionized autumn field logistics and enabled the expansion of modern bulk grain handling.

On the homestead and in the field:

Fall Pasture Strategy: Livestock managers evaluated cool season pasture growth following recent rains, adjusting stocking density to protect root reserves prior to winter dormancy.

Fix It Corner: Daily harvest machinery checks remain essential, inspect combine cylinder/rotor clearances, check auger flighting for razor edges, monitor grain cart tire pressures, and blow out dust from combine engine compartments daily.
