text:
A daylight saving historian says candy makers once left a candy-filled pumpkin on every lawmaker's seat in the Capitol. The candy industry says it never took a single pumpkin to Capitol Hill. Somebody's wrong about pumpkins, and honestly I can't let it go.

What's on the record is almost as good. In 1985 the House voted to stretch daylight saving time, and the sponsors tossed in an extra week in the fall so trick-or-treaters would get more light.

Then a Kentucky lawmaker threatened a filibuster over dark fall mornings for farmers and kids on school buses. Halloween got cut, and the 1986 law only moved the spring start.

The man running the daylight coalition told the LA Times four candy groups would be disappointed, then offered this: "People will be eating more candy bars while they play more softball." His coalition also had the barbecue industry and the softball association in it. What a lineup.

Halloween finally got its hour in 2007, when the clocks started falling back in November. And the candy association's own account? About $200 chipped in back in the early '80s, then it sat the issue out.

Personally I want the pumpkins to be real. Historian or candy guys, who are you believing?

text: 67/100 Practice six: waking up on purpose. The anchor checks where your mind is. Waking up is what you do when you catch it on autopilot. The moment you realise you've been scrolling for twenty minutes, or rehearsing an argument in the shower, or driving with no memory of the last ten kilometres, skip the scolding. Self-criticism just launches a fresh story in the default mode network. Name it lightly instead, almost with a smirk: "Ah. Autopilot." Then make one deliberate micro-choice. Phone face down. Feel the water temperature. Look at one real object for three seconds. Lucid dream research offers a nice parallel. In the 1980s Stephen LaBerge at Stanford showed that some people can realise they're dreaming while still inside the dream and signal it with pre-agreed eye movements. Later work, such as a 2009 study by Ursula Voss and colleagues, found distinctive brain activity in lucid dreams, including more activity in frontal areas. Lucid dreaming is a niche field and no goal of this book. It does give you a powerful image: you can be inside an experience and know at the same time that you're inside it. That double awareness is the whole skill, and the daytime version is available right now, no pillow required.

text:
Gen Z doesn’t think their degrees will land them work anymore, so they’re becoming their own bosses instead—and these college towns are thriving | Preston Fore, Fortune

College degrees are increasingly leaving graduates questioning whether the time and money were worth it as underemployment, unemployment, and an uncertain job market cloud their career prospects.

But rather than waiting for the right job opportunity to come along, some young people are taking matters into their own hands—and turning to entrepreneurship. New data shared exclusively with Fortune by GoDaddy finds that microbusiness activity is growing across college communities nationwide, with several smaller university towns emerging as particularly strong entrepreneurial hubs.

Stanford, Calif.,—home to Stanford University—has long been an entrepreneurial hotspot and led the ranking with 20.2% growth in microbusiness activity between July 2025 and June 2026. But smaller college communities weren’t far behind: Warrensburg, Mo., home to the University of Central Missouri, saw 16.1% growth, while Newark, Del., home to the University of Delaware, recorded 16% growth. Elon, N.C., and Cortland, N.Y., rounded out the top five, with growth of 15.5% and 14.6%, respectively.

“What surprised me is the diversity of schools and towns that made the top 10,” Alexandra Rosen, economist and head of GoDaddy’s Small Business Research Lab, told Fortune.

“They range from the more high-tech hubs, with Stanford coming in first place, but also with rural areas like two SUNY schools being in the top 10, showing that entrepreneurship really is growing everywhere.”

The study identified college towns by combining GoDaddy’s city-level microbusiness data with U.S. Census and federal education data. To qualify, a community needed a population of at least 10,000, a college or university with at least 5,000 students, and at least 20% of its residents enrolled in college or graduate school.

AI is lowering the barriers to entrepreneurship—and college towns are seeing a surge

While the GoDaddy data isn’t exclusive to students or recent graduates, it offers a broader snapshot of entrepreneurial activity in and around college communities. A microbusiness could belong to a professor publishing a book, a local resident opening a coffee shop, or a student testing a business idea—and it speaks to the entrepreneurial energy universities can help cultivate in the communities around them.

“The optimism of opportunity and making an impact on the world—in college towns, you’re encountering the real world and probably asking, ‘What is your place in that world and what are you going to do with it?’” Rosen said.

College towns have long been breeding grounds for innovation, producing some of today’s biggest companies. For example, Mark Zuckerberg launched Facebook (now Meta) while attending Harvard University, and Michael Dell founded what would become Dell Technologies from his dorm room at the University of Texas at Austin.

But a new wave of technological change is something of a double-edged sword for aspiring entrepreneurs. On one hand, AI is transforming the job market and raising questions about which entry-level opportunities will remain available to young workers. On the other, AI tools are lowering the barriers to starting a business, making it easier for aspiring founders to develop business plans, build websites, test ideas, and get a venture off the ground without the same resources they might have needed in the past.

Overall, Rosen said entrepreneurship offers young people a way to “take the reins or to bet on yourself,” rather than wait for an employer to give them an opportunity.

Universities themselves have been a major source of making the process less intimidating. According to business school accreditor AACSB, the number of undergraduate entrepreneurship programs increased by nearly 25% between 2017–18 and 2019–20.

“It is inviting more students to feel it more accessible and less scary, and as a more likely outcome or potential path forward,” Rosen said. “It feels less risky because it’s more familiar. Everybody knows somebody that has a small business now.”

CEOs see a golden opportunity for Gen Z entrepreneurs—but Jeff Bezos says don’t skip the experience

Some of the world’s most prominent business leaders are also urging young people to take a closer look at entrepreneurship, arguing that rapid technological change is creating an unusually fertile environment for aspiring founders.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called it “absolutely the single greatest time to start a company,” during a conversation earlier this year with Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The 63-year-old even said he was “jealous” of the opportunities ahead for young founders. For those intimidated by the changes in the world, he encourages entrepreneurs to approach any challenge with one simple question: “How hard can it be?”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman sees a similar opening for young people willing to take advantage of the AI revolution. Speaking to Stanford students earlier this month, he argued that entering the workforce during a period of rapid change can give ambitious people an advantage.

“If you’re heading into the world right now to work on something, I think you want to start your career at a time of the greatest change, when the playing field is most open,” Altman said.

“I think people with high potential, drive, ideas, a new way of looking at things, and new skills tend to do relatively well when the ground is shaking the most.”

Still, not every billionaire business leader thinks young people should rush to strike out on their own. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has cautioned against treating well-known college dropouts as blueprints for success.

“It is possible to be 18, 19, 20 years old, drop out of college and be a great entrepreneur,” Bezos said on stage at Italian Tech Week 2025. “We have famous examples of that working, Bill Gates, Mark Zuckerberg, etc. But these people are the exception.”

Bezos, now the world’s second-richest person with an estimated $355 billion fortune, graduated from Princeton University in 1986 and didn’t launch Amazon until nearly a decade later. That extra time gaining work experience, he said, improved his odds of success.

“I started Amazon when I was 30, not when I was 20, and I think that extra 10 years of experience actually improved the odds that Amazon would succeed,” Bezos added. “So that would always be my advice: I finished college, and I think it’s been helpful to me.”

"Cross River Bank’s early ties to Ripple go back to the mid-2010s, when Ripple was still mainly pushing its payment protocol (the predecessor to today’s RippleNet / On-Demand Liquidity stack) rather than the broader institutional products it offers now.

What happened around 2014

Cross River was among the first U.S. banks to experiment with Ripple’s protocol for real-time cross-border payments. At the time, Ripple was marketing a distributed ledger that could settle payments in seconds without traditional correspondent banking chains. A handful of early-adopter banks and payment companies integrated the protocol to test faster, cheaper foreign-exchange and remittance flows.

Cross River, already positioning itself as a tech-forward community bank that powered fintechs, was a natural fit. It used the Ripple protocol to explore real-time settlement options for its partners. Contemporary reports and later retrospective comments from people familiar with the bank describe this as one of the earliest U.S. bank integrations of the protocol.

How it fit Cross River’s strategy

Cross River had been chartered in 2008 and quickly moved into “banking-as-a-service” for fintechs.
Adding a real-time cross-border rail aligned with its goal of giving fintech partners more modern payment tools than traditional ACH/wire infrastructure alone.
The integration was relatively limited compared with today’s RLUSD/XRPL work; it was primarily about the messaging and settlement protocol rather than on-chain digital assets or stablecoins (which largely came later).

Evolution since then

The 2014-era protocol work was an early proof-of-concept. Over the following years Ripple shifted emphasis toward RippleNet, then On-Demand Liquidity (using XRP as a bridge asset), and more recently stablecoins (RLUSD) and deeper bank integrations. Cross River’s October 2026 announcement of embedding RLUSD (issued on the XRP Ledger) into its Core Operating System is a much more mature, production-oriented version of the same idea: giving fintechs access to faster settlement rails without forcing them to build blockchain infrastructure themselves.

In short, the “2014 Ripple protocol connection” was Cross River being an early U.S. bank tester of Ripple’s real-time cross-border settlement technology. That historical relationship is why the bank’s logo appears in the satirical XRP video—you’re seeing a nod to both the old protocol experiments and the new RLUSD integration."

text:
Hermes yesterday: you could delete a cron job mid-run and it kept going anyway, paying for model calls toward a result Hermes then threw away. Now cron jobs have a Stop button. 91 commits landed on main, almost all of them fixes, and here are the 10 that matter.

1️⃣ Cron jobs get a Stop button, and each job picks what happens to missed runs

Before: a running cron job had no stop command, so you waited for its timeout or killed the process by hand, and deleting a job mid-run let it keep going, model and tool calls included, until it booked failed with its result discarded. After: hermes cron cancel, a Stop button on the job in Desktop, the dashboard API and the cronjob_manage cancel action stop a live run, which books cancelled with the reason, with no failure alert and no bump to the failure streak; deleting a job now stops its live run too. In the PR's test, an agent run stopped inside a 75-second terminal command was cancelled in about 4 seconds, its command killed. Each job can also choose what happens to runs missed while the machine was off: --catch-up on or off in hermes cron create and edit, or Missed runs in the Desktop editor (use the default, run once when back, skip them); the global cron.catch_up_missed stays the default, and every skipped or collapsed slot now shows in run history as one missed row. Limits: pause still does not stop a live run, only cancel and remove do; a one-shot job missed by more than 120 seconds still skips unless it sets catch_up; and the external scheduler provider's misfire backstop ignores the per-job setting.

2️⃣ Desktop stops dropping healthy connections when you switch back to it

Before: every focus, wake or network-online event made Desktop probe its socket with a 5-second ping, and the backend answered that ping only after every control request queued ahead of it, so one slow request (a manual compression, resuming a large chat, a slow slash command, a slow remote host) turned the next alt-tab into connection lost and a full reconnect. By the opt-in telemetry quoted in the PR, about 2,000 of roughly 11,500 daily Desktop installs hit it, about 2.8 times a day each. After: the probe uses https://t.co/L5bFLtfb0s, which the backend's socket reader answers at once, remote and Hermes Cloud backends included (an older backend without it counts as alive), and a heartbeat tick that itself ran late after a frozen window or a sleep sends one more probe instead of dropping a socket whose answer is still queued. A peer that never answers still drops. Limit: a stall that starts right after an already-late tick can still close a healthy socket.

3️⃣ A gateway caught in a boot loop now starts

Before: at startup, the gateway's sweep that closes orphaned local sessions opened a database read inside another read. When the read pool is unavailable (no WAL journal, the network-filesystem fallback, or every read permit spent), reads go through one lock that cannot be taken twice, so the startup thread waited on itself forever: the control socket never answered, Desktop showed Gateway inaccessible or Gateway starting: deadline, the liveness watchdog exited, and the service manager restarted the gateway into the same wedge. It was seen on a live macOS gateway; the code path is the same on every platform. After: the sweep resolves its target before opening the read, so it takes exactly one read. The slower degraded read path itself is unchanged.

4️⃣ Docker: the CLI and Desktop share one sandbox again

Before: with the persistent Docker backend and docker_mount_cwd_to_workspace off (both defaults), since October 17 a Desktop session got its own per-folder container while the CLI kept the profile's, so the two saw different /workspace and /root files in the same profile, and the Desktop file panel could preview a leftover copy instead of the live file. After: with mounting off, CLI, gateway and Desktop sessions of a profile share one sandbox, and the file panel reads and saves in it; with mounting on, nothing changes (one container per profile and folder). Heads-up: files written into the per-folder sandboxes in between (the _ws_ folders under the profile's Docker sandbox directory) are not migrated; they are kept but no longer used, so copy anything you still need into the profile sandbox's workspace or home folder.

5️⃣ A local model server that is down stops looking like a sign-in problem

Before: with Hermes's managed llama.cpp server as the main model, a server that was down (stopped when Desktop closed, still loading, or switched off) made the Webapp open the provider sign-in screen, and a message sent anyway got a card saying the AI service rejected your API key. After: the app stays open with a Local model unavailable notice, with Open Local models on Desktop and Choose another model in the Webapp; a failed turn reads Can't reach your model server, with Switch provider, and Retry only while the server is still starting. The TUI, the dashboard and messaging replies name the local server too and point to both ways to start it, the desktop app or hermes model; Desktop backs off re-checking a server that stays down and clears the notice when it comes back. Failures of other kinds, like a missing credential, still open setup as before. Limit: the Desktop side was covered by unit tests, the live run was on the Webapp.

6️⃣ Several clarify questions become one form

Before: on Desktop and the Webapp, when the agent asked several questions in one clarify call, you got one card at a time, and the next question appeared only after you answered the one before. After: every question shows at once in one form with one submit, and plain Enter sends the set only once every question is answered. Limits: a Desktop app paired with an older backend falls back to one card per question, an edited queued prompt still gets one card per question, and a reply typed into the composer still answers only one question of a set, a separate bug.

7️⃣ Attention alerts you can actually notice

Before: when a chat needed you (an approval, a question, a finished or failed turn), the Webapp only put a small mark in the tab title and asked for notification permission at the moment of the event, which browsers ignore, and clicking a notification did nothing; Desktop showed a toast that left no trace once the window was minimized. After: an unfocused Webapp tab alternates its title with the alert every second and gets an amber dot on its icon until you come back; browser notifications work once you click Allow under Settings, Notifications, Browser notifications (Hermes never asks on page load), and clicking one opens that chat; Desktop flashes the taskbar on Windows, bounces the dock on macOS and sets the urgency hint on Linux while unfocused. It reuses the existing notification toggles, so a kind that is off flashes nothing. Limit: browser notifications need HTTPS (Tailscale serve, for example); over plain HTTP on a LAN only the title flash works.

8️⃣ Desktop error cards get one fix each

Before: the inline card on a failed Desktop turn used raw provider text as its headline, offered three or four equal buttons, and the same failure could show up as a card, a toast and a banner at once. After: each card is either blocking or degraded (degraded ones can be closed), carries a short title naming the provider or model, one main action and at most one second option (new ones include Continue for a reply cut off at the token limit and Setup guide for TLS and local-server failures), plus a View error details toggle with copy, logs and diagnostics. The chat on screen gets no duplicate toast, and out of credits lives in the composer banner. Two follow-ups the same day fixed what review found: Continue now really sends, and never picks up or erases your unsent draft; Open billing settings goes to the failing provider's own billing page, or Settings, Billing for Nous; and a plain Retry appears only after a usage limit has actually reset.

9️⃣ hermes plugins doctor stops copying what it should not

Before: hermes plugins doctor run on a folder that merely contained a plugin (a home folder next to .hermes, a Downloads folder with an extracted plugin and large files) could copy the whole folder into its temporary Hermes home, and with TMPDIR inside the plugin, or a link in the plugin pointing at TMPDIR, it copied the plugin into its own temporary folder until the path got too long or, on a big plugin, the disk filled. After: a folder without its own manifest counts as a category only when every subfolder is a plugin, Doctor copies only the one plugin it validates, a category of several plugins is refused before anything is copied, and the self-copy cases stop with an error telling you to point TMPDIR outside the plugin. It is the same bug family as an earlier fix, after a run copied 461 GB from a home folder.

🔟 The Webapp on a slow link: big videos play, media stops re-downloading

Before: in the Webapp, chat videos over 100 MiB did not play, a clip was fetched again every time its row re-rendered, transcript images were downloaded in full on every remount, and after a reconnect the next send hid the subagent and background-task bar until the chat resumed. After: videos of any size stream one range at a time, SSH profiles included; a remounted clip reuses its stream URL; an unchanged image costs a 304 answer of about 173 bytes from the browser cache, while a rewritten file still shows its new version; and a reconnect keeps the open chat bound, so the bar stays. Limits: images from SSH profiles still re-read on remount, and on a slow link a remount still waits one round trip.

━━━━━━━━━━

⚙️ Meanwhile, in the engine room

Dozens of fixes landed yesterday that most users never see, and the cron Stop work and config loading took most of them.

• A Cloud agent using the remote config backend never booted: its first config read waited on a lock its own thread held while loading the sign-in module; loading the config and sign-in modules now reads no config, and the credential is resolved before the fetch lock
• Discord's /model picker overwrote a finished switch or cancel with Selection expired when its 120-second timeout fired; it now releases the picker as soon as it is answered and keeps the result
• hermes config set on MoA preset fields such as fanout and reference_timeout saved working values and then warned that Hermes might not read them; preset fields are now recognized under any preset name, and typos still warn
• In a gateway Group Chat, a member addressed directly that answered with a pass left the user with nothing; the member is now asked for an answer, a result or a blocker, and a pass that still comes back shows as a failed turn with an explanation

If you noticed none of this, it worked.

All on main, ships in the next release (Desktop app changes reach the Microsoft Store app with the release and the .exe and .dmg app with its next bundled release). Latest stable: v0.22.5.

Which one hits you most? 👇

I visited my friend last weekend, and what happened in her house still annoys me.

When I arrived, she welcomed me warmly and offered me food. I noticed she had a house help, so I assumed everything was fine.

Only for her husband to come out and tell the house help to serve me food.

The girl served me a plate of rice with one small piece of meat.

I didn’t complain.

But when my friend came out, she shouted at the girl, collected the meat from my plate and said, “Didn’t I tell you that visitors should not eat the meat meant for the family?”

I was embarrassed.

I told her not to worry, that I was okay with the food.

Then she said something that shocked me.

“Don’t mind her. Even my husband doesn’t eat meat every day.”

I dropped my spoon and asked for my bag.

Because how can you invite someone into your house and make them feel like a burden over one piece of meat?

text:
#Meta, #TikTok, and #X Lose London Court Battle: UK Demands Disclosure of How Many Children See Harmful Content

On October 30, 2026, the High Court of Justice in London dismissed lawsuits brought by Meta, TikTok, and X against the UK regulator #Ofcom, which demanded access to internal statistics on moderation and the spread of harmful content. The tech giants attempted to challenge the scope of the requests and the regulator's authority, arguing that compliance would cost millions of pounds and require restructuring their analytical systems. Judges Rabinder #Singh and Beverly Collins-#Rice ruled the demands lawful and refused to overturn them. The decision marks the first judicial test of Ofcom's powers under the #Online #Safety #Act 2023, reports Reuters.

On February 10, Ofcom issued information notices to Meta Platforms, WhatsApp LLC, X Internet Unlimited Company, and TikTok Information Technologies UK. The regulator requested data covering from January 1, 2024: user numbers categorized by age groups, volumes of removed and restricted content, banned accounts, moderation speeds, the number of UK users—including children—who viewed later-deleted posts, outcomes of user complaints, and appeal timelines. The data spans three periods: 2024–2025, H1 2026, and H2 2026. Initial submission deadlines were set for June 15, September 22, 2026, and March 25, 2027.

Three judicial proceedings—No. AC-2026-LON-002160, AC-2026-LON-002053, and AC-2026-LON-001872—were heard jointly. In judgment No. [2026] EWHC 2779 (Admin), the court outlined the tech companies' arguments. X estimated compliance costs in the millions of pounds, requiring 3–4 months of specialist work and hundreds of hours from at least ten employees. Meta reported mobilizing up to 20 internal teams, while TikTok cited more than 1,000 staff members across 80 teams dedicated to UK compliance. The judges ruled that the companies failed to provide sufficiently detailed calculations of additional costs to prove the demands were disproportionate, rejecting all challenges to Ofcom's statutory authority, procedures, and objectives.

The court validated Ofcom's authority to demand such data under Section 100 of the Online Safety Act. Serious violations of the act carry potential fines of up to £18 million or 10% of a company's qualifying global turnover, whichever is higher. The current ruling does not impose fines; rather, it upholds the legal obligation to supply the data. Meta expressed disappointment with the ruling, TikTok is reviewing potential next steps, and X initially offered no comment.

On October 6, Ofcom opened a separate investigation into Meta regarding the "Instagram Instants" feature launched on May 13, where photos and videos disappear after viewing. The regulator is assessing whether the company conducted adequate risk assessments concerning illegal content and threats to children prior to launch, as mandated by Sections 9(4) and 11(4). Concurrently, Meta is challenging the calculation of regulatory fees and potential penalties, as well as WhatsApp's classification. Since January 23, Ofcom has also been independently auditing the accuracy and completeness of data regarding WhatsApp Business requested under the #Communications #Act 2003. The October 30 ruling secures the regulator's access to detailed moderation, complaint, and child audience statistics that tech corporations sought to withhold from mandatory reporting.

Unbelievable, but true…

Drastic Reduction in Property Taxes Would Put Local Services at Risk

Property taxes help fund the crucial local services that families rely on in Florida, including disaster response, hospitals and health services, public safety, fire and rescue, waste management, libraries, children's services councils, and more.

However, Amendment 3, which is on the ballot in Florida in 2026, would reduce local revenue by roughly $12 billion on a recurring basis. The proposed amendment to Florida’s constitution would increase the state’s homestead exemption, create a pathway for the full elimination of non-school property taxes on homesteads, and reduce the assessment growth cap on non-homesteaded properties.

Local lawmakers, if faced with a drastic reduction in property tax revenue, would have to increase other taxes and fees or cut services. 

For example, in response to Amendment 3, a local government might: eliminate firefighter positions or close fire stations; close the local library, reduce library staff, or implement charges for programs traditionally offered for free; implement solid waste fees, stormwater fees, fire service assessments, impact fees, or permit and licensing fees; or increase the price of municipality-run summer camp.

Expectations for South Carolina are clear and uncompromising: another Final Four appearance and a national championship run. Dawn Staley has assembled a challenging non-conference schedule, featuring high-profile matchups in Paris, marquee non-conference tests against elite rivals, and a grueling SEC slate. 

While early-season chemistry and backcourt rotation adjustments may produce moments of adaptation, the roster’s sheer depth, defensive versatility, and interior dominance make the Gamecocks the early favorite to reign over women's college basketball.

What a week. Here are the top 10 national stories of Oct. 25 to 31, and why each one mattered.

1. The Fed held rates, and two members wanted a hike. In Chair Kevin Warshâ€™s first decision, the Fed kept its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% on a 10 to 2 vote Wednesday, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voting for another quarter point hike. A day later the economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, the fastest in a year, but the Fedâ€™s preferred inflation gauge rose to 3.6%, the Commerce Department said. Why it was big: futures now point to a December hike, which means higher costs on mortgages, car loans and credit cards.

2. The AI trade cracked. Alphabet dropped about 10% after its first miss on revenue and profit in nearly four years, Amazon fell after its AI spending pushed free cash flow negative, and Intel plunged 29% Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, CNBC reported. The Nasdaq lost 2% for the week, the S&P 500 0.6% and the Dow 0.9%, while small caps gained. Why it was big: a lot of retirement money rides on the AI story, and investors are starting to ask when the spending pays off.

3. Iran escalated in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranâ€™s Revolutionary Guard said four oil tankers hit mines and caught fire Friday, and Reuters reported a small boat stuck limpet mines on a tanker Thursday, the first successful attack of its kind in this war. CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said the main shipping lanes have been cleared of Iranian mines and U.S. forces have escorted more than 3,000 ships. Brent crude ended the week near $117.55 a barrel. Why it was big: this fight sets the price of every gallon you buy.

4. Texans broke turnout records. More than 6.6 million Texans voted through Thursday, about 34.5% of registered voters, and Harris and Travis counties set midterm early voting records, per state data and the Houston Chronicle. Early voting closed Friday ahead of Tuesdayâ€™s Nov. 3 election. Why it was big: a surge like this can swing close races up and down the ballot.

5. Courts fought over noncitizen voting. The Justice Department charged 48 noncitizens in five states with illegal voting, false registration or false citizenship claims. In California, Judge David O. Carter refused to make the state set aside up to 20,000 mail ballots, and Friday night Judge Trina Thompson barred DOJ and DHS from threatening election officials with prosecution over voters the administration calls ineligible. Why it was big: the rules for counting ballots are being decided days before Election Day.

6. Trump ended Bidenâ€™s methane rules in West Texas. At a Lubbock rally, the President said heâ€™s â€œofficially terminating Bidenâ€™s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations,â€ and the EPA proposed rewriting the 2024 rules, which it says would add 210 million barrels of oil. The Energy Department also offered up to $5 billion in loans to boost output at eight existing nuclear plants. Why it was big: cheaper energy is the fastest relief for family budgets.

7. Big Oil cashed in while diesel hit $6.32. ExxonMobil and Chevron beat profit forecasts Friday and their stocks touched all time highs, with Exxonâ€™s profit roughly doubling to $15.4 billion, CNBC reported. AAA had diesel at $6.32 a gallon, up more than 70% from a year ago. Why it was big: diesel moves everything we buy, from groceries to building materials.

8. SpaceX is all in on Starship. The ship and booster for Flight 15 both finished full engine tests at Starbase in South Texas, and SpaceX expects the FAA license to allow catching both stages with the tower. Ars Technica reported SpaceX told NASA it will stop flying Crew Dragon by 2030 and stopped selling Falcon 9 launches after 2028. Why it was big: Americaâ€™s ride to space is about to depend on one giant rocket built in Texas.

9. Anthropic filed to go public. The maker of the Claude chatbot filed for a Nasdaq listing under â€œANT,â€ showing $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026 and an $80.7 billion net loss, mostly from accounting charges, CNBC and The Verge reported. The filing lists deals worth about $3.1 billion a month to SpaceX for chip access. Why it was big: itâ€™s one of the biggest tests yet of whether AI companies can make real money.

10. Border agentsâ€™ personal info leaked, and Washington went after fraud. A leak site posted names, cell numbers and office locations for more than 41,000 DHS employees and contractors, including about 21,000 at CBP, Reuters and WIRED reported. In Minnesota, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel and Dr. Mehmet Oz launched a fraud tip line with rewards up to $30,000. Why it was big: one story puts agents at risk, and the other goes after your tax money being stolen.

Facts and details in these stories are still being verified and may change as the stories develop.

My take: Inflation at 3.6%, diesel over $6 and record Texas turnout tell you where this election is. Vote Tuesday. Thoughts?

text:
⚖️ THE NIGHT HISTORY LOST ITS SENSE OF PROPORTION

══════════════ ❧ ════════════════

THE WEIRDEST EVENTS IN HISTORY 🤯

══════════════ ❧ ════════════════

Stranger Than Fiction — October 31st Halloween Edition

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🗺️ CONSPECTUS

📜 EPIGRAPH: The guiding principle of the newsletter and the lens through which the day’s stories are viewed.

🎬 INTRO: Sets the tone, introduces the day’s theme, and previews what’s ahead without giving away the stories.

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY: A quick history test. The answer awaits near the end.

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS: Five featured historical events, each with historical context, a trivia tidbit, and a brief source reference.

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER: A longer, story-driven feature in the tradition of classic radio storytelling. Settle in for the day’s centerpiece.

⚖️ CLOSING: Draws together the day’s events, revealing the common thread behind their historical absurdities and human consequences.

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: Reveals the correct answer to the day’s quiz, with a brief explanation.

🍬 CANDY: One last sweet bite before you go, with a quick look at tomorrow’s edition.

💋 SEND-OFF: A brief, personal farewell and an invitation to share the newsletter.

📚 SOURCES & FURTHER READING: References and links for further exploration.

✒️ PUDD'NHEAD WILSON HAS THE LAST WORD: A monthly decree from Mark Twain’s Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar (1894)—because some wisdom deserves the final word.

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

📜 EPIGRAPH

“Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn't.” ~ Mark Twain, Following the Equator, Chapter XV, “Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar” (1897) ☄️

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🎬 INTRO

Well, look who's crawled back out of the void. Welcome to Halloween—humanity's annual celebration of dressing up like monsters, frightening the neighbors, and handing children enough sugar to keep a small power station running. It's the one night of the year when people actually enjoy being scared. The other 364 days, they call it reading the news.

Tonight the porch lights come on, the costumes come out, and the neighborhood fills with creatures of the night. By tomorrow morning, they'll all be back at work pretending to be respectable citizens. Some will even be promoted. That's the really frightening part.

History, meanwhile, is sitting in the corner with a drink it didn't order, watching us make the same mistakes we've been making for centuries. It has seen wars, revolutions, spectacular miscalculations and people who thought they had everything under control. It has kept the receipts, too. And believe me, nobody is getting out of this without an itemized bill.

On tonight's program: a theological disagreement that helped ignite a religious upheaval lasting centuries. A state admitted to the Union at a politically convenient moment—so convenient, in fact, that coincidence might want to consult a lawyer. A cavalry charge that looked at modern warfare and decided the rules were merely suggestions. A prison escape involving a helicopter landing in the prison yard. Because when the front door is locked, apparently the sensible thing is to try the roof. And an anonymous announcement to a cryptography mailing list that introduced an entirely new form of money. Just what the world needed: something else nobody completely understands, but everybody wants to argue about.

Five historical events. Five reminders that humanity has never been short of confidence. Good judgment, on the other hand, has had a rather difficult time getting invited.

We are extraordinary planners. We raise armies, draft constitutions, build institutions, invent financial systems and devise prison escapes involving aircraft. We can organize thousands of people to accomplish almost anything. Getting them to agree on where to have lunch remains a different matter.

And there's the problem. We make the plan, admire the plan, congratulate ourselves on the plan—and then reality walks into the room without an appointment. Sometimes the result changes the world. Sometimes it changes a prison's security procedures. And sometimes it leaves everybody standing around asking the same question: Who thought this was going to work?

So keep a light on if it makes you feel better. Sharpen your skepticism, secure the candy, and remember: not everything that sounds impossible is fiction. Some of the strangest things on record happened in broad daylight, with witnesses, paperwork, and people afterward insisting that everything had gone exactly as intended.History does not need Halloween to be frightening.

It has us.

Cue the chaos. Let’s roll. 💥

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

On October 30, 1974, Muhammad Ali faced heavyweight champion George Foreman in one of boxing's most famous bouts.

What was the name given to this historic fight in Kinshasa, Zaire?

[A] The Thrilla in Manila
[B] The Rumble in the Jungle
[C] The Fight of the Century
[D] The Long Count Fight

👇 (Scroll down to the bottom of today's issue for the answer!)

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS

⚒️ 1517 — MONK CHALLENGES THE CHURCH, AND EUROPE GETS A REFORMATION 📜

On October 31, 1517, German theologian and professor Martin Luther sent the Archbishop of Mainz a document challenging the Catholic Church's sale of indulgences. Its 95 propositions were intended to provoke theological debate.

Tradition holds that Luther nailed the theses to the Castle Church door in Wittenberg, though that famous scene remains disputed. What is certain is that his challenge helped ignite the Protestant Reformation, transforming Europe's religious and political landscape.

An invitation to debate became one of history's most consequential arguments. One might say things got slightly out of hand.

🧩 TRIVIA: The first of Luther's 95 Theses begins by quoting Jesus: “When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, ‘Repent,’ he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance.”

Sources: Lutheran Quarterly — Reformation Timeline · German History in Documents and Images — Luther's Ninety-Five Theses

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🇺🇸 1864 — LINCOLN TELEGRAPHS AN ENTIRE STATE INTO EXISTENCE BECAUSE THE POSTMAN WAS TOO SLOW FOR AN ELECTION 🗳️

On October 31, 1864, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed Nevada the 36th state of the United States. The timing was hardly accidental. With the presidential election only days away, Nevada's admission was expected to strengthen support for Lincoln and the Union cause.

There was just one small complication: Nevada's population was well below the usual threshold for statehood. But the Civil War had changed the political calculations, and the territory's mineral wealth and expected loyalty to the Union made it strategically valuable.

The final rush was so urgent that Nevada's lengthy state constitution was transmitted to Washington by telegraph. Statehood, it seems, could not wait for the postman.

🧩 TRIVIA: The constitution sent by telegraph contained 16,543 words. The transmission cost $4,303.27—a remarkable bill for a document that arrived one Morse-code click at a time.

Sources: U.S. National Archives, DocsTeach — Nevada's Constitution by Telegraph · American Presidency Project — Lincoln's Nevada Statehood Proclamation

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🐎 1917 — BEERSHEBA: WHERE THIRSTY TROOPS CHARGED MACHINE GUNS WITH HORSES AND BAYONET-SWORDS BECAUSE THE 20TH CENTURY WAS TAKING TOO LONG ⚔️

On October 31, 1917, Australian and New Zealand mounted troops took part in the Battle of Beersheba, a major engagement during the First World War's Sinai and Palestine campaign.

As the day wore on, the British-led forces faced a pressing problem: water. Beersheba's wells were essential, and the opportunity to capture the town before nightfall was slipping away.

The Australian 4th Light Horse Brigade launched a daring mounted charge against Ottoman defensive positions. Rather than dismounting and advancing as conventional cavalry tactics often required, the horsemen rode directly toward the enemy positions, using bayonets as swords.

The attack succeeded. Beersheba fell, and the victory helped open the way for the subsequent advance toward Jerusalem.

In an age increasingly dominated by machine guns, trenches, and modern artillery, a mounted charge helped turn the tide. Sometimes the old-fashioned approach still has a few surprises left.

🧩 TRIVIA: The Australian 4th Light Horse Brigade suffered 67 casualties in the charge: 31 killed and 36 wounded.

Sources: Australian War Memorial — The Attack on Beersheba · Australian War Memorial — The 4th Light Horse Brigade

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🎃👻 1936 — HOUDINI GHOSTS HIS OWN WIFE FOR TEN YEARS, THEN FAILS TO APPEAR FOR THE GRAND FINALE ☠️

Ten years after Harry Houdini's death, his widow Bess kept the promise they had made: if one of them died first, the survivor would attempt to make contact from beyond the grave.

The agreement included a secret code. If Harry could communicate with Bess, he would deliver the word “Rosabelle,” followed by a sequence of words that carried a hidden message.

On October 31, 1936, Bess held the final séance on the roof of the Knickerbocker Hotel in Hollywood. The date marked the tenth anniversary of Houdini's death. Spiritualists and spectators had spent years waiting for the great escape artist to return from the one place no magician had ever demonstrated an ability to leave.

But no message came.

Bess announced that Houdini had not come through. She declared her belief that communication with the dead was impossible, extinguished the candle that had burned beside his photograph, and brought the ten-year vigil to an end.

The final act was not an escape. It was a goodbye.

🦇🧩  TRIVIA: The Library of Congress preserves the séance's radio script—and it reveals that the event was scripted in advance, complete with stage directions such as “Pause. Speak slowly.” Even the final attempt to contact the spirit world had its cues.

Sources: Library of Congress — Hollywood, Houdini and the Halloween Séance of 1936 · Houdini Museum — Bess Houdini's Final Séance

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🚁 1973 — WHEN THE PRISON YARD BECAME A HELICOPTER PAD AND NOBODY THOUGHT TO ASK FOR A FLIGHT PLAN 🚨

On October 31, 1973, three Provisional IRA prisoners escaped from Dublin's Mountjoy Prison in a fashion that sounds less like a prison break and more like a rejected film script.

A helicopter landed in the prison exercise yard. The aircraft had been hijacked, and its pilot, Captain Thomson Boyes, was forced to cooperate. The prisoners climbed aboard and flew away while prison authorities watched an escape unfold in the most conspicuous way imaginable.

The helicopter had reportedly been hired under the pretense of an aerial photography assignment. The operation turned that innocent-sounding cover story into one of the most audacious prison escapes in Irish history.

A prison built to keep people in had just been given an aerial exit. One can only imagine the awkwardness of explaining that security failure at the next staff meeting.

🧩 TRIVIA: The three escapees were J. B. O'Hagan, Seamus Twomey, and Kevin Mallon. The pilot later described being held at gunpoint and forced to fly the helicopter into the prison yard.

Sources: RTÉ Archives — The Mountjoy Prison Helicopter Escape, October 31, 1973

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

₿ 2008 — ANONYMOUS GHOST POSTS PDF TO A LISTSERV AND ACCIDENTALLY INVENTS MONEY THE BANKS CAN'T CONTROL 🕵️

On October 31, 2008, a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto announced a paper titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System to a cryptography mailing list.

The proposal introduced a digital payment system that required no central financial institution or trusted intermediary. It offered a way to prevent digital money from being spent more than once without a central authority keeping the books.

There was no press conference, fanfare, or celebrity endorsement—just a message on an obscure mailing list. Its author remained anonymous, and that mystery became part of the story.

The financial world had no idea what was coming. The internet had just received the blueprint for a new kind of money—and a mystery that remains unsolved.

🧩 TRIVIA: Nakamoto's original announcement was timestamped 18:10 UTC on October 31, 2008. The identity behind the name Satoshi Nakamoto remains unknown.

🔑 ESOTERIC: The original proposal described a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that could operate without a trusted third party. Its underlying innovation was not simply digital money; it was a way for participants to agree on transaction history without handing control to a central authority.

Sources: Satoshi Nakamoto — Original Bitcoin Announcement · Satoshi Nakamoto Institute — Email Archive

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🎙️ HARVEY'S CORNER

THE MAN WHO COULDN'T ESCAPE DEATH

Good day, everybody.

Imagine making a living by escaping things that were never supposed to let you go.

Handcuffs. Chains. Locked trunks. Sealed containers. Straitjackets. Houdini faced them all, and time after time, he emerged where no one expected him to be. His audiences watched in disbelief. His reputation grew. He became the man who could escape almost anything.

His name was Harry Houdini.

By 1926, Houdini was one of the most famous entertainers in the world. But there was another side to the man behind the spectacle. He had become a determined opponent of fraudulent spiritualists, exposing mediums who claimed they could communicate with the dead. He believed that grief was too precious to be exploited, and he was prepared to challenge anyone who made a business of it.

Then came October 1926.

While in Montreal, Houdini was speaking with students when one of them struck him several times in the abdomen. The incident would become one of the most repeated stories about his death. The popular version says those blows ruptured his appendix.

But the truth is less certain. Houdini had already been suffering from illness. Although the punches became inseparable from the story of his death, there is no established medical evidence that they caused his appendicitis or ruptured appendix.

He continued performing as his condition worsened, eventually requiring emergency surgery. He died on October 31, 1926, from peritonitis following a ruptured appendix.

At fifty-two, the world's most celebrated escape artist had reached the one locked door no human being can open.

Death.

But there was one final challenge Houdini had arranged before he died.

He and his wife, Bess, had agreed upon a secret code. If Harry could somehow communicate with her after death, he would use that code to prove the message was genuine. No vague whispers. No convenient interpretations. No clever medium claiming to know what a grieving widow wanted to hear.

There would be a test.

Bess promised to keep trying.

And she did. For ten years, she held to the possibility that her husband might find a way to reach her. Each Halloween brought another attempt, another séance, and another opportunity for the promised message to arrive.

But it never did.

On October 31, 1936, ten years after Houdini's death, Bess held the final séance. The agreed-upon message had not come. She brought the experiment to an end.

In later years, she explained the decision with words that carried the weight of a decade:

"Ten years is long enough to wait for any man."

Think about that for a moment.

Harry Houdini had spent his life escaping restraints, defeating locks, and making the impossible appear possible. He had challenged the world to distinguish genuine wonders from carefully constructed illusions.

Yet the final story was not about an escape.

It was about a wife who waited ten years for a message that never came.

And perhaps the most remarkable thing about Houdini's final mystery is that, after all his years of exposing deception, the one thing he could not prove was the one thing his wife most wanted to believe.

And now you know the rest of the story.

Good day!

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

⚖️ CLOSING

What links these October 31 stories is not coincidence of date alone. It is the gap between what people intended and what actually followed.

Martin Luther wanted a debate. He got a fracture that remade Europe. Nevada’s admission was a wartime expedient to secure three electoral votes; it also permanently enlarged the Union at a moment when the Union’s survival was still in doubt.

The horsemen at Beersheba needed water before nightfall and answered the need with a charge that modern doctrine had already ruled impractical. The men who left Mountjoy in a helicopter solved the immediate problem of confinement and, in doing so, exposed how brittle even a guarded perimeter can be. Satoshi Nakamoto offered a technical solution to double-spending; the result was a monetary system whose social and political consequences remain unsettled more than a decade later. And Bess Houdini kept a ten-year appointment with a husband who had promised, if it were possible, to return. The message never came.

In each case the actors were competent, deliberate, and limited. They could see the problem in front of them. They could not see the full shape of what their solution would become, or the parts of the problem that would remain after they had done their best. History is full of such moments. The unusual thing about this particular day is how clearly the pattern appears: careful plans, real intelligence, incomplete information, and outcomes that outrun the people who set them in motion.

That does not make the efforts futile. Nevada did enter the Union. Beersheba’s wells were taken. The Mountjoy prisoners did escape. Bitcoin’s ledger continues. Bess kept her word. It simply means that human agency is real and still not sovereign. We can alter the conditions we face. We cannot fully dictate the meaning those alterations will later carry.

On Halloween it is easy to treat the past as a collection of oddities. These stories resist that. They are ordinary human actions—argument, political calculation, military necessity, escape, invention, and the long loyalty of a widow—whose results proved larger, stranger, or quieter than anyone involved could guarantee. The mystery is not that such things happened. The mystery is that we keep being surprised when they do.

Happy Halloween. 🎃🍬👻

text:
Democratic Secularism vs. Totalitarian Secularism

In the modern world, public opinion is often trapped in simplistic assumptions. We tend to believe that if a country is “secular,” it must necessarily be free and democratic, while if a state is “religious” or “theocratic,” it must be backward and undemocratic.

But if we look beyond political labels, we discover some of the most fascinating geopolitical paradoxes.

The British Example

Let me begin with the United Kingdom.

Britain is a country where the state is formally religious, yet its society is among the most secular and liberal in the world.

From a legal and institutional perspective, Britain is far from being a secular state:

An established church: The Church of England is the country's official state church.

The monarch as a religious leader: King Charles III is not only the Head of State but also the Supreme Governor of the Church of England and holds the historic title “Defender of the Faith.”

Clergy in Parliament: Twenty-six Anglican bishops, known as the Lords Spiritual, automatically hold seats in the House of Lords, without being elected, and participate in the country's legislative process.

Yet despite this seemingly medieval institutional arrangement, religion plays a remarkably limited role in the everyday lives of most British people.

Sociological research, including the respected British Social Attitudes survey, shows that:

The decline of religious identity: More than half of Britain's population, and over 60% of younger people, identify with no religion.

Liberal values: British society is broadly tolerant. The rights of marginalized communities, gender equality, access to abortion, and freedom of expression are widely accepted and protected.

Religious indifference: For many people, churches are primarily beautiful architectural landmarks, while Anglican ceremonies such as royal weddings and coronations are viewed as elements of national tradition and cultural heritage rather than expressions of religious doctrine.

Why does this system work peacefully?

The answer lies in British pragmatism.

Britain has effectively stripped its established church of political power. The Church retains symbolic and constitutional status, but it is not allowed to dictate how people live their private lives or interfere with their individual freedoms.

What matters is not simply what a country's constitution says, but the values upon which its society is built.

Britain is formally religious, yet practically free and liberal. North Korea, by contrast, is formally secular, yet in reality it is a totalitarian nightmare.

This paradox touches on one of the most fundamental questions in political science and sociology.

To understand it, we must recognize that secularization—the decline of religious influence—can occur through two fundamentally different processes: organic secularization and forced, totalitarian secularization.

1. The First Group: The Czech Republic, Scandinavia, the Netherlands, and Others — Organic Secularization

In these countries, the declining influence of religion was largely a natural consequence of social development.

The Enlightenment and institutions: Over centuries, these societies developed political and legal systems in which the rule of law, human rights, and individual freedom became fundamental values.

Prosperity and security: Sociological research, including the Inglehart-Welzel Cultural Map, suggests that the greater a country's economic security, social protection, and educational attainment, the less society depends on religion as a psychological or social support system.

The result: Society became secular because it became free. The state did not prohibit anyone from attending church. People simply made their own choices and voluntarily adopted a less religious way of life. Democracy and liberalism remained intact.

2. The Second Group: China, North Korea, and Azerbaijan — Forced and Political Secularization

In these countries, non-religiosity is not necessarily the result of people's free choices. Instead, it has been shaped by authoritarian or totalitarian state policies.

Eliminating ideological competition: In China and North Korea, communist regimes have historically used violence, repression, the destruction of religious institutions, and the imprisonment of believers to suppress religion. The logic is straightforward: a dictatorship does not want citizens who recognize an authority higher than the state ideology, whether that authority is God or the Church. It wants people whose ultimate loyalty belongs exclusively to the ruling party and its leader.

The Aliyev model in Azerbaijan: Here, we are dealing with a form of post-Soviet secular authoritarianism. Soviet state atheism weakened religion's social influence, while today's Aliyev regime uses secularism as a political shield: on the one hand, to contain political Islam and Iranian influence, and on the other, to present an image of “progressiveness” to the West.

The result: Society is less religious not necessarily because it is free, but because it is politically constrained. The state has forcefully replaced traditional religious authority with its own system of control.

Secularism is not a prerequisite for democracy. It is a byproduct of democracy only when it develops in an environment of freedom.

When a society becomes less religious through education, economic prosperity, and the expansion of individual freedoms, the result is Sweden or the Netherlands.

But when religion is suppressed by secret police, the military, and state propaganda, the result is North Korea or China.

The label may be the same—non-religiosity—but the underlying reality and purpose are radically different.

American Exceptionalism

The United States is one of the greatest exceptions in the Western world.

In sociology, the term “American Exceptionalism” is often used to describe the fact that the United States remains a highly developed, wealthy Western democracy with a population that is still remarkably religious, especially when compared with Europe.

1. The Free Market of Religious Freedom

Historically, most European countries had an established state church: Anglicanism in Britain, Catholicism in France, and Lutheranism across much of Scandinavia.

When Europeans began challenging the state in their struggle for freedom, they often came to reject the established churches as well.

The American experience was different.

The Founding Fathers prohibited the establishment of a state religion through the First Amendment to the Constitution.

As a result, America developed something resembling a free market of religion.

Since no single church enjoyed guaranteed state funding, religious institutions had to become flexible and competitive, much like businesses in a capitalist economy. They had to attract congregations and offer meaningful social, educational, and cultural programs.

This competition helped keep religion vibrant and attractive in American society.

2. Immigration and the Religious Motive

The United States — an ideological and religious foundation: Many of America's early European settlers, including Puritans and Quakers, were religious dissenters. They left Europe not simply to explore new territories or seek economic opportunities, but also to establish communities where they could practice their faith freely and, in some cases, build deeply religious societies inspired by the idea of a “City upon a Hill.”

Religion was one of the primary motivations behind significant waves of early American migration.

3. The Church as a Social Safety Net

European and Scandinavian countries developed what is known as the Welfare State.

The state provides education, healthcare, unemployment benefits, and social protection during times of crisis. As a result, people are less dependent on religious institutions for practical assistance.

The United States, by contrast, has a more capitalist and individualistic system, with a comparatively limited social safety net.

When people lose their jobs, face financial difficulties, or experience family tragedies, local religious communities often provide essential financial, psychological, and humanitarian support.

For many Americans, therefore, the church is not merely a spiritual institution. It is a practical pillar of everyday life.

4. Politicized Religion — The Religious Right

Beginning in the 1970s and 1980s, religion became increasingly intertwined with American politics, particularly with the Republican Party.

Powerful movements, such as the Moral Majority, emerged and turned religion into a major force in America's cultural wars over abortion, family values, and traditional social norms.

Religion increasingly became part of political identity.

For many conservative Americans, religious affiliation and patriotism became closely connected.

The United States had broken away from Britain through revolution and a bloody war. It rejected the old European ecclesiastical hierarchies and developed thousands of independent Protestant congregations and denominations, including Baptists, Methodists, and Pentecostals, many of which proved remarkably dynamic and resilient.

Yet, despite its deeply religious society, secularism and democracy continue to function in the United States because the country's political system was designed, in large part, by religious people seeking to protect their own freedom.

Unlike the European model, where secularism was often achieved through conflict with religion and anti-clericalism, American secularism is rooted in an entirely different philosophy.

Secularism as a Protector of Religion, Not Its Enemy

The American Founding Fathers—Jefferson, Madison, and Washington—had witnessed Europe's devastating religious wars, in which governments used state power to force people into belonging to particular churches.

They therefore established two fundamental principles in the First Amendment:

The Establishment Clause: The government cannot establish an official state religion or favor one religion over another.

The Free Exercise Clause: The government cannot prohibit or unduly interfere with the free exercise of religion.

American secularism was designed to prevent the state from interfering in religious affairs.

Religious groups themselves—Baptists, Catholics, Quakers, and others—had strong reasons to support a secular state. They understood that if the government were not religiously neutral, one powerful denomination could seize political control and begin persecuting the others.

In this sense, religious diversity itself created the need for a secular state.

2. Constructive Distrust and an Independent Judiciary

The American Constitution is built upon a profound distrust of human nature, an idea that has interesting parallels with the Christian doctrine of human sinfulness.

The Founding Fathers believed that any person—whether a president, judge, or priest—could become a tyrant if given absolute power.

That is why they created the unique system of Checks and Balances:

The executive branch (the President), the legislative branch (Congress), and the judiciary operate independently and limit one another's power.

Even when a religious majority attempts to pass discriminatory legislation, an independent Supreme Court can act as a constitutional safeguard, ensuring that the law remains subordinate to the Constitution rather than to the interests of a ruling party or religious majority.

3. Civil Religion

America also developed what sociologists call “Civil Religion.”

The Constitution, democratic institutions, and the very idea of freedom became almost sacred elements of national identity.

Even for a conservative Christian, the Constitution can carry an authority approaching that of a sacred text.

As a result, religious identity does not necessarily lead to opposition to democracy. On the contrary, many religious Americans see American democracy and individual liberty as a system blessed by God and therefore worthy of protection.

The secret of genuine democracy is not how religious or non-religious a society is, but how strong its institutions are.

If a country has an independent judiciary, a strong constitution, a free press, and a genuine separation of powers, its society can be deeply religious, like the United States, or highly secular, like Sweden, and still remain free and democratic.

But if these institutions do not exist and power is concentrated in the hands of one individual, the country will remain a tyranny—whether it is an Islamic theocracy like Iran or a secular dictatorship like North Korea or Azerbaijan.

The New Zealand Model

New Zealand fits remarkably well into the broader geopolitical and sociological model shared by Canada and Australia.

It is a country where society is highly secular and liberal, while its democratic institutions rank among the strongest and most trustworthy in the world.

New Zealand consistently ranks near the top internationally in democratic performance, low levels of corruption, and the protection of individual freedoms.

Unlike the United States, however, these achievements have developed alongside strong secular tendencies rather than a deeply religious public culture.

1. The Decline of Religious Majoritarianism

New Zealand's historical and cultural DNA is largely British, much like that of Australia and Canada. Consequently, it followed a path of gradual, organic secularization.

The decline of religion: Over recent decades, Christian identification has fallen significantly. According to recent census figures, approximately 48–50% of New Zealanders identify with no religion, making the non-religious the largest religious-identification category in the country.

The British model: Early migration to New Zealand was largely driven by the desire to settle new territories and pursue economic development, rather than by the ambition to establish an ultra-religious utopia, as was the case with some of the Puritan settlers in America.

2. Māori Culture and Integration

New Zealand's secularism has a unique local dimension that distinguishes it from Australia and the United States.

It is rooted partly in the Treaty of Waitangi and the deep integration of Māori culture into the country's public life.

Traditional Māori worldviews contain profound spiritual and animistic elements, emphasizing the relationship between people, nature, and the spiritual world. However, they do not necessarily operate through the same institutional structures as conventional organized religions.

New Zealand has developed an approach that recognizes and respects Māori spiritual traditions while grounding political decision-making in rational, liberal, and secular principles.

3. Strong Institutions

New Zealand has a strong independent judiciary, a free media environment, and a comparatively transparent public administration.

Its social consensus is built around social justice, equality, and the rule of law. People do not need to rely exclusively on religious institutions to feel socially protected and secure because an effective democratic state provides many of these functions.

New Zealand is therefore another classic example of the first category: a society in which freedom, education, and strong institutions have produced organic and peaceful secularization, without totalitarian violence or religious prohibitions.

The Icelandic Model

Iceland is another particularly fascinating—and arguably unique—example on this geopolitical and sociological map.

It combines elements of both the British and Scandinavian models: it has an officially established state church, yet its society is among the most secular and democratic in the world.

1. A Formal State Church vs. A Secular Society

Like Britain, Iceland has an established church. Under Article 62 of its Constitution, the Evangelical Lutheran Church is recognized as the national church and receives official state support and funding.

Yet the reality of everyday life tells a very different story.

“Nominal believers”: Approximately 56% of Icelanders are formally registered members of the National Church, a dramatic decline from around 92% in 1990. For many, this registration is primarily a matter of tradition and family background rather than active religious belief.

A generation of young atheists: Sociological surveys suggest that belief in the biblical account of creation is extremely uncommon among younger Icelanders. Scientific explanations of the origins of the universe, particularly the Big Bang theory, are widely accepted, while many young people openly identify as atheists or agnostics.

2. The Parish Tax (Sóknargjöld) and Neo-Paganism

Iceland has a special system of religious congregation contributions.

A small portion of each taxpayer's income tax is allocated to the religious organization with which that person is registered. If someone does not belong to a recognized religious organization, the corresponding funds are allocated through the state's designated system.

This arrangement has contributed to a particularly interesting phenomenon:

Ásatrú: Iceland has witnessed the revival of the ancient Norse pagan tradition, associated with Viking-era beliefs and deities such as Odin and Thor. Some people have left Christian institutions and registered with this organization as an alternative expression of religious or cultural identity.

3. Althingi — The Foundation of Democratic Tradition

Iceland is home to one of the world's oldest continuously operating parliamentary traditions: the Althingi, founded in 930 AD.

For Icelanders, democracy, equality, and the rule of law are not merely political concepts. They are fundamental elements of the country's national identity and historical survival.

Iceland is also a global leader in gender equality. It became the first country to introduce legislation requiring equal pay for men and women performing equal work, and it maintains strong public healthcare and education systems alongside very low levels of corruption.

The Peak of Organic Secularization

Iceland is one of the clearest examples of the first category: organic secularization.

Its society became increasingly non-religious not because someone destroyed its churches, as happened under totalitarian regimes, but largely through education, economic security, scientific progress, and changing social values.

The existence of an established state church does not prevent Iceland from being highly liberal and democratic because religion has very limited political power.

The church remains largely a cultural and traditional institution, while everyday public life is governed by strong, transparent, and accountable secular institutions.

The Bigger Picture: Institutions Matter More Than Labels

All of these examples demonstrate that official labels—“secular” or “theocratic”—can create a deeply misleading picture of how a country actually functions.

A state's freedom is not determined by the words written in its constitution, but by the strength of its democratic institutions and the values of its society.

If independent courts and respect for human rights exist, a political system can protect individual freedom equally well in officially religious London and officially secular Washington.

Conversely, when these institutions are absent, so-called secularism in China, North Korea, or Azerbaijan can become just as powerful an instrument of tyranny as religious fundamentalism.

Ultimately, the real dividing line is not between religious and secular societies. It is between free societies and authoritarian ones.

text:
Werner Herzog on "The Wheels on the Bus":
(Sound of wind, perhaps a distant, discordant hum)

"Observe the bus. A hulking metal carcass, commandeered by an unseen, perhaps nonexistent, intelligence. Its wheels, they turn, 'round and 'round, with a mindless, algorithmic insistence. This, they tell us, is the vehicle of civilization, ferrying its passengers towards an ever-receding horizon of promised destinations.

But who, one must ask, truly grips the wheel? Who navigates by the stars of emotional truth, by the magnetic north of accountability? The answer, I suspect, is a void, an empty driver's seat. The passengers, lulled into a state of bovine placidity, sing their 'merry song.' A song of conformity, a childish rhyme to drown out the grinding of gears, the screech of metal against metal as the chassis strains. The music, you see, is so very loud, designed to obscure the silence from the driver's seat, to mask the chilling truth that this colossus, this societal omnibus, might possess no functioning brakes.

And so it hurtles onward, 'round and 'round, or perhaps, in a terrifyingly straight line towards a precipice only a few dare to acknowledge. The landscape outside is a blur of fleeting distractions. Inside, the song drones on, a mantra of oblivion. The wheels, indifferent to the fate of their cargo, simply continue their rotation, a perfect, mechanical metaphor for a journey undertaken without wisdom, careening towards a future shaped not by conscious design, but by the blind, idiot force of unexamined momentum. One day, the singing will abruptly cease. If emotional intelligence is not taught to fix the brakes then I imagine the view from the window wont matter much anymore if the brakes on the bus aren't fixed as soon as possible."

...

Werner Herzog on "The Itsy-Bitsy Spider":
(Sound of dripping water, a faint, skittering noise)

"And then, we have the arachnid. The 'Itsy-Bitsy Spider.' A creature of almost ludicrous fragility, attempting its ascent up the 'waterspout' – this, we are told, is the grand edifice of societal norms, the slick, vertical promise of promotions, of accumulating currency. The spider, driven by some primal, unarticulated yearning, perhaps what it dimly perceives as 'up,' begins its climb. It is a creature already bearing the weight of an unseen burden – its emotional suffering, a private, internal weeping.

But societal structures, much like the indifferent plumbing of the universe, are not designed for such delicate ascents. The 'rain,' you see, is not mere water. It is the rotting accumulation of unprocessed human suffering within a collective that has systematically failed to educate its smallest members in the language of the heart, in emotional intelligence. It is the downpour of a thousand unmourned griefs, a torrent of unspoken anxieties, and it washes the spider out, a predictable, almost banal tragedy.

Then, the 'sun' appears – the so-called 'help.' A course of medication, perhaps, designed to numb the fall. Or the therapist, offering a different 'tube' to climb. Society, with a benign, almost patronizing smile, gestures towards a new structure. Perhaps it is no longer the waterspout of raw commerce, but a 'metal pole' of 'wellness,' of 'self-improvement.' Yet, this new edifice, for all its gleaming surfaces, shares the same flaws as the old. The spider, still unversed in emotional literacy, still carrying its residual emotional pain, attempts the climb again, with almost the same vulnerabilities as before.

The cycle is complete, only to begin anew. The climb, the rain, the fall, the superficial drying, the redirection to another treacherous ascent. The spider, in its Sisyphean toil, becomes the individual ensnared in systems that offer the illusion of progress, while the core deficit – the profound, societal neglect of emotional understanding – ensures each climb is merely a prelude to the next fall. The spout changes; the suffering, and the ignorance that perpetuates it, remain."

What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.
