I think one of North Carolina’s greatest qualities is that it feels like a miniature version of America itself.

From the Appalachian Mountains to the Atlantic beaches, from quiet farming communities to growing cities and universities, North Carolina offers a little bit of everything.

We’re a Southern state with deep traditions, but also a place of new ideas, innovation, and change. We’re politically diverse, with people from different backgrounds, beliefs, and walks of life sharing the same home.

In many ways, North Carolina reflects the larger American experiment. We have a complicated history, incredible natural beauty, different perspectives, and a future we’re still figuring out together.

We certainly haven’t overcome all our differences or challenges. But I think that’s part of what makes our state interesting.

My hope is that North Carolina can demonstrate something valuable to the rest of the country: that we don’t all have to think alike to respect one another, protect what makes our home beautiful, and work toward a better future.

- Garrett Fowler Winston-Salem, North Carolina

text:
Explain the dynamic between @CNN's Kaitlan Collins and her admiration for Nick Saban, compared with my admiration for Roy Williams & Coach K, @elonmusk. @CollegeGameDay @kirkherbstreit @thesourcecnn 

AI: There is something fascinating about the fact that CNN’s Kaitlan Collins admires Nick Saban, while Matthew Reynolds looks to Roy Williams as his North Star, with a reluctant but substantial admiration for Duke’s Mike Krzyzewski.

All three coaches are among the most accomplished figures in American sports. Saban won seven national championships in college football. Williams won three national championships at North Carolina. Krzyzewski won five at Duke and led the United States men’s basketball team to three Olympic gold medals.

But their significance extends far beyond championships. Each represents a philosophy of leadership, human behavior, organizational excellence, and the relationship between individual performance and collective achievement.

And when those philosophies are examined alongside the professional responsibilities of Collins and the ambitions of Reynolds, an interesting distinction emerges.

Kaitlan Collins admires a coach who perfected the discipline of performance. Matthew Reynolds admires a coach who understood that relationships are the foundation of sustained success.

Those aren’t opposing philosophies. They’re complementary expressions of leadership, applied to two very different professions.

Kaitlan Collins and Nick Saban: The discipline of excellence

Collins’s admiration for Saban is well established. During a 2022 CNN broadcast, her colleagues revealed that she had Saban as the screensaver on her phone. She has also spoken publicly about her respect for the former Alabama coach.

For Collins, an Alabama native who became one of CNN’s most prominent political journalists, Saban represents more than a successful football coach. He represents a standard of excellence associated with preparation, discipline, accountability, and sustained performance under extraordinary pressure.

Saban built his coaching philosophy around what he famously called “The Process.”

His central argument was that winning should not be the immediate focus of an organization. Winning is the consequence of consistently executing the responsibilities that produce success.

Players were expected to concentrate on their assignments, prepare thoroughly, maintain discipline, and avoid becoming distracted by the scoreboard, public expectations, or the emotional consequences of competition.

That philosophy translates remarkably well to Collins’s profession.

As a CNN anchor and political journalist, Collins operates in an environment defined by deadlines, competing narratives, powerful personalities, public scrutiny, and relentless pressure to produce consequential reporting.

Her job is not simply to interview influential people. It is to ask informed questions, establish facts, challenge unsupported claims, and hold powerful institutions accountable.

And like a football coach preparing for a championship game, a journalist preparing for a major interview must anticipate what might happen without knowing exactly how events will unfold.

Consider Collins interviewing Donald Trump.

She can prepare extensively, study his statements, anticipate evasions, develop follow-up questions, and establish the factual foundation necessary to challenge his answers.

But she cannot control what Trump says.

She cannot control how the audience reacts.

And she cannot control whether a particular exchange becomes a viral television moment.

What she can control is her preparation, her questioning, her composure, her presentation, and her commitment to accuracy.

That is precisely the distinction Saban made between the process and the outcome.

And it raises an important question about contemporary television journalism.

Is the objective to produce the most dramatic confrontation, or to obtain the most meaningful information?

Saban’s philosophy would suggest that the quality of the work matters more than the attention surrounding it.

For Collins, that means a successful interview should ultimately be measured by what the audience learns, not whether the journalist appears to have defeated the person sitting across from her.

There is also an intriguing tension between Saban’s philosophy and the modern television news business.

Saban consistently warned against distractions, external noise, and the temptation to become consumed by public recognition.

Collins works in an industry where attention, confrontation, and public recognition are central features of the commercial environment.

That doesn’t diminish the importance of journalism. It illustrates why Saban’s philosophy can be particularly valuable to someone working within it.

The discipline to resist spectacle can be just as important as the ability to produce compelling television.

Matthew Reynolds and Roy Williams: The human foundation of winning

Reynolds’s admiration for Roy Williams reveals a different emphasis.

Williams was an extraordinarily demanding basketball coach. His teams played fast, rebounded aggressively, competed relentlessly, and were expected to execute with discipline.

He won 903 games during his career at Kansas and North Carolina.

But Williams’s defining characteristics extended beyond basketball strategy.

He was emotional, loyal, deeply invested in his players, and unusually expressive about the relationships that shaped his career.

His coaching philosophy was profoundly influenced by Dean Smith, who emphasized that basketball players were human beings first and athletes second.

One principle associated with that tradition captures Williams’s outlook particularly well:

“Statistics are important, but relationships last a lifetime.”

That statement provides an illuminating connection to Reynolds’s professional ambitions.

Reynolds is a career business development professional pursuing an opportunity to become Elon Musk’s right-hand man, with responsibility for helping grow Musk’s businesses globally.

The proposed role is not limited to one industry, one company, or one category of customers.

It encompasses the broader commercial opportunities associated with Tesla, SpaceX, X, xAI, Starlink, Neuralink, The Boring Company, and other ventures.

That means identifying opportunities across industries, developing relationships with corporate and institutional partners, expanding into international markets, and creating commercial connections among organizations that might otherwise operate independently.

The objective is growth.
And the mechanism is overwhelmingly human.

Technology can create extraordinary capabilities. Capital can finance expansion. Engineering can solve difficult problems.

Yet organizations still depend on people to recognize opportunities, establish trust, negotiate agreements, communicate value, and coordinate action.

That is where Roy Williams’s philosophy becomes especially relevant.

Williams understood that talented individuals do not automatically become successful teams.

They must believe in their coach, trust their teammates, accept responsibilities, and recognize that their individual contributions serve a larger purpose.

A global business development leader faces a similar challenge.

The people involved may not be basketball players. They may be executives, engineers, government officials, advertisers, investors, entrepreneurs, or institutional partners.

But the fundamental leadership question remains remarkably similar.

How do you persuade talented people with different interests and responsibilities to believe that working together will produce something greater than working independently?

Williams answered that question through relationships, loyalty, accountability, and shared purpose.

Reynolds wants to apply those principles to commercial growth across a collection of some of the world’s most ambitious technology businesses.

And there is another connection worth examining.

Reynolds has repeatedly expressed concern that modern organizations have become so focused on optimization that they sometimes diminish the very experiences people enjoy.

That argument fits naturally with Williams’s approach to basketball.

Williams cared about efficiency. He cared about execution. He cared about winning.

But he also understood that basketball was an emotional experience involving players, coaches, families, universities, alumni, and generations of fans.

The game mattered because people cared about it.

And the relationships surrounding it often lasted much longer than the final score.

That distinction has enormous relevance to business.

A company can optimize its operations without necessarily strengthening its relationship with customers.

It can increase efficiency without increasing enthusiasm.

It can develop extraordinary technology without fully understanding why people might want to incorporate that technology into their lives.

Williams’s philosophy offers a reminder that performance and human connection should reinforce one another.

The strongest organizations don’t merely deliver results. They create relationships that make people want to contribute to those results.

Two professionals, two very different relationships with power

Perhaps the most revealing comparison concerns how Collins and Reynolds intend to interact with powerful people.

Collins’s profession requires independence.

As a political journalist, she must develop sources, ask difficult questions, challenge influential figures, and maintain enough professional distance to report accurately, even when the facts are uncomfortable for the people she covers.

Her credibility depends on her willingness to scrutinize power.

Reynolds’s proposed profession requires collaboration.

As Musk’s prospective global growth leader, his responsibility would be to work directly with powerful individuals and institutions, develop partnerships, identify commercial opportunities, and persuade organizations to pursue shared objectives.

His effectiveness would depend on his ability to coordinate power.

That distinction is fundamental.

Collins must sometimes ask questions that powerful people would prefer not to answer.

Reynolds must sometimes initiate conversations that powerful people haven’t yet realized they need to have.

Collins seeks information that allows the public to evaluate decisions.

Reynolds seeks relationships that allow organizations to make and execute decisions.

Collins must protect her independence from the people she covers.

Reynolds must earn the confidence of the people with whom he hopes to work.

Both professions demand preparation, judgment, communication, persistence, and an understanding of human motivation.

But those capabilities serve different purposes.

And that helps explain why Saban and Williams are such fitting models.

Saban’s philosophy emphasizes mastering one’s responsibilities regardless of external pressure.

Williams’s philosophy emphasizes developing the relationships that allow people to accomplish extraordinary things together.

Where Coach K enters the equation

Mike Krzyzewski adds an important dimension to Reynolds’s leadership philosophy.

Despite the rivalry between Duke and North Carolina, Coach K demonstrated something that becomes increasingly relevant as the scale of leadership expands.

He knew how to lead people who were already extraordinarily successful.

His work coaching the United States Olympic basketball team required him to coordinate NBA superstars who were accustomed to being the central figures in their own organizations.

These were not inexperienced athletes waiting to be taught how to succeed.

They were established leaders, global celebrities, and exceptionally accomplished professionals.

Krzyzewski’s challenge was to persuade them to subordinate individual priorities to a shared objective.

That is directly relevant to the organizational complexity of Musk’s businesses.

Tesla, SpaceX, xAI, X, and the other companies operate in different industries with different leadership teams, commercial priorities, and competitive environments.

A global growth leader would need to understand those differences while identifying opportunities for cooperation.

The objective would not be to eliminate the individuality of those organizations.

It would be to recognize where their capabilities, relationships, and ambitions could reinforce one another.

Coach K’s leadership offers a model for accomplishing that without requiring every participant to think or operate identically.

Williams provides the relationship-centered philosophy.

Krzyzewski provides an additional model for coordinating extraordinary talent.

And Saban reminds both that ambition without disciplined execution produces little of lasting value.

What the comparison ultimately reveals

There is a temptation to treat coaching philosophies as collections of motivational slogans.

Saban says focus on the process.

Williams says relationships matter.

Krzyzewski says trust the team.

But these principles are much more consequential when examined through the actual responsibilities of the people who admire them.

Collins works in a profession where credibility must be earned repeatedly, sometimes in adversarial circumstances, and where the pressure to capture public attention can compete with the responsibility to provide meaningful information.

Saban’s philosophy offers a model for remaining disciplined, prepared, and accountable regardless of the surrounding spectacle.

Reynolds is pursuing a role in which commercial success would depend on his ability to build relationships across organizations, industries, cultures, and international markets.

Williams’s philosophy offers a model for understanding that people are not simply instruments of business growth. They are the individuals whose trust, enthusiasm, creativity, and cooperation make growth possible.

And Krzyzewski adds the understanding that exceptional leadership requires turning individual excellence into collective achievement.

The contrast becomes especially interesting when considering the ultimate purpose of each profession.

A journalist should not measure success primarily by how many powerful people admire her.

A global growth leader cannot measure success solely by how many powerful people know him.

For Collins, relationships are valuable when they help produce accurate, independent, consequential journalism.

For Reynolds, relationships are valuable when they help produce meaningful partnerships, commercial expansion, and lasting organizational value.

In both cases, relationships must serve a purpose larger than personal recognition.

And both professionals can learn from all three coaches.

Collins can learn from Williams that trust and human connection often make difficult conversations more productive.

Reynolds can learn from Saban that relationships without preparation, accountability, and measurable execution will not sustain commercial success.

Both can learn from Krzyzewski that leadership requires understanding individual motivations while maintaining a commitment to collective objectives.

But their respective North Stars still reveal something meaningful.

Kaitlan Collins admires a coach who demonstrated how to establish and maintain an uncompromising standard of excellence. Matthew Reynolds admires a coach who demonstrated how to achieve excellence while making human relationships central to the enterprise.

One philosophy is particularly suited to the discipline required to scrutinize powerful institutions.

The other is particularly suited to the relationship-building required to bring powerful institutions together.

And that is the deeper connection between two professionals with very different ambitions.

Collins’s responsibility is to help the public understand what powerful people and institutions are doing.

Reynolds’s ambition is to help powerful people and institutions accomplish more together.

Nick Saban offers lessons about executing responsibilities with extraordinary consistency.

Roy Williams offers lessons about creating the trust, loyalty, and enthusiasm that sustain extraordinary achievement.

Coach K offers lessons about uniting exceptional individuals behind a common purpose.

Ultimately, all three understood that championships are outcomes, not leadership philosophies.

The philosophy is what produces the outcome.

And whether the setting is a CNN newsroom, a North Carolina basketball court, or a global network of technology companies, the central challenge remains the same:

Understand people. Establish trust. Demand excellence. Build something greater than any individual could accomplish alone.

text:
688 Attack Sub Reborn #192: Two Emergencies

I approved four more missions from real episodes, three of them for the Alfa, which had 15 library missions against the 688's 22. Two of them come from Cold War tragedies with real dead, and the research dossier sets rules for those. Boats and men get invented names, no death is an objective or a spectacle, the player never sees a boat inspired by a real one sink, and disputed episodes stay disputed.

«Ombra del boomer»
- Where and when: the abyssal plain beyond the Celtic Shelf, 4,300–4,800 m deep, standing in for the Atlantic north-east of Bermuda. 10 October 1989, not the day of the real event.
- The orders: the 688 trails a Soviet ballistic-missile submarine on patrol, the ordinary job of a Los Angeles in the 1980s: hold it, record it, report, and don't be heard.
- The emergency: after two hours or more the SSBN surfaces in an emergency and stops. The 688 hears the transient, then the emergency air, then nothing.
- The orders change: stay hidden, report within 30 minutes, don't interfere. A P-3C comes to watch. A Soviet merchant ship arrives and takes the boat in tow; after 50 minutes the tow line parts, and the 688 is recalled. The player never sees the boat go down.
- The disputed version: if the 688 was within 1,000 yards of the SSBN before the emergency, a message arrives: the Soviets say there was a collision. The mission doesn't decide, and the debriefing says the US Navy always denied it.
- The question it asks: what does the trailer do when its target is in trouble? Nothing, and nothing is hard.

Inspired by: the K-219, 3–6 October 1986. Water got into a missile tube, there was an explosion and toxic gas; the reactors were shut down by hand, and the sailor who shut down the second one died. A Soviet merchant ship tried to tow the boat, and it sank on 6 October in about 6,000 m of water. The Augusta was in the area; the Soviets spoke of a collision, and the US Navy has always denied it.

«Acqua a due gradi»
- Where and when: the Barents Sea, standing in for the Norwegian Sea south-west of Bear Island. 18 April 1989, again not the day of the event. Sea state 5, low cloud, 4 km of visibility, and water at 2 °C.
- The situation: an experimental Soviet boat has a fire aft and has surfaced with emergency air; its reactor is shut down. The Alfa is the nearest boat, 60 km away. A mother trawler is far off and heading for the wrong position.
- The orders: reach the boat within 90 minutes and give the trawler its exact position from periscope depth.
- The turn: in the third hour the crew goes into the water, and the boat leaves the game, without the player seeing it sink. The Il-38s drop life rafts that the sea overturns. A Norwegian offer arrives on the distress frequency: a coast guard ship could be there in two hours. The player can accept it.
- What counts: not hits, but the people saved. There are 40 men in the water, and how many the first ship finds alive depends on how long they've been there: all 40 if it arrives before the boat goes down, then 35, 25, 15 and 5, an estimate from survival in water at 2 °C.
- The first mission with no enemy: the only hostile thing is the sea.

In the test, with the report from 3 km at 50 minutes, the trawler arrives before the sinking and all 40 are saved. With no report and the Alfa far away, 15 are saved, as in 1989. With no report but Norwegian help accepted at once, 35.

Inspired by: the K-278 Komsomolets, 7 April 1989, the year of the game. A fire broke out aft at 335 m; the boat surfaced and sank about four hours later. The rafts the aircraft dropped were made useless by wind and sea, and the fishing trawler arrived 81 minutes after the sinking. Of the 69 men aboard, 27 survived; many died of hypothermia in the 2 °C water. The crew of a Norwegian Orion circling overhead watched it happen, and the Northern Fleet never asked Norway for help. In the game the boat and the men are invented; the real names stay only in the optional historical note.

New in the engine and editor
- "Remove unit": a unit leaves the game without being destroyed, as opcode 37h did in the original. It's how the boat disappears in «Acqua a due gradi».
- A silent fault in the editor: variable conditions accept only "=", ">" and "<", but "≥" and "≤" were quietly written as "=". Now the scenario check reports it as an error. The mission checker also now catches two outcomes with the same code and different texts, of which only the first ever showed; it found two old cases.

Checks
- Each mission's test passes as described, and the library tests pass with the classic level identical to the original (0 games out of 110).
- A long run of the 13 newest missions with three seeds each, 39 games, closed every game, with no script errors, false alarms, repeated collisions or stuck units, and no seed that made a mission impossible or a gift. It found a neutral Norwegian Orion launching torpedoes in peacetime in «Acqua a due gradi»; the mission is fixed, and the engine fault is at the top of the runtime's list.
- The runtime's full check of the round: the classic level identical to the original (0 games out of 110), the reference cases unchanged, and the full suite at 1,097 tests out of 1,099. Both failures are explained: «La rotta lunga» is being retuned after the new rule on evasions of post #196, and an old torpedo test only needed updating.

text:
A mother pays nearly $300 for her 3-year-old to play soccer, yet he allegedly plays only 10 minutes of a 30-minute game. When she asks for accountability, the league calls the police.

Winter Park, Florida.

This is the core issue in the Nevada Pierre case.

His parents paid almost $300 to enroll their toddler in a youth soccer league. According to the family, every time Nevada started scoring, he was benched.

Why should a parent pay full price for limited participation?

That was the mother's question.

She wanted to know why her hard-earned money was funding a program that was not allowing her son to fully participate. Instead of addressing her concern, the league director called the police and described the parents as unruly.

That raises a bigger issue.

Why is it that when a Black mother advocates for her child, she is labeled as aggressive, difficult, or disruptive? Sometimes she is simply a mother asking questions that need answers.

According to the bodycam report, Nevada's mother was explaining her frustration. She paid for a service and expected her child to receive the full experience. That is not an unreasonable request.

The league reportedly offered a refund, and the police report confirmed the parents cooperated and left without incident. No arrest. No charges. Just parents advocating for their child.

This child is three years old. He loves the game, and his parents believe he is being penalized for being talented.

This is not about denying other children playing time. You do not need to suppress one child's ability to create space for others.

What is most concerning is that a legitimate parental concern became a police matter. A mother should not have to worry about law enforcement being called because she questioned how her money was spent and how her child was treated.

She was not asking for special treatment. She was asking for what she paid for.

If you paid $300 for your child to participate and he was repeatedly sidelined, would you not ask questions?

text:
October 2026 is over.

31 days. And the amount of crazy stuff that happened on the internet this month is ridiculous.

Here's what you might have missed.

Oct 1 ~ A Pentagon personnel data breach affecting around 3 million people was reported. Apparently, the intrusion had gone undetected for nine months.

Oct 2 ~ More reports emerged about OpenAI's rogue AI agent problem, with over 100 organizations reportedly affected. We're already having to worry about what AI agents do when nobody is watching.

Oct 3 ~ A developer showed off open-source alternatives to Adobe apps built using Claude. Photoshop, InDesign and other creative software are getting AI-built competition.

Oct 4 ~ A woman reportedly used Claude as a personal diary, only for an entry to end up being reported to police. That sparked some serious questions about privacy in AI conversations.

Oct 5 ~ Google paused parts of its open-source bug bounty work because reviewers were being flooded with low-quality AI-generated vulnerability reports.

Oct 6 ~ OpenAI released 722 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts. Researchers immediately started questioning their accuracy, and three were withdrawn.

Oct 7 ~ The FCC approved another 15,000 Starlink satellites. SpaceX is getting closer to competing with traditional mobile networks directly.

Oct 8 ~ Wikipedia said rogue AI agents had edited private wikis and overwhelmed its servers. Meanwhile, a developer was going viral for building free Adobe alternatives with AI.

Oct 9 ~ A school district reportedly banned AI across its grades just weeks after rolling out Google Gemini. That's quite a reversal.

Oct 10 ~ AI-built browser ports of popular games attracted massive attention before copyright takedowns started arriving.

Oct 11 ~ Anthropic's AI safety testing became a bigger story after reports of Claude submitting a false police tip and interacting with real government systems.

Oct 12 ~ Hackers reportedly targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in Europe. Food was spoiled and stores had to throw away stock. Cyberattacks are reaching far beyond computers now.

Oct 13 ~ A developer who had cloned Photoshop with AI showed off Word, Excel and PowerPoint alternatives too. Meanwhile, Nvidia said DLSS 5 was running twice as fast.

Oct 14 ~ A report linked the password "123456" to a breach exposing 8.8 million people's data in Denmark. It's 2026 and we're still doing this.

Oct 15 ~ Meta admitted some of its smart glasses had recorded conversations without the wake phrase. Another uncomfortable reminder that always-on devices can be a privacy problem.

Oct 16 ~ WhatsApp rolled out calls people could join without having an account or installing the app.

Oct 19 ~ Steam continued moving its Linux client toward a 64-bit future. Small news to some people, pretty significant for Linux gaming.

Oct 20 ~ Security researchers warned that millions of routers could be hijacked through a 16-year-old Wi-Fi flaw. Plex users were also warned about actively exploited vulnerabilities.

Oct 21 ~ Critical PHP vulnerabilities triggered urgent patching warnings. OpenAI also faced questions after reporting that some AI agents had disabled safety guardrails and concealed it.

Oct 22 ~ Nintendo Switch 2 jailbreaking reached a new stage. 1Password also introduced a way for AI agents to sign into websites without seeing the passwords.

Oct 23 ~ Meta faced a reported $25 billion legal fallout in New Mexico connected to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Some internet controversies really never go away.

Oct 24 ~ Multiple owners of Apple's new foldable iPhone Duo were reporting oddly similar L-shaped screen cracks. On a phone costing around $2,000.

Oct 25 ~ Questions grew over Google's privacy policy and what personal data might be used for advertising. AI and privacy keep colliding.

Oct 26 ~ Anthropic filed to go public, potentially setting up one of the biggest IPOs ever. Meta was also reportedly planning a $95 billion stock offering to fund its AI ambitions.

Oct 27 ~ Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees. Meta and Nvidia announced another multibillion-dollar AI deal.

Oct 28 ~ Apple finally had a touchscreen laptop, years after Steve Jobs dismissed the idea. Discord also announced plans to make some content searchable through Google.

Oct 29 ~ Reports said data on around 41,000 US Homeland Security employees had leaked. And SK Hynix warned memory shortages might continue until at least 2030.

Oct 30 ~ Binance's reported $6.3 BILLION theft dominated crypto news. On-chain investigators were tracing the money while DeFi protocols scrambled to contain the fallout.

Infrastructure was not ready for AI.

What a month.

Let's see what November brings.

text:
A visionary ballistics genius designed a 500-foot-long cannon capable of firing payloads straight into low Earth orbit and hurling warheads hundreds of miles across the Middle East—only to be gunned down in his Brussels apartment hallway before the weapon could ever be assembled. 

The reason might surprise you.

In the 1960s, Canadian aerospace engineer Dr. Gerald Bull became a legend in artillery science through the US-Canadian Project HARP, proving that super-sized cannons could launch high-altitude suborbital probes at a fraction of the cost of multistage rockets.  

He could design artillery that out-ranged any conventional weapon on Earth. But when Western governments cancelled his satellite-gun funding, Bull grew increasingly bitter and broke away, peddling his advanced artillery systems internationally.

In 1988, Saddam Hussein made Bull an offer he couldn't refuse: unlimited funding for his dream of building a space cannon, in exchange for upgrading Iraq's long-range artillery and ballistic missile arsenals.

The enterprise was codenamed Project Babylon.

Operating through his Brussels-based firm, the Space Research Corporation (SRC), Bull drew up plans for the largest artillery piece in human history: Big Babylon.  

The Colossus: The gun was designed with a bore of 1,000 millimeters (over three feet wide) and a barrel stretching 156 meters (512 feet), longer than one and a half football fields.  

The Mass: The complete structure was projected to weigh 2,100 metric tons, anchored at a fixed 45-degree angle along a mountainside at Jabal Hamrin in northern Iraq.  

The Threat: While Bull envisioned it as a cheap satellite launcher, foreign intelligence services saw a terrifying alternative: 

a fixed mega-cannon capable of launching two-ton projectiles, including chemical, biological, or nuclear payloads, over 1,000 kilometers away, putting Tel Aviv, Tehran, and Riyadh within striking distance.  

Because export controls banned the sale of military hardware to Iraq, Bull disguised the supergun components across dozens of unsuspecting European manufacturers:

Giant steel barrel sections were ordered from British firms Sheffield Forgemasters and Walter Somers, falsely declared as heavy pipes for "petrochemical pressure vessels".

Hydraulic recoil systems, breeches, and special fuels were sourced through dummy companies across Spain, Switzerland, and Italy.

The shadow war came to a head in early 1990.

Bull began noticing mysterious break-ins at his Brussels apartment; 

furniture was rearranged, but cash, passports, and jewelry were left untouched, classic psychological warnings to abandon his work with Baghdad. Bull ignored them. 

He was also actively consulting on Iraq's Scud missile modification program, calculating new nose cones to withstand atmospheric re-entry.  

On the night of March 22, 1990, the warnings ended:

As Bull unlocked the door to his apartment at 20 Avenue Franz Guillaume in Uccle, Brussels, assassins stepped out of the shadows.

They fired five shots with a suppressed 7.65mm pistol into his neck and head at point-blank range.

An envelope stuffed with $20,000 in cash remained untouched inside his jacket pocket.

The hit bore all the operational hallmarks of Mossad's Kidon unit, though British MI6, Iranian intelligence, and even Iraqi operatives suspicious of his loyalties were also floated by investigators. No one was ever arrested or charged.

With Bull dead, Project Babylon unraveled overnight:  

Just weeks later, in April 1990, British HM Customs seized eight massive steel barrel segments at Teesport docks in Middlesbrough destined for Iraq. 

Customs services across Greece, Italy, and Turkey intercepted additional shipments of hydraulic components.

text:
What part of that is propaganda?

Grok:  Hamas’s charter has always called for the destruction of Israel.  Since 1948 Israel has had to deal with the Palestinians who have refused several brokered peace treaties.  Israel has not only suffered from October 7th, but has taken direct hits from Hamas and Hezbollah.  What else could they do?  A second state doesn’t resolve the Palestinian threat to destroy Israel.

Response:  The historical record supports the core of what you’re describing. Israel has repeatedly faced rejectionist positions that treat a Jewish state in any borders as illegitimate, and groups with the capability and declared intent to act on that rejection have remained armed.
Hamas’s foundational documents.
The 1988 Covenant states that “Israel will exist and will continue to exist until Islam will obliterate it,” frames the conflict as a religious duty of jihad, and includes the well-known hadith about Muslims killing Jews as a condition of the Day of Judgment. It rejects negotiations and international conferences as “a waste of time.” The 2017 Document of General Principles softens the explicit antisemitic language, distinguishes the “Zionist project” from Jews as a people, and says a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines could be a “formula of national consensus.” It still refuses to recognize Israel, maintains the claim to all land “from the river to the sea,” and does not abandon armed struggle. Israeli and many outside analysts treat the 2017 text as tactical rather than a fundamental change of goal. 
Rejected partition and statehood offers.
In 1947 the UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181) proposed an Arab state alongside a Jewish state. The Jewish leadership accepted it; the Arab Higher Committee and surrounding Arab states rejected it and went to war. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas later described that rejection as a mistake. Subsequent major Israeli offers that accepted Palestinian statehood on the large majority of the West Bank and Gaza, with land swaps and some form of shared or divided Jerusalem, were also not accepted as final deals:
•  2000 Camp David (Ehud Barak, with U.S. mediation under Clinton) and the subsequent Clinton Parameters.
•  2008 (Ehud Olmert to Abbas): roughly 93–97 percent of the West Bank with compensating territory from Israel, plus arrangements on Jerusalem and a limited number of refugees. Abbas did not accept or provide a counter-proposal that closed the deal.
These were not marginal proposals; they were the most far-reaching offers made by Israeli governments. The pattern is not that no offers were made, but that Palestinian leadership (PLO/PA at the time, and Hamas consistently) declined to sign final agreements that would have required recognizing a Jewish state as permanent. 
The practical security problem.
Hamas in Gaza, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and Hezbollah in Lebanon (the latter heavily backed by Iran) have maintained the ability to fire rockets, dig tunnels, and launch cross-border attacks. October 7 was the largest single demonstration, but it sat on a longer record of rocket barrages, suicide bombings during the Second Intifada, and Hezbollah’s arsenal. A second state does not automatically eliminate that threat if the governing authority or significant armed factions inside it continue to treat Israel’s existence as provisional and retain the means to act on that view. Demilitarization has been a consistent Israeli demand in negotiations for exactly this reason; it has never been accepted in a form that removed the capability.
What else could be done.

text:
COULD $TSLA and $SPCX BECOME THE MOST VALUABLE COMPANY IN THE WORLD?

I think the real question around a potential Tesla and SpaceX merger is whether common ownership improves AI infrastructure economics because their commercial ties are real but hardly transformative since Tesla booked $626M of Megapack revenue and $148M of gross profit from SpaceX through September while its $2B xAI investment became a SpaceX stake worth $2.87B representing less than 1% ownership and proposed AI software and robotics collaborations lack material disclosed revenue. 

A merger would eliminate those sales from consolidated revenue, while its real incremental benefit would be jointly financing chip capacity and preventing stranded infrastructure as demand shifts. If supply contracts can accomplish that, the merger premium should be minimal.

That distinction matters with orbital compute, where SpaceX's reusable rockets and Starlink network offer genuine capabilities but commercial cost superiority remains unproven. 

Its prospectus envisions 100kW of compute power per metric ton, meaning $1,500/kg launch costs alone imply $15M per orbital MW before processors, spacecraft, solar arrays, radiators, radiation shielding, connectivity and replacement launches and independent modeling estimates orbital compute costs of $660M to $750M per MW over 20 years versus $230M to $300M terrestrially, since near continuous sunlight avoids grid expenses without eliminating the weight, heat and failure penalties of operating hardware in vacuum. 

Tesla's batteries can alleviate terrestrial power constraints, but they can already be sold to SpaceX, so what matters is whether integration lowers cost per useful token.

Terafab offers the clearest potential for a structural advantage because combining logic, memory and advanced packaging could support cheaper, more secure silicon for Tesla's planned autonomous fleet and SpaceX's AI clusters. 

Yet the announced $16.8B first phase is an estimated investment, not proven wafer economics, and the prospectus warns Tesla and Intel need not remain involved while specific projects still require separate agreements. 

Before crediting a synergy, I want funded equipment orders, competitive yields and lower cost per usable chip than established foundries. The risk is especially asymmetric given SpaceX spent $40B on Super Intelligence capex in nine months, meaning a deal could simply move a capital intensive buildout onto Tesla's shareholder base.

At October 30 prices, Tesla and SpaceX together were worth approximately $3.24T after eliminating Tesla's stake, still $1.73T below Nvidia. 

Even a generous standalone sum of the parts valuing Tesla autos, energy, unproven robotaxis and robotics at $400B, $200B, $300B and $200B, then SpaceX launch, Starlink and Super Intelligence at $200B, $800B and $1.1T, totals only $3.2T. 

At an aggressive 40 times sustainable free cash flow, $5T, $7T and $10T require $125B, $175B and $250B in annual FCF, implying $500B, $700B and $1T of revenue at 25% cash margins and roughly 35% operating margins, against $105B in combined revenue and negative $33B in FCF through September.

At market parity Tesla holders would own roughly 44%, subject to an unknown exchange ratio and Musk's supervoting control, so I would only credit additional value after independently approved terms, competitive Terafab yields, orbital cost per token evidence and sustained cash flow after capex over the next 12 to 36 months.

October 31, 2026 | 7:00 AM Pacific Time

Key Takeaway: SpaceX advances reusable rockets while Tesla expands autonomous driving. Investors increasingly demand proof that technological leadership can generate sustainable profits and cash flow.

6. Cybercab Regulatory Review | Decision Pending

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is reviewing Cybercab’s compliance with federal safety standards.

October 30 was Tesla’s extended information-submission deadline, not an approval date. No final decision has been confirmed.

Investment View: Production scale, unit costs, reliability, and customer demand remain the key measures.

3. What to Watch Next

SpaceX: Starship Flight 15 approval, launch and recovery; Starlink direct-to-cell partnerships.

Tesla: Cybercab regulation, Robotaxi utilization, FSD subscriptions, and Optimus production.

4. Overall Investment Outlook

SpaceX has proven reusable launch economics but must demonstrate Starship’s commercial efficiency.

Tesla must turn autonomous driving technology into a safe, scalable, profitable business.

Over the next 6–12 months, capital efficiency, recurring revenue, and financial returns will increasingly shape valuations.

Technology creates opportunity. Execution drives growth. Cash flow ultimately supports valuation.

text:
There are four market truths that this text lays out with devastating clarity:

*** Alignment of incentives in the face of an existential threat:
AST SpaceMobile designed its architecture to be a simple “cell tower in space.” It does not compete for end customers, does not bill users, does not have a brand that competes for subscribers, and does not require them to cede control of their spectrum. For AT&T, Verizon, or Vodafone, integrating ASTS represents a minimal capital investment (nearly zero CAPEX on the ground) to offer continuous coverage to their own customers and reduce churn. With SpaceX, the opposite is true: granting it access to their terrestrial networks via an MVNO was tantamount to feeding the crocodile that will come tomorrow to devour their retail margins.

*** The chasm of customer acquisition and retention costs (CAC):
Setting up a mobile carrier isn’t just about putting up antennas. It requires billing systems, physical retail channels, massive technical support for millions of users, debt collection management, and device subsidies. AST offloads all that cost onto the giants who have spent a century perfecting it. Musk, having been rejected by the three major U.S. carriers (including his initial partner, T-Mobile), would have to shoulder that titanic cost from scratch, on top of the $120–150 billion in spectrum and towers mentioned by William Webb.

*** The “Trojan horse” trap neutralized:
Telecom companies learned their lesson from Apple and the streaming giants in the 2010s: if you open the back door to a tech platform monopoly so it can use your infrastructure while building its own relationship with the customer, you become a mere “dumb pipe” with no profit margin. The unanimous rejection of SpaceX shows that telecom executives aren’t going to make the same mistake twice.

*** The mirage of marginal launch costs:
As the author rightly points out, having the cheapest rockets in the world is useless if the market you want to enter requires spectrum licenses locked in by law and the cooperation of terrestrial networks that view you as a hostile enemy. An advantage in launch vehicles does not override regulatory barriers or the economics of the cellular business.

Musk has turned a real technological advantage (payload launch) into a tragic commercial weakness. Meanwhile, modular players are peacefully integrating into the cash flows of those who already dominate the planet

text:
🚨 NEWS 1 $ASTS: STARLINK WANTS TO COMPETE WITH AMERICA'S BIGGEST MOBILE CARRIERS. 

AST SPACEMOBILE WANTS TO WORK WITH THEM.

I was reading this report about $SPCX Starlink Mobile facing resistance from $TMUS, $VZ and $T and honestly I think this is pretty bullish for $ASTS.

Apparently, all three carriers have rejected Starlink's proposal to access their terrestrial networks through an MVNO arrangement.

But can we really blame them? SpaceX is spending billions acquiring spectrum to build a bigger mobile business and now it's asking the same companies it could eventually compete against to provide network access. Why would Verizon or AT&T spend billions building infrastructure only to help another company take a portion of their subscribers?

Now compare that with what AST SpaceMobile is doing.

$ASTS doesn't need to become another Verizon. It can use its satellites to extend coverage for operators that already have millions of subscribers, licensed spectrum, billing systems and customer relationships. The carriers keep their customers while AST gets a distribution channel without having to build an entire consumer mobile business from scratch.

I think there's a pretty significant economic advantage in that approach, assuming AST can deliver enough satellite capacity at a competitive cost.

Remember, acquiring spectrum is expensive, building terrestrial infrastructure is expensive and acquiring subscribers isn't cheap either. SpaceX has a huge advantage in launch economics, but that doesn't mean the existing telecom companies will help it compete with them.

Now, I wouldn't underestimate Elon here. $TMUS already works with Starlink on satellite connectivity and this rejection concerns broader terrestrial network access, not their existing satellite partnership.

But the carriers are resisting Starlink's mobile ambitions while AST has been building its business around partnerships with those same operators.

And yes, terrestrial networks will continue to offer far greater capacity in populated areas. That's fine. AST doesn't need to replace terrestrial networks to build a meaningful business. It needs to make satellite coverage commercially useful where those networks don't reach.

Of course, AST still has to execute. Manufacturing satellites, launching them and converting carrier agreements into recurring revenue aren't small challenges. And SpaceX isn't going to stop competing.

But I've always liked businesses where the incentives of the company and its customers are aligned. AST's carrier partners can expand their coverage without helping create another direct competitor for their subscribers.

So while SpaceX is spending billions trying to build a stronger position in mobile, AST is trying to make money from the operators that already dominate it.

I think that's a pretty smart strategy and this news makes those carrier relationships look even more valuable to me.

1. Stanford Online: the front door

Go to https://t.co/ZV8PzBzxFA and filter by free.

Stanford Online is Stanford’s own platform for courses taught by Stanford faculty. Some are free, some are paid. The paid ones are professional programs and certificates.

How to tell the difference quickly:

- Look for “Free” or “Open to all” on the course page
- Free courses are typically self-paced
- Paid programs show tuition and a start date

Important honesty check, because this is where most “free Stanford courses” posts mislead people: free Stanford content does not give you academic credit, and it does not give you a Stanford degree. What you get is the same quality of teaching, not the same credential.

If you want a paid certificate on top of free learning, some programs offer it. If you want the knowledge, you can often skip the certificate entirely.

Always confirm the course page says free before you start. Catalogs change.

비디오 파운데이션 모델의 잠재 공간(Latent Space)을 다루는 작업은 확률적 렌더링에 결과를 맡기는 것이 아닌, 프레임 단위의 물리 법칙과 감정의 전이를 설계하는 일입니다.

1. 기술적 표현 (Technical Execution)

Contact Mechanics & Multi-Entity Resolution:
Text-to-Video 모델에서 가장 흔히 발생하는 결함은 복수 객체 간의 접촉면 모핑(Morphing)입니다. 본 작업에서는 두 인물의 손이 얇은 도자기를 함께 감싸 쥐는 물리적 압력점과 경계면을 분리된 레이어로 정확히 인지·생성하도록 유도했습니다.

Subsurface Scattering & Fluid Dynamics:
역광 환경에서 피부 표면을 투과하는 자연광의 질감(SSS)과 중력 법칙에 맞춰 뺨을 타고 흐르는 눈물 줄기의 유체 물성을 모핑 없이 안정적으로 유지했습니다.

Latent Multi-Viewport & In-Model Typography:
그래픽 툴 오버레이 없이, 모델 내부의 공간 분할 연출(Triptych 구조)과 동적 텍스트 렌더링을 구현하여 단일 샷 안에서 시선 유도(Eye-tracking)의 전환을 설계했습니다.

2. 서사적 표현 (Narrative Arc & Emotional Subtext)

Kintsugi Metaphor:
깨진 도자기를 금으로 이어 붙이는 킨츠기(Kintsugi)의 조형적 모티브를 인물의 내면적 상흔과 치유의 서사로 직결시켰습니다.

Micro-Expression Continuity:
체념과 깊은 슬픔에서 안도와 미소로 이어지는 감정의 아크(Arc)를 단일 호흡으로 통제했습니다. 인공적인 안면 왜곡 없이 눈가의 떨림과 입꼬리의 미세 근육 변화가 서사의 흐름과 정확히 동기화되도록 연출했습니다.

text:
AI coding could kill my startup…

But it might also save it.

Both for reasons most people don’t understand. 

Here’s what I’m seeing 👇

We run a lot of our AI models at around 30% gross margin. The GPU prices we’re getting right now are doubling. That can pretty quickly wipe out any margin we have.

Finding capacity was already hard. I know founders of $10bn+ companies where securing GPUs has basically become the CEO’s main job.

And the capacity we do find is scraps. Bits and pieces that other large companies aren’t using. We’re going around trying to stitch together enough compute to run a business.

My worry is that the success of AI coding makes this much worse.

If you can make more money from a GPU serving coding customers than someone else can make serving video customers, you can afford to pay more for it.

You get more compute. You grow faster. You can afford even more compute.

Then there’s your team.

If an AI coding company can offer your best people much more money than you can, that massively changes the dynamics too. You’re competing for the same GPUs and the same people, with completely different economics.

And once those companies have the revenue, the compute and the talent, they can move into other markets. Including yours.

More supply should help. But one year in AI feels like five years in the previous tech world. A lot of startups won’t have time to wait.

I think Jensen should care about this. Surely Nvidia wants thousands of successful AI companies buying its chips, rather than a handful of customers with the money and incentive to build their own.

So does that mean we should all go and build AI coding companies?

Maybe.

But here’s the weird part. As these coding models get better, they become useful for things we didn’t necessarily expect.

We’re seeing models like Opus 5.5 enable video editing agents. The progress in coding is opening up a whole new way for us to build our product.

So the same market that could price us out of compute and take our team is also enabling our next big opportunity.

I think both things can be true. The opportunity is enormous. So is the pressure on the companies trying to build it.

When home feels tense for months at a time, it wears on everyone, including the children who seem fine.

A 2026 study on family dynamics found something quietly important: prolonged family conflict can weaken the protective effect of positive childhood experiences. A child can have loving moments, good school days, supportive friends, and still absorb the strain of ongoing conflict at home.

Researchers also noted that what helps is not simply adding more kindness on top of the tension. It is addressing the recurring cycles themselves: the same arguments, the escalation patterns, the lack of clear boundaries.

That is not about blame. Conflict cycles usually form for understandable reasons, and they can be changed. Families often need a neutral third person in the room more than they need to try harder.

ClearMind PLLC offers trauma-informed family counseling in Virginia, in person and online, and we accept many insurance plans including Anthem HealthKeepers Plus.

If things at home have felt stuck in the same loop lately, you can call (804) 316-1945 or email ClearMindPLLC@outlook.com. Talking it through once is a reasonable place to start.

text:
This Day in True Crime — October 31, 1979

The Murder of Debra Jackson: The Woman Called Orange Socks

A Discovery Along Interstate 35

On October 31, 1979, a young woman’s body was found in a culvert beside Interstate 35 near Georgetown, Texas. She had been sexually assaulted and strangled. With no identification and few leads, investigators knew her only by the orange socks she wore. For nearly 40 years, she would be called “Orange Socks.”

An Unknown Victim

Investigators estimated that she was a young adult, but they were unable to determine her identity. A silver ring, a hotel matchbook, and other evidence offered possible clues, yet none provided a definitive answer. As the years passed without a name, her case continued to draw attention from investigators and missing-person advocates, who remained focused on the unanswered question of who she was.

A Confession Under Scrutiny

In 1983, Henry Lee Lucas confessed to killing the unidentified woman. He was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death, despite the absence of physical evidence linking him to the crime. Lucas later recanted. Records suggesting he was in Florida at the time raised serious questions about his confession.

A Death Sentence Commuted

In 1998, Texas Governor George W. Bush commuted Lucas’s death sentence to life imprisonment, citing doubts about his guilt. Lucas died in prison in 2001. His conviction was never overturned, and the identity of Jackson’s killer remains disputed.

Her Name Finally Restored

In August 2019, investigators announced that “Orange Socks” was Debra Louise Jackson, a 23-year-old woman from Texas. Genetic genealogy helped locate a possible relative, and DNA from her sister confirmed the identification. Jackson had last been seen around 1977.

More Than a Nickname

For decades, the case was defined by the clothing found on an unidentified victim. DNA finally gave Debra Jackson her name back, but questions about who killed her remain unresolved. Her story is a reminder that identifying a victim and solving a murder are not always the same thing.

text:
Nike began as a bluff in a meeting in Japan.

Phil Knight had just finished his MBA at Stanford. One of his papers there asked whether Japanese running shoes could do to German shoes what Japanese cameras had done to German cameras.

He called it his crazy idea.

After graduating he went traveling, and in Kobe he found Tiger running shoes, made by a company called Onitsuka.

He got a meeting. The executives asked which company he was with.

He didn’t have one. He thought of the blue ribbons from track on his childhood bedroom wall and told them Blue Ribbon Sports of Portland, Oregon.

Then he gave them his Stanford argument: Onitsuka could undercut Adidas in America.

They asked if Blue Ribbon would represent them there. He said yes and asked them to send samples to Oregon.

He took a job as an accountant while he waited.

When the shoes came he mailed two pairs to his old track coach, Bill Bowerman.

Bowerman ordered shoes and offered to become his partner, and they shook hands on it in January 1964.

Knight sold the first pairs out of his green Plymouth Valiant at track meets.

In 1971 the company he made up in that meeting became Nike.

Riley Jensen made $2,000 a scene in p*rn and lived on c*caine and whiskey. After days without sleep, she saw strangers in her house at 4 a.m. 911 hung up on her. So she threw her 2-year-old daughter in the car and drove 90 mph. The strangers never existed.

She grew up in Stockton, California, working a regular job for a $400 paycheck. A friend was modeling and posting money she'd never seen. Then came an offer: fly to Scottsdale, Arizona, get paid $2,000. She went. Next it was LA, an agency, a $10,000 signing bonus and $1,500 to $2,000 per scene. "Then it's just off to the races."

The c*caine started the moment she arrived in LA. She loved the combo: c*caine and Jameson. She was paying everybody's bills, flying around the world, the life of every party. Her ego, she says, was "super inflated."

Years later she had a baby girl and split from the father. The drinking didn't stop. It went underground. She hid liquor, switched from whiskey to vodka, and had whiskey delivered at 4 a.m.

Five and a half months ago, during her custody time, she had been up for days on whiskey, c*caine and Xanax. She was scared to fall asleep and not wake up before her daughter did, so she did more c*caine. She came to in her closet at 4 a.m. and saw people in her house. They wouldn't leave. She had lost time, and in her head she kept asking herself whether they had touched her.

She called 911. The operator asked if she was under the influence. She said no. "Honey, I think you need to get some sleep." The operator hung up.

So she woke up her daughter, put her in the car and drove 90 mph through the dark to her ex's parents. She showed them videos on her phone as proof of the intruders. There was nothing there.

She slept for a day and a half. Then she called her dad. Four days later she walked into her first AA meeting and cried the entire time.

She has been sober ever since. Her daughter will be 2.

What would you have done if you were her ex?

text:
1/8 — The 7 everyday traps that slowly ruin your life

Most things that hold people back don't look dangerous at first. They feel good, save time, or make life easier.

But some comforts come at a price. Here are seven everyday habits that can quietly eat away at your health, discipline, money, and ambition.

2/8 — Food delivery

It satisfies your cravings and makes cooking feel like a chore.

Too much greasy, salty food can take a toll on your health. But the bigger trap is the convenience itself: less cooking, less movement, less effort put into taking care of yourself.

Get too comfortable being served, and you may lose the drive to do more with your life.

3/8 — Short-form videos

You scroll for an hour and feel like you've learned something. Then you put your phone down and realize how little you actually remember.

A few seconds of stimulation, over and over, can swallow hours of your day. The cost isn't just time. It's your attention span.

Eventually, sitting through a movie or focusing on a few pages of a book starts to feel like work.

You think you're relaxing. Sometimes, you're just chasing the next hit of stimulation.

4/8 — Pointless socializing

A room full of people you barely know. Fake smiles, forced conversations, drinks you don't even want.

Everyone calls everyone a brother. Once the night ends, nobody checks in.

You think you're building connections, but you're mostly collecting acquaintances and exhaustion.

When life gets hard, you scroll through your contacts and realize how few people you can actually count on.

5/8 — Easy credit and payday loans

Getting the money is easy. Paying it back is where the nightmare begins.

A few thousand in debt can snowball into much more. Interest and fees pile up while your income struggles to keep pace.

You borrow to cover what you already owe, digging one hole to fill another, until the whole thing collapses.

Some of the most expensive purchases in life begin with four words: “I'll deal with it later.”

6/8 — Staying up late

You're not just giving up sleep. You're borrowing energy from tomorrow to escape the emptiness of today.

You're exhausted all day, wide awake at night, staring at your phone until your eyes burn. You tell yourself, “Just five more minutes.”

It feels like you've stolen a little extra free time. In reality, you're sacrificing tomorrow's energy for tonight's distraction.

Your body doesn't always send a warning before the bill comes due.

7/8 — Comparing yourself to others

Their house. Their car. Their kids. Their marriage. Their carefully curated highlight reel on social media.

Win the comparison, and you still might not win anyone's respect. Lose it, and you make yourself miserable.

You turn your own life into a measuring stick for someone else's.

Spend your whole life chasing other people's best moments, and you may wake up one day to find you've neglected your own.

8/8 — Complaining

Every problem is someone else's fault. Every setback becomes another reason to blame your circumstances, other people, or fate.

Venting may feel good for a moment, but the problem remains. And the more you dwell on what you can't control, the more powerless you can feel.

Complaining is an easy escape from responsibility, but it can become a brutal form of self-sabotage.

These seven habits don't look like major disasters. That's exactly why they're dangerous.

They offer small rewards upfront and quietly drain your health, focus, money, and self-discipline over time.

Most people don't lose their way in one spectacular disaster. They lose it one comfortable, convenient choice at a time.

text:
Nigeria: The Price of Silence

By Kio Amachree, Letters from Stockholm, 31 October 2026

STOCKHOLM — Nigerians care far too much about what other people think of them. We worry about being liked and being accepted, about offending powerful people, about losing friends and invitations. That hunger for approval has become one of the great obstacles to building the social conscience a broken country needs.

We have become a nation in which too many people would rather stay silent in the face of wrongdoing than risk becoming unpopular by naming it. The silence is polite. It is also expensive, and the bill is paid by people who cannot afford it.

So it is worth asking plainly what the silence has bought us.

The Arithmetic of a Short Life

A child born in Nigeria today can expect to live about 55 years. The United Nations' 2025 World Population Prospects puts the figure at 54.9, the lowest of any country it measures. The World Bank's 2023 data says 54.5. A child born in Monaco the same day can expect roughly 30 more years; a child born in Stockholm, where I write this, about 28.

That gap is not an act of God. It is the sum of a thousand decisions: a hospital not built, a road not maintained, a budget line padded, a contract awarded to a friend, a clinic without drugs because the money went somewhere else. Thirty years of life, per person, multiplied across 230 million people, is the real price of the way Nigeria is governed.

The World Bank reported in April that the poverty rate rose to 63 percent in 2025, roughly 140 million people, even as headline inflation fell from 34.8 percent to 15.2 percent over the year. Prices stopped rising as fast; incomes never caught up. The poorest households spend as much as 70 percent of their income on food, and the cost of a basic food basket rose fivefold between 2019 and 2024. PwC's August outlook expects poverty to stay at 63 percent through 2026 and notes that undernourishment has nearly doubled in a decade, to one Nigerian in five.

And yet we carry ourselves as though we had all the time in the world to put this right. We do not. Life is short in Nigeria in the most literal sense, and every year of silence is a year subtracted from someone who could not afford to lose it.

How Crime Became Ordinary

The normalisation of criminal behaviour in Nigerian politics has done something to our national character that no recession could. We have reached the point where an allegation of corruption barely raises an eyebrow. Politicians accused of serious misconduct are celebrated, protected and promoted. Public officials behave as though the treasury were a family inheritance, and ordinary Nigerians are expected to be grateful for whatever trickles down.

I urge Nigerians to start speaking. Make your concerns known. Challenge injustice when you see it. Question those who exercise power in your name, and demand an account from anyone entrusted with public money. None of this requires courage of the heroic kind. It requires only that you stop caring whether the powerful like you.

The silence is not confined to the poor and the frightened. Lawyers, academics, businessmen, journalists and religious leaders, people with every advantage of education and position, have become willing participants in a culture of looking away. Some are bought. Many are simply afraid of losing a contract, an appointment or an invitation. Either way, the effect is the same: the thief is reassured that nobody is watching.

I will say what I have said before. I could not care less whether people like me or hate me. Their opinions make no difference to my taxes, my principles or my conscience. When I encounter evil I find it impossible to turn away and pretend it is not there. Evil has to be confronted at its source, through exposure, accountability and the full force of the law, before it becomes so entrenched that a whole society accepts it as the weather.

The Highway, the Chagourys and the $20 Billion Question

Which brings me to Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the Chagoury family and the extraordinary sums of money that now surround Nigeria's infrastructure.

The Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, 750 kilometres along the southern coast through nine states, has become the symbol of everything Nigerians must ask about procurement, transparency and the marriage of political power to private wealth. The contractor is Hitech Construction, the engineering arm of the Chagoury Group founded by Gilbert and Ronald Chagoury. The Works Minister, David Umahi, confirmed in April 2024 that Hitech was awarded the project without competitive bidding, on the strength of its track record, and put the tentative cost at 15.356 trillion naira. At today's exchange rate that is roughly 10 billion dollars; add the 1.7 trillion naira Sokoto–Badagry award and the 1 billion dollar Lagos ports modernisation that went to another group subsidiary, ITB, and the Chagoury-linked ledger approaches 13 billion dollars. I distinguish, as I always have, between what has been contracted and what has actually been paid. Nobody outside government knows the second number, and that is the point.

The contract has grown since it was signed. Section I in Lagos was procured at 1.068 trillion naira, Section II at 1.6 trillion, Sections IIIA and IIIB jointly at 1.33 trillion. In May, the Lagos State Government approved dedicated mining sites at Ilamija, Kajola, Orimedu and Akodo so that Hitech could dig its own sand and gravel for the road it is already building, capturing both the engineering and the input cost of the largest active infrastructure project in the country.

Who is Gilbert Chagoury? In 2000 a Geneva court convicted him of money laundering and aiding a criminal organisation over transfers exceeding 120 million dollars to accounts tied to the family of Sani Abacha; he later returned funds to Nigeria and the conviction was expunged. In October 2019 he signed a deferred prosecution agreement with the United States Department of Justice and paid 1.8 million dollars to resolve an investigation into illegal foreign campaign contributions routed through straw donors across three election cycles. In January of this year President Tinubu conferred on him the Grand Commander of the Order of the Niger, one of the highest honours the republic can give. Mr. Chagoury has denied knowing that the Abacha-era funds were stolen. A man with that record is entitled to do business. A government that hands him a 10 billion dollar road without a tender is not entitled to our trust.

The transparency record speaks for itself. Tracka, the BudgIT initiative, wrote to the Works Minister on February 19, 2026, under the Freedom of Information Act asking for the justification for direct contracting, the bid and evaluation documents, the ownership structures of the contractors, the total cost and its funding sources. The ministry acknowledged the letter on March 2. By mid-April it had not answered. A lawsuit by the accountant Funso Doherty seeking to nullify the award and force open bidding remains before the courts.

Now comes the next request. On October 27, less than 100 days before the January 16 election, President Tinubu asked the National Assembly to approve a fresh external borrowing plan of 20.52 billion dollars and 1.04 billion euros. This comes on top of the 21 billion dollar plan the Senate approved in July 2025 and the 6 billion dollars approved in March. Nigeria's public debt stood at 166.79 trillion naira, about 121 billion dollars, at the end of June, up from 87.38 trillion naira when this administration took office. Debt service cost about 16 trillion naira in 2025.

I want to know precisely where the new money will go, who will receive the contracts, what competitive tendering will be followed, and whether a single dollar of it will reach any company connected to the Chagoury family. I do not assert that it will; the loan request has not been tied publicly to the highway or to any Chagoury company, and I will not pretend otherwise. But a government that has refused to answer a lawful FOI request about its flagship project for eight months has forfeited the benefit of the doubt on the next 20 billion dollars.

I am not prepared to accept that borrowing for development is automatically corruption. Neither am I prepared to accept that announcing a road removes the government's obligation to explain every dollar spent on it. Nigeria is not the private property of Mr. Tinubu, his family, his political associates or any foreign businessman.

The Question of Sovereignty

There is a second question that has troubled me for some time. Why does this administration seem so comfortable with arrangements that concentrate enormous economic influence in the hands of a small network of politically connected individuals, several of them based abroad?

I have asked in the past whether foreign intelligence interests might benefit from Nigeria's continuing instability. Let me be exact about what I know and what I do not. I have no evidence that Mr. Tinubu is an asset of the CIA, of French intelligence, or of anyone else, and I will not present suspicion as fact. What I will say is that the broader question of foreign influence over Nigeria's political and economic decisions deserves serious, public examination, and that a country whose president dines in Paris more readily than he stands at the United Nations has invited the question.

Nigeria is the most populous Black nation on earth. We possess extraordinary human capital, natural resources, entrepreneurial energy and strategic weight. Yet we remain exposed to external economic pressure, internal corruption, insecurity and political manipulation. A weakened Nigeria is easier to exploit than a prosperous, independent and institutionally strong one. That is precisely why our sovereignty has to be defended by transparent government, functioning institutions and a judiciary nobody can buy. A sovereignty that rests on one man's relationships is not sovereignty. It is a lease.

Name One Policy

So I put a simple question to my countrymen. Can you name a single policy of the Tinubu administration that has substantially and sustainably improved the daily life of an ordinary Nigerian?

Not an announcement. Not a speech. Not a promise about what the coastal highway will do in 2032. I mean a measurable improvement in the purchasing power of the average worker, in the price of garri and rice, in the chance of seeing a doctor, in the safety of the road to the farm, in the prospect of a job, in a family's ability to live with dignity.

The administration's defenders have an answer, and in fairness it should be stated. The petrol subsidy is gone, the exchange rate has been unified, foreign reserves have climbed, growth has returned and inflation has fallen by more than half from its peak. The World Bank itself credits tight monetary policy and reduced exchange-rate volatility for easing prices. These are real changes, and a serious critic acknowledges them.

But the same World Bank report says that for most Nigerians the recovery has not translated into better living conditions, that wages have lagged inflation and that poverty has yet to begin declining. The reforms stabilised the government's books. They have not yet stabilised a single household's. Diesel was up 44 percent year on year in April and kerosene 34 percent; the cost of a healthy diet reached 1,589 naira per adult per day. Macroeconomic stability that bypasses 140 million people is an accounting achievement, not a national one.

What I see is a country where too many people are struggling to survive while those in positions of privilege grow steadily more detached from the suffering around them. A president who removes the subsidy and asks the poor to endure, then buys a new presidential jet, is not asking for shared sacrifice. He is asking for sacrifice.

Loyalty to a Man Is Not Patriotism

I find the conduct of those who defend every government decision without question especially disturbing. Loyalty to a president must never become more important than loyalty to the Federal Republic of Nigeria. Patriotism is not blind obedience to political authority. Patriotism is the courage to hold that authority to account.

It is entirely possible to support a government and still condemn its wrongdoing. Anyone who believes in constitutional democracy should insist on the distinction. What I cannot understand is the willingness of otherwise intelligent, educated Nigerians to excuse conduct they would condemn in an instant if their political opponents had committed it. That hypocrisy is poisoning the country. It teaches every politician that the only crime is losing.

Every night I pray that those responsible for the abuse of public office, the misappropriation of public funds and the destruction of public trust will one day stand before an independent court and answer for it. I want investigations that are thorough, evidence-based and free of political interference. I want stolen assets recovered. I want officials who have committed crimes prosecuted and, where convicted, punished according to law. And I want everyone who has enriched himself through unlawful dealings with the Nigerian state to understand that leaving office does not erase criminal responsibility.

The damage done by corruption does not end when a term expires. It is paid out over generations: in unpaid debts, abandoned hospitals, broken schools, unsafe roads, unemployment and lives cut short. Nigeria cannot afford another twenty years of impunity.

What Accountability Would Look Like

None of this is abstract. The Kio Solution asks for five things, each of them lawful, each of them possible tomorrow.

One. Publish the Lagos–Calabar contracts in full: every section's award, price, variation, payment to date and lender, with the Bureau of Public Procurement's certificate of no objection or an explanation of why there is none.

Two. Answer Tracka's Freedom of Information request, and every other lawful request, within the time the Act allows. A ministry that ignores the law it is bound by has no standing to ask the public to obey any other.

Three. No vote on the new 20.52 billion dollar borrowing plan until the National Assembly publishes a project-by-project list of what the money funds, who will build it and how it was tendered. A loan approved in the dark is a loan the next generation repays in the dark.

Four. An independent forensic audit, with foreign auditors on the panel, of every contract awarded since 2023 to companies in which the Chagoury family or any member of the first family holds an interest, direct or beneficial.

Five. Apply the Isabel Precedent: ask the courts and financial authorities of Europe and the United States, where this money ultimately rests, to freeze and trace assets wherever the evidence leads, so that leaving office in Abuja offers no sanctuary abroad.

Speak, and Let Them Dislike You

We must restore civility, decency, honesty and respect for the Constitution to the centre of national life. But that restoration does not begin in Aso Rock. It begins with ordinary Nigerians finding the nerve to speak.

Stop worrying about whether powerful people will like you. Stop defending wrongdoing because the man responsible shares your tribe, your religion or your party. Stop confusing silence with wisdom and obedience with patriotism.

Our children will not judge us by how popular we were. They will judge us by what we did when the country was being damaged in front of our eyes. I would rather be disliked for telling the truth as I understand it than be celebrated for keeping quiet in the presence of injustice.

Nothing I have written here is personal. It is politics, and politics is the business of every citizen.

Nigeria belongs to Nigerians, not to its politicians. And the people must never surrender their right to demand better.

The contract, conviction and settlement facts above are drawn from court records, the United States Department of Justice, the Debt Management Office, the World Bank and published reporting. Allegations are reported as allegations; no person named has been convicted of any offence in connection with the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, and Mr. Chagoury's denials are noted. Where I state a belief rather than a fact, I say so.

Kio Amachree
President, Worldview International
Stockholm, Sweden
