text:
👻🎃 HALLOWEEN —
HOUDINI'S CENTURY AND THE NIGHT BEHIND THE MASK 🗝️
— The Full Story ▸ ▸ ▸ 📖 Special Edition ✨
Houdini died at 1:26 p.m. on Halloween 1926, a century ago today. Tonight magicians try again to reach him, on a holiday whose oldest-sounding stories are among its newest.

✍️ By 3 Star Media — The BX Files 🏇💨

🕰️ ONE HUNDRED YEARS

That afternoon, in Grace Hospital in Detroit, the most famous escape artist in the world died of peritonitis at 52. A burst appendix had done what no handcuff, straitjacket or sealed coffin ever managed.

A century later the anniversary is a holiday inside the holiday. The Detroit Historical Museum holds a Houdini evening tonight, and in Austin, Texas, the Harry Ransom Center has opened an exhibition called Houdini's Library. And at 5 p.m. Pacific, at the Magic Castle in Hollywood, the Official Houdini Séance will try once more to reach him, guided by the medium Rob Zabrecky, with Houdini's grandniece Debbie Hardeen Bloom in the inner circle.

This is the first Saturday Halloween since 2020 and the last until 2037. Derry, in Northern Ireland, marks the 40th year of Europe's largest Halloween festival. Manhattan's Village Halloween Parade steps off at 7 p.m. for the 53rd time, under the theme Body & Soul.

Halloween tells a story about itself: an ancient Celtic new year, a Roman harvest goddess, poisoned candy. Read against the record, the date is a Christian feast, the customs are mostly Gaelic and Scottish folk practice, the phrase trick or treat was first printed in Canada, and the money is American. Several of the oldest-sounding parts were first argued in print during Houdini's own lifetime. He spent his last years exposing people who claimed to speak for the dead, and he would have recognized the method.

▸ ▸ ▸

⛪ ALL HALLOWS

Halloween is a contraction of All Hallows' Eve, the night before All Saints' Day. Merriam-Webster dates the short form to about 1700.

All Saints came first, and it did not start on Nov. 1.

On May 13 in 609 or 610, Pope Boniface IV dedicated Rome's Pantheon to Mary and the martyrs. Pope Gregory III, who reigned from 731 to 741, dedicated a chapel in St. Peter's to all the saints on Nov. 1. Churches in England and Germany were keeping the feast on Nov. 1 by about 800, and in 835 the emperor Louis the Pious ordered it kept across Gaul and Germany.

⚖️ Two Irish church calendars from the early ninth century, the Martyrology of Tallaght and the Félire Óengusso, keep a feast of all the saints of Europe on April 20, and University College Dublin's cultural heritage blog notes that the April feast carried more weight there than Nov. 1. The historian Ronald Hutton, in The Stations of the Sun, reads the April date as evidence that the November feast was a Germanic idea that Rome itself adopted, not a Christian cover laid over an Irish festival.

The same Irish calendar complicates that. The Félire Óengusso also places a great crowd of saints on samain, Nov. 1. By the ninth century, Irish monks were already setting their saints on the old festival's day.

▸ ▸ ▸

🔥 SAMAIN

Irish literature from the ninth century onward treats samain, Nov. 1, as the beginning of winter and a time of gatherings, feasts and danger, when the burial mounds open onto the Otherworld. In the saga The Adventure of Nera, in Kuno Meyer's translation, Nera is told that "the fairy-mounds of Erinn are always opened about Halloween."

On the Hill of Ward in County Meath, which the 17th-century historian Geoffrey Keating named as the center of samain rites, a University College Dublin dig led by Steve Davis in 2014 and 2015 dated the great ringed enclosure of Tlachtga to around the fifth century, built over earthworks from the Late Bronze Age.

That is the strongest case for continuity, and the folklorist Jack Santino made it in the journal Western Folklore in 1983. The sagas were written down by Christian monks centuries later, he argued, but they draw on long oral traditions that likely preserve pre-Christian practice. He linked saga figures who demand a share of the harvest at samain to the costumed visitor at the door who demands candy now.

The famous origin stories built on top of that are another matter.

🔬 The new-year reading has one pre-Christian anchor. The bronze Coligny calendar from second-century Roman Gaul opens with a month called Samonios, a name linked to samain, though scholars disagree on whether that month fell in autumn or early summer.

❌ The Celtic New Year is a modern inference. The label traces to the Welsh scholar John Rhys, who drew partly on Isle of Man folklore, where Oct. 31 was sometimes called New Year's Night. James Frazer, author of The Golden Bough, spread the idea and made samain a pagan festival of the dead, while conceding at times that the evidence was inconclusive. Hutton calls the new-year evidence flimsy, and finds no medieval record that Nov. 1 was a major festival across all the Celtic lands.

❌ The Roman connection traces to a single book. In The Book of Hallowe'en, published in 1919, Ruth Edna Kelley described Pomona, goddess of fruit, honored in "a grove near Ostia where a harvest festival was held about November first." No surviving Roman calendar records that festival, and the Halloween historian Lisa Morton has rejected the link between Pomona and Halloween's apples.

💡 The bottom line: samain was real, and its reputation as a night when the other world comes close is genuinely old. The Celtic New Year and the Roman harvest goddess are inferences that writers put in print within Houdini's lifetime.

▸ ▸ ▸

🏮 SOULS AND LANTERNS

The customs are better documented than the origins, and most of them come down to food.

📊 Souling, going door to door for food in return for prayers for the dead, is on record by 1511, according to Morton. Shakespeare could count on his audience knowing it. In The Two Gentlemen of Verona, a servant mocks his lovesick master for learning "to speak puling, like a beggar at Hallowmas," Hallowmas being All Saints.

Robert Burns gave the night its great poem, Halloween, written in 1785 and published in the 1786 Kilmarnock edition, with notes explaining the customs: young people pulling kale stalks and burning nuts in the fire to read their futures in love.

In Ireland the night meant barmbrack, a fruit loaf with a ring baked inside to tell who would marry first, and lanterns carved from turnips. The National Museum of Ireland adds marriage divination, ghostly masks, and bands of men or children going house to house in disguise, on what was also called ghost night or spirit night, when the souls of the dead were expected home.

The jack-o'-lantern was a man before it was a pumpkin.

In 17th-century English the word meant a night watchman, a man carrying a lantern, and the will-o'-the-wisp, the ghost light over a marsh. By the 1830s it named a carved lantern. Immigrants likely swapped turnips for pumpkins, Merriam-Webster says, though a turnip has to be scraped out by hand and a pumpkin comes with its hollow built in.

💬 Stingy Jack, the drunk who tricks the devil and wanders with a coal in a turnip, is a folk tale, told far more often than it is sourced.

▸ ▸ ▸

🍁 TRICK OR TREAT

🔬 Puritan New England largely ignored Halloween. The usual account has it spreading across America after the Irish famine migration of 1845 to 1852, with Scottish customs traveling alongside.

Before trick-or-treating, New York children had a begging day of their own, and it fell on Thanksgiving.

From about the 1870s, children in masks went door to door asking, "Anything for Thanksgiving?" They were called ragamuffins. In the 1930s the city's schools superintendent condemned the custom, a 1936 New York Times headline read Ragamuffins Frowned Upon, and the Times found it hanging on in Flatbush, the Bronx and Greenpoint. The last recorded traditional Ragamuffin Day was in the Bronx, in 1956. Bay Ridge in Brooklyn later revived it as a parade.

Trick or treat was first printed in Canada.

The Dictionary of Canadian English on Historical Principles, published by the University of British Columbia, cites the Sault Star of Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, on Nov. 1, 1917, reporting "tricks or treats" being called out by gangs that Halloween. A 1927 headline about the Alberta village of Blackie read: "Trick or Treat" Is Demand. American papers had it by 1928, in Bay City, Michigan.

The treats came because the tricks had become a problem. By the 1920s and 1930s, Halloween pranks were destructive enough that towns organized parties and parades to steer them somewhere else.

Anoka, Minnesota, held a civic Halloween celebration in 1920, often called the nation's first, with a parade, a bonfire and candy for the children. It still calls itself the Halloween Capital of the World.

▸ ▸ ▸

Then the candy ran out.

Sugar rationing began in the spring of 1942 and lasted until June 1947, and Anoka canceled its celebration in 1942 and 1943.

When the sugar came back, so did the door-to-door holiday.

In 1950, in Philadelphia, Clyde and Mary Emma Allison sent children out to collect coins for UNICEF instead of candy, and raised $17 the first year. Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF has raised more than $175 million since.

On Oct. 27, 1966, 60 years ago this week, It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown aired for the first time, with Linus spending the whole night in a pumpkin patch waiting for a visitor who never comes. Few holiday traditions are built so faithfully around a no-show.

▸ ▸ ▸

🌽 CHICKEN FEED

Soul cakes, apples, nuts and barmbrack gave way to candy, and candy corn's inventor is a story, not a record.

💬 The National Confectioners Association credits George Renninger of the Wunderle Candy Company in Philadelphia in the 1880s, and calls the account oral history.

A 1910 patent does tie Renninger to Wunderle. The Goelitz company, now Jelly Belly, began making candy corn around 1900 and sold it as Chicken Feed, which may be the most honest name in the history of candy marketing. Jelly Belly says plainly that it did not invent the candy.

⚖️ Newark newspaper accounts from 1948 and 1964 credit William Kolb, a Newark candy maker, with inventing the candy apple, dipping apples in red cinnamon candy in 1908 and selling them for 5 cents. But toffee apples were already being sold in London in the 1890s.

Illinois grows more pumpkins than any other state, about 533 million pounds in 2025, and nearly 70 percent of its pumpkin acreage goes to processing, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service. Most of the nation's biggest pumpkin crop never meets a carving knife.

💬 Michael Downing, author of Spring Forward, a history of daylight saving time, says candy makers left candy pumpkins on senators' seats during 1985 hearings on extending daylight saving time, hoping for one more hour of evening light on Halloween. The 1986 law that came out of that fight did not reach Halloween.

The Energy Policy Act of 2005 did. Since 2007, daylight saving time has ended on the first Sunday in November, after Halloween rather than before it. David Prerau, another historian of the clock, says the candy industry played a smaller part in that change than the story gives it. Either way, tonight is the last evening of daylight saving time, so trick-or-treaters get the later sunset.

▸ ▸ ▸

💵 THE MONEY

Americans will spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, up from $13.1 billion in 2025, according to the National Retail Federation's survey of 7,889 consumers, released Sept. 22. That is $115.14 a person. Seventy-four percent plan to celebrate, up from 68 percent in 2019.

The money splits almost evenly three ways: $4.4 billion on costumes, $4.3 billion on decorations and $4.1 billion on candy. The witch is the top adult costume, and the top pet costume is a pumpkin, chosen by 11.6 percent of pet owners, comfortably ahead of the hot dog.

❌ Halloween is often called America's second-biggest holiday for spending, but NRF puts Valentine's Day at $29.1 billion and Mother's Day at $38 billion this year, both far above Halloween.

In 1985 the sociologists Joel Best and Gerald Horiuchi noted that folklorists, Santino among them, considered Halloween one of the least commercialized holidays of the modern calendar. Forty years later, Americans spend more on decorations than on the candy they hand out, $920 million on pet costumes alone, and half start shopping by September, up from a third in 2016. That is the strongest case that money changed the night.

The decorations business is older than it looks: the Dennison Manufacturing Company published its first Bogie Book, a party guide built around its crepe paper and cutouts, in 1909. Spirit Halloween began in 1983, when Joe Marver opened a Halloween store in Castro Valley, California. It now opens more than 1,500 seasonal stores a year. In 2020 Home Depot introduced a 12-foot skeleton for $299 that sold out again and again, and front lawns have not been the same since.

🔍 What the evidence shows: the same survey answers the charge that money spoiled it. The most common way Americans celebrate is still handing out candy to whoever knocks, 61 percent, ahead of wearing a costume, 50 percent. The money buys the candy, but the biggest single act of the holiday is still a neighbor opening a door.

▸ ▸ ▸

🚸 THE REAL DANGER

🎯 THE KEY QUESTION Has a stranger ever poisoned a child's Halloween candy?

Best and Horiuchi went looking and reported in the journal Social Problems. Searching newspaper coverage from the late 1950s to 1984, they counted 76 reported incidents. Twenty involved an injury, and the worst needed 11 stitches. Two children died, and in both cases the cause was inside the family: one boy got into heroin at his uncle's home, and another was poisoned with cyanide by his own father. Neither was the work of a stranger. Best kept looking after 1985, and as of 2019 had still found no child killed by a stranger's Halloween candy.

In 1982, after the Tylenol poisonings, 12 Halloween cases were reported. Of 270 possible Halloween candy tamperings that year, an FDA review cited in the paper found more than 95 percent involved no tampering at all, and an FDA official called the wave "psychosomatic mass hysteria."

🔍 What the evidence shows: the danger on Halloween is not in the candy bag. It is in the street. In JAMA Pediatrics in 2019, a team led by John Staples and Donald Redelmeier compared 42 Halloween evenings from 1975 to 2016 with the same weeknight a week before and a week after: 608 pedestrian deaths against 851 on twice as many ordinary evenings. That is 43 percent higher odds of a pedestrian death, about four extra deaths every Halloween. For children ages 4 to 8, the odds were 10 times higher.

In Detroit, the city where Houdini died, the three nights ending on Halloween, Devil's Night among them, brought 810 fires in 1984, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. By 1996, with 33,615 volunteers patrolling the streets, the count was down to 142. The patrols became Angels' Night, and since 2018 the city has thrown Halloween in the D.

◆ ◆ ◆

🪄 THE ESCAPE ARTIST

He was born in Budapest in 1874 and raised in Appleton, Wisconsin, the son of a rabbi. As a teenager he took his stage name from Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, the French performer often called the father of modern magic. In 1908 he published a book attacking his own namesake, The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin, calling him "a mere pretender."

That book points at the obsession underneath the act. He built one of the great libraries of magic history.

The Library of Congress, which received his magic and spiritualism holdings under his will, calls him a formidable collector and writes that his "formal education was slight; his self education immense." He combed old bookshops, interviewed retired magicians and kept a 53-page typed catalogue of what he owned, The Art Newspaper reports. The Harry Ransom Center holds his drama collection.

Among the books in the center's centennial exhibition is Reginald Scot's Discovery of Witchcraft, from 1584, which explained conjurors' tricks in order to argue against the persecution of accused witches, along with a book of sermons printed in Strasbourg in 1497. "Houdini felt very strongly that all of human knowledge was in books," the center's curator, Eric Colleary, told The Art Newspaper.

The other hunt was for his mother.

Cecilia Weiss died in 1913. In A Magician Among the Spirits he wrote of sitting with mediums "for the solace of one word from my loved departed." What he found were tricks he knew how to do himself.

📊 The test that ended his friendship with Arthur Conan Doyle came in June 1922, at the Ambassador Hotel in Atlantic City. Doyle's wife, Jean, produced pages of automatic writing she said came from Houdini's mother, headed with a cross. Cecilia Weiss was a rabbi's wife, and Houdini wrote to Doyle that his "sainted mother could not read, write or speak the English language." He also said the séance fell on her birthday, which the message never mentioned, though his own notes put it a day later. Doyle answered in print that his wife "always puts a cross on her paper when she writes under inspiration," and that such writing carries thoughts, not "a verbatim message in a strange language."

In hearings that opened Feb. 26, 1926, on a bill to ban fortune-telling for pay in the District of Columbia, Houdini offered $10,000 to any medium who could produce a genuine psychic phenomenon, and called the mediums "frauds from start to finish." The bill failed. Two years earlier, on a Scientific American committee, he had concluded that the Boston medium Mina Crandon rang the séance bell with her feet. She did not get the $2,500 prize.

💬 One medium at the 1926 hearings, Madame Marcia, predicted he would be dead by November, according to Atlas Obscura's account. He died on Oct. 31.

▸ ▸ ▸

🥊 THE LAST SHOW

⚖️ In October 1926, in his dressing room at the Princess Theatre in Montreal, a McGill University student named J. Gordon Whitehead struck him in the stomach, testing his boast that he could take any blow above the waist. The details depend on who is telling it. McGill's Office for Science and Society has the blows landing before Houdini could brace. Whitehead's own sworn statement, taken in 1927 for the estate's claim against Houdini's life insurer, says Houdini invited the blows and showed no sign of pain. Accounts do not even agree on the date. His doctors blamed the blows, History*com reports, and in June 1927 The New York Times reported that New York Life had paid his widow $50,000, double the policy, for accidental death. That is the punch theory at its strongest: an insurer with $25,000 at stake paid on it.

🔬 What Smithsonian magazine's account adds is the part the legend leaves out: Houdini had likely been suffering from appendicitis for weeks, and his appendix would probably have burst without any blow at all.

What killed him was the thing that made him. He did not stop.

He opened at the Garrick Theater in Detroit on Oct. 24 with a fever of 104 degrees, and it was his last performance. At Grace Hospital, surgeons found that the appendix had ruptured. He died a week later, at 1:26 p.m. on Halloween.

That is the human center of the legend. A man who spent his life proving a body could be chained, locked and sunk and still come out would not leave a stage while there was an audience in it.

📊 He was buried at Machpelah Cemetery in Queens, in a plot he shares with his mother, in a bronze casket with a sealed liner that, by Smithsonian magazine's account, he had used underwater in his act, with his head resting on a packet of her letters. That August he had lasted 91 minutes sealed in a coffin at the bottom of a New York hotel pool, to beat a rival's hour.

▸ ▸ ▸

🌹 ROSABELLE

Harry and Bess Houdini agreed that whoever died first would try to reach the other, using a code from their old mind-reading act: the word Rosabelle, followed by a string of code words that spelled believe. If nothing came in 10 years, the question would be settled. Bess held a séance on the anniversary each year. The last, at 8 p.m. on Oct. 31, 1936, on the roof of the Knickerbocker Hotel in Hollywood, went out over the radio. Nothing came, and Bess closed it herself: "I now, reverently, turn out the light. It is finished. Good night, Harry!"

The magicians did not take her word for it. Oct. 31 is observed as Magic Day because Houdini died on it, and the Official Houdini Séance describes itself as a 100-year tradition.

▸ ▸ ▸

📜 THE OBJECTIONS

Not everyone keeps this night, and the strongest objections to it are religious, not commercial.

Jehovah's Witnesses do not celebrate Halloween. Their official website traces its customs to the occult and cites Deuteronomy 18:10 to 12, which forbids divination and consulting the dead. On this report's own evidence the charge lands twice: the old night's customs, Burns's kale stalks and the barmbrack ring, were fortune-telling, and its most famous modern ritual is a séance.

In 1972 Jerry Falwell's ministry in Lynchburg, Virginia, opened Scaremare, the forerunner of the Hell House, a haunted attraction built to frighten visitors toward faith. Trunk-or-treat, candy handed out from decorated car trunks in church parking lots, dates to 1989, according to Merriam-Webster.

Others in the church claim the night back. In 2019 Vatican News, the Holy See's news service, called it "one of those feasts on the Catholic calendar that is celebrated on the eve of a great solemnity," its ghoulish trappings "supposed to be reminders of death and of the last things."

Many observant Jews skip the night, citing Leviticus 18:3, read as a ban on imitating other peoples' rites, while more liberal Jews treat it as secular, My Jewish Learning notes. Purim already has the costumes.

▸ ▸ ▸

🗺️ BEYOND THE FRONT DOOR

Mexico's Día de Muertos, Nov. 1 and 2, is a separate tradition, recognized by UNESCO in 2003, and Mexico City's giant parade for it is newer than it looks: it began in 2016, inspired by the opening scene of the James Bond film Spectre.

In the Philippines, families crowd the cemeteries for Undas, and the old custom of pangangaluluwa, singing door to door for the souls, is a near cousin of English souling. Germany keeps Oct. 31 as Reformation Day, for Martin Luther's 95 Theses. Wiccans keep Samhain as the witches' new year, a reading that took shape with Gerald Gardner in the mid-20th century.

In Tokyo, Halloween grew into a street party big enough that Shibuya now bans drinking on its streets from 6 p.m. to 5 a.m. all year, and its mayor, Ken Hasebe, asks revelers to keep the party off the streets. Across the sea in Seoul, the night carries the memory of the 159 people who died in the Itaewon crowd crush in 2022.

💡 The bottom line: Halloween's date is a Christian feast that most likely spread from England and Germany. Its customs of food, fire, disguise and fortune-telling are Gaelic and Scottish folk practice, carried across the Atlantic by immigrants. Its famous phrase was first printed in Canada, and its candy and its money are American. What the continuity camp gets right is the belief. Medieval Ireland already treated this as the night the wall between the worlds runs thin, and that idea has outlived every theory about where it came from.

◆ ◆ ◆

🎭 THE NIGHT BEHIND THE MASK

At 5 p.m. Pacific the lights will go down in the Magic Castle, and someone will say the word Rosabelle.

Houdini spent his life proving that every locked box has a way out, and his last years proving that no medium had found the way back. A hundred years later, his fellow magicians still sit in a circle on the night he died and leave the door open for him. Tonight the clocks fall back, and the night itself runs an hour longer. They will have a little extra time to wait.

A note on sources: this report draws on medieval Irish texts in translation; archaeology; dictionaries; historians and folklorists; museum and library collections; trade survey data; peer-reviewed research; federal reports; sworn testimony and hearing records; religious publications; and news reporting.

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

ANNALS OF THE DAY  🪔

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

A Historical Chronicle: October 31 Edition

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🪔 EPIGRAPH  

“We carry yesterday like a lantern—not to live in its light, but to see how far we’ve already come, and how much farther we need to go.” ~ Hodgepodgery, 2026

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📜 INTRO

Some dates are remembered for what happened. October 31 deserves attention for what people set in motion. A few words would challenge an institution that had stood for centuries. A seemingly impossible gamble on a battlefield would produce an astonishing result. An act of political violence would unleash consequences far beyond the killer's intentions. And an idea, introduced almost unnoticed, would eventually shake the foundations of an established system. Add a masterpiece that took years to complete and a moment when the boundaries of human achievement were pushed further than anyone thought possible, and this date becomes anything but ordinary. Some of these stories changed the world. Others are remarkable for reasons you may never have heard.

────────────────────────────────

🧭 CALENDAR OVERVIEW

October 31 is the 304th day of the year in the Gregorian calendar (≈83.29% of the year completed). There are 61 days remaining after this date, representing ≈16.71% of the year. The year 2026 is a common year (365 days). Today is Saturday, falling in ISO week 44. Verified observances for this date include Halloween, Reformation Day, and World Savings Day.

────────────────────────────────

🏛️ MAJOR HISTORICAL EVENTS

From religious upheaval and territorial expansion to military breakthroughs and technological transformation, October 31 has repeatedly placed history at a crossroads.

1517 — Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses Challenge Church Practices 📜

Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and theology professor in Wittenberg, dated a letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz enclosing ninety-five propositions challenging the sale of indulgences and other church practices. The document helped ignite the Protestant Reformation, transforming Christianity and European political life. The familiar account of Luther dramatically nailing the theses to the Castle Church door remains disputed; the dated letter and its accompanying propositions provide firmer evidence of his action.

🧩 TRIVIA: Luther's original propositions were written in Latin, the scholarly language of European universities and theological debate.

📜 APOCRYPHAL: The famous door-nailing episode should not be presented as established fact. Historians disagree over whether it occurred, although the dated letter itself is documented.

1864 — Nevada Becomes the Thirty-Sixth State 🗽

President Abraham Lincoln issued the proclamation admitting Nevada into the Union as the thirty-sixth state. Its admission during the Civil War strengthened the Union politically and added another Republican-leaning state before Lincoln's November re-election. The presidential proclamation was formally dated October 31, 1864.

🧩 TRIVIA: Nevada was admitted only eight days before the presidential election of November 8, 1864.

1917 — British War Cabinet Approves the Balfour Declaration 📜

The British War Cabinet approved the wording of a statement supporting the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people. Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour subsequently issued the declaration in a letter to Lord Rothschild dated November 2. The decision became one of the most consequential diplomatic statements in the history of the modern Middle East.

🧩 TRIVIA: The declaration also stated that nothing should prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities in Palestine.

1917 — Australian Light Horse Captures Beersheba in Daring Mounted Charge ⚔️

Late in the afternoon, the 4th and 12th Australian Light Horse Regiments charged Ottoman defensive positions at Beersheba, Palestine. The assault overwhelmed the trenches, secured the town's essential water supplies, and broke the Gaza–Beersheba defensive line. Thirty-one Australians were killed and thirty-six wounded among the Light Horse casualties.

🧩 TRIVIA: The mounted troopers carried their bayonets in their hands and used them as swords because the Light Horsemen were not equipped with traditional cavalry sabres or lances.

🌀 OBSCURE: The surprise attack depended partly on the discovery that the Ottoman trenches lacked barbed-wire entanglements in front of them, allowing the horses to jump the defenses.

1940 — Battle of Britain Reaches Its Official End ✈️

October 31 is recognized as the conventional closing date of the Battle of Britain, the German air campaign fought over southern England and the English Channel from the summer of 1940. Britain's Royal Air Force had prevented the Luftwaffe from securing the air superiority necessary for a German invasion. The invasion plans were consequently postponed and ultimately abandoned.

🧩 TRIVIA: The Luftwaffe's failure did not end the bombing of Britain; the Blitz continued into 1941.

1941 — USS Reuben James Sunk by German Submarine ⚓

The American destroyer USS Reuben James was torpedoed by the German submarine U-552 while escorting convoy HX-156 near Iceland. The ship sank rapidly, with heavy loss of life among its crew. It became the first United States Navy vessel lost to enemy action during the Second World War, more than a month before the attack on Pearl Harbor brought America formally into the conflict.

🧩 TRIVIA: The destroyer had been commissioned in 1920 and was named after an American sailor who distinguished himself during the Barbary Wars and the War of 1812.

🌀 OBSCURE: The ship was protecting a British-bound convoy, illustrating how deeply American naval forces were already involved in the Atlantic struggle before the United States officially entered the war.

1941 — Mount Rushmore Declared Complete 🗿

After fourteen years of construction, Mount Rushmore National Memorial was declared a completed project in South Dakota's Black Hills. The monumental presidential sculpture depicts George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln. Gutzon Borglum had died earlier that year, leaving his son Lincoln to supervise the final work.

🧩 TRIVIA: More than 400 workers participated in carving the four presidential faces into the granite mountain.

🌀 OBSCURE: The original vision included a massive Hall of Records inside the mountain, intended to preserve important documents and tell the story of the United States. The chamber was never completed.

1984 — Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi Assassinated 👑

Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated at her New Delhi residence by two members of her Sikh security detail. The killing followed months of tension surrounding her government's military operation at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. Her assassination was followed by widespread violence against Sikhs, particularly in Delhi.

🧩 TRIVIA: Her son Rajiv Gandhi was sworn in as India's prime minister later that same day.

🤫 SPOILER: In Delhi, organized mobs targeted Sikh neighborhoods, homes, businesses, and places of worship. Thousands were killed or displaced in the violence.

2008 — Bitcoin White Paper Introduces a New Form of Electronic Money 💻

An anonymous author using the name Satoshi Nakamoto sent an announcement to the Cryptography Mailing List linking a paper titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System. It proposed a decentralized payment system designed to operate without a trusted financial intermediary. The proposal became the foundation of Bitcoin, which launched in January 2009.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original version linked in the October 31 announcement was eight pages long; the familiar nine-page version represents a later revision.

🌀 OBSCURE: The announcement appeared on a specialized cryptography mailing list rather than through a financial institution, government agency, or mainstream technology publication.

These pivotal events continue to shape the course of history.   🌍

────────────────────────────────

🔬 SCIENTIFIC, TECHNOLOGICAL, AND CULTURAL MILESTONES

October 31 also witnessed artistic revelations, scientific reassessments, and technological achievements that expanded humanity's understanding of its world and itself.

1541 — Michelangelo Completes The Last Judgment 🎨

Michelangelo completed his monumental fresco on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City. Painted between 1536 and 1541, the enormous composition depicts Christ presiding over the final judgment of humanity. Pope Paul III celebrated Vespers before the newly revealed masterpiece on October 31, making the occasion one of the great artistic milestones of the Renaissance.

🧩 TRIVIA: The fresco contains approximately 391 figures, making it one of the most densely populated compositions of Michelangelo's career.

🌀 OBSCURE: The painting's nude figures provoked such controversy that later church authorities ordered painted coverings over many of them. The artist Daniele da Volterra acquired the nickname Il Braghettone, or "the breeches maker," for carrying out some of those alterations.

1992 — Vatican Formally Addresses the Galileo Affair 🔭

Pope John Paul II addressed the Pontifical Academy of Sciences and reflected on the seventeenth-century condemnation of Galileo Galilei. He acknowledged that theologians involved in the controversy had made errors in their judgment and called for a more constructive relationship between scientific inquiry and religious understanding. The address marked an important public acknowledgment of the Church's historical failure in the Galileo affair.

🧩 TRIVIA: Galileo was condemned in 1633 and spent the remaining years of his life under house arrest.

2000 — First Permanent International Space Station Crew Launched 🚀

A Russian Soyuz spacecraft lifted off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome carrying American astronaut William Shepherd and Russian cosmonauts Sergei Krikalev and Yuri Gidzenko. The Expedition 1 crew reached the International Space Station on November 2 and began the era of continuous human habitation in orbit, a presence that has continued ever since.

🧩 TRIVIA: The three crew members represented two space agencies and began the first long-duration occupation of the orbital laboratory.

2011 — United Nations Marks the Seven Billion Population Milestone 🌍

The United Nations Population Fund marked October 31 as the symbolic date when the world's population reached seven billion. The milestone highlighted the challenges of population growth, including urbanization, food security, healthcare, and access to education. The figure was based on demographic projections rather than the identification of one verifiable seventh-billionth birth.

🧩 TRIVIA: The United Nations launched its Seven Billion Actions campaign to encourage individuals and organizations to address the opportunities and challenges associated with global population growth.

Human creativity and scientific inquiry continue to expand our horizons. ✨

────────────────────────────────

English Romantic poet whose odes, including Ode to a Nightingale, Ode on a Grecian Urn, and To Autumn, became enduring masterpieces of English literature. Born in London, England.

American humanitarian and founder of the Girl Scouts of the USA, creating an organization that encouraged generations of girls to develop confidence, independence, leadership, and practical skills. Born in Savannah, Georgia, USA.

American actor, writer, director, and producer remembered for his beloved television roles in Bonanza, Little House on the Prairie, and Highway to Heaven. Born in Forest Hills, New York, USA.

Happy birthday to them all!  🎉

────────────────────────────────

🥀 MEMORIAM

We pause with gratitude and affection to remember those whose remarkable lives, achievements, and individual stories remain part of our shared history.

1926 — Harry Houdini (aged 52)

Born Erik Weisz, the Hungarian-born American magician and escape artist became one of the most celebrated entertainers of the twentieth century. His extraordinary escapes, public challenges, and determination to expose fraudulent spiritualists made him an international sensation. He died in Detroit from peritonitis following a ruptured appendix.

🧩 TRIVIA: On October 31, 1936, ten years after Houdini's death, his widow Bess held her final séance in an attempt to contact him. When no message came, she declared her vigil over and extinguished the shrine's light.

📜 APOCRYPHAL: The popular claim that a student's punches to Houdini's abdomen caused his appendix to rupture has never been conclusively established. His illness and the timing of the blows are documented, but a direct medical connection remains uncertain.

1983 — George S. Halas (aged 88)

American football pioneer, coach, executive, and founder of the Chicago Bears, George Halas helped establish the National Football League and shaped professional football for more than six decades. Known affectionately as Papa Bear, he died in Chicago from pancreatic cancer.

🧩 TRIVIA: Before becoming one of football's most influential figures, Halas briefly played professional baseball for the New York Yankees.

1984 — Indira Gandhi (aged 66)

India's first woman prime minister and one of the most influential political leaders of the twentieth century, Indira Gandhi guided the country through war, political upheaval, and sweeping social change. She oversaw India's role in the creation of Bangladesh in 1971 and served two periods as prime minister. She was assassinated by two of her bodyguards.

🧩 TRIVIA: She was the daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, independent India's first prime minister.

Italian film director and screenwriter whose imaginative, dreamlike cinema helped redefine international filmmaking. His celebrated works included La Dolce Vita, 8½, La Strada, and Amarcord. He died in Rome from cardiac arrest following a stroke earlier that year.

🧩 TRIVIA: Fellini won four Academy Awards for Best Foreign Language Film, a record achievement in that category at the time.

American actor whose performances in Stand by Me, Running on Empty, and My Own Private Idaho established him as one of the most promising young actors of his generation. His artistic talent and humanitarian interests left a lasting impression despite his tragically short career. He died in West Hollywood following an accidental drug overdose.

🧩 TRIVIA: Phoenix was a committed environmental and animal-rights activist who used his public profile to support causes beyond the film industry.

Scottish actor who became internationally famous as the original cinematic James Bond, defining the role in seven films. His distinguished career also included acclaimed performances in The Untouchables, The Hunt for Red October, and Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. He died peacefully in his sleep at his home in the Bahamas. His death certificate listed pneumonia, respiratory failure, old age, and atrial fibrillation.

🧩 TRIVIA: Connery received the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance as Chicago police officer Jim Malone in The Untouchables.

In fond remembrance of them all.  🕯️

────────────────────────────────

🏟️ SPORTS HIGHLIGHTS

October 31 has also produced pioneering achievements, remarkable individual performances, and unforgettable victories in the sporting world.

1950 — Earl Lloyd Breaks the NBA's Color Barrier 🏀

Earl "The Big Cat" Lloyd took the court for the Washington Capitols against the Rochester Royals, becoming the first African American to play in an official NBA game. His appearance marked a milestone in the integration of professional basketball and opened the way for generations of Black players.

🧩 TRIVIA: In 1971, Lloyd became head coach of the Detroit Pistons, breaking another barrier as one of the NBA's pioneering Black head coaches.

1964 — Kelso Wins His Fifth Consecutive Jockey Club Gold Cup 🐎

The legendary thoroughbred Kelso captured the Jockey Club Gold Cup at Aqueduct Racetrack, completing an extraordinary fifth consecutive victory in the prestigious two-mile race. His remarkable consistency established him as one of the greatest American racehorses of his era.

🧩 TRIVIA: Kelso was named American Horse of the Year five consecutive times, from 1960 through 1964.

1987 — Chris Antley Wins Nine Races in One Day 🏇

American jockey Chris "The Antman" Antley achieved a remarkable riding feat by winning nine races on a single calendar day. He recorded four victories at Aqueduct in New York and five more at the Meadowlands in New Jersey, establishing a record recognized by Guinness World Records.

🧩 TRIVIA: The nine victories were divided between two separate racetracks, with four afternoon wins followed by five evening wins.

2015 — New Zealand Retains the Rugby World Cup 🏉

The All Blacks defeated Australia 34–17 in the Rugby World Cup final at Twickenham Stadium in London. New Zealand became the first nation to retain the men's Rugby World Cup, securing its third championship overall in a performance led by the outstanding Dan Carter.

🧩 TRIVIA: Carter scored a long-range drop goal in the second half, helping New Zealand regain control after Australia had begun its comeback.

These sporting achievements remind us of the power of talent, determination, discipline, and perseverance. 🏆

📝 HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

October 31, 2026

❓ Question: Which historical event on October 31, 1917, involved Australian mounted troops using their bayonets as swords while charging Ottoman defensive positions?

[A] The Battle of Gallipoli
[B] The Charge at Beersheba
[C] The Battle of Passchendaele
[D] The Battle of Megiddo

👇 (Scroll down to the bottom of today's issue for the answer!)

────────────────────────────────

CLOSING

What a day to take stock of human achievement—and human folly. October 31 gave us Martin Luther challenging an empire of religious authority, Australian horsemen risking everything at Beersheba, and Houdini's widow finally accepting that the secret message she had waited ten years to hear would never come. It gave us Michelangelo's vision, Galileo's vindication, and a permanent human presence in space. It brought Keats, Juliette Gordon Low, Zaha Hadid and John Candy into the world, while taking Houdini, Fellini, River Phoenix and Sean Connery from it. Earl Lloyd broke a colour barrier in professional basketball; Kelso kept rewriting the record books; Chris Antley produced a day in the saddle few jockeys could imagine; and New Zealand conquered the rugby world.

There is no tidy moral to October 31. Its stories offer courage and cowardice, genius and injustice, triumph and loss. But they leave little doubt about one thing: the people who make history are rarely ordinary, and the consequences of what they do are rarely small.

History has had its turn. Now go make yours. ✨

────────────────────────────────

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: [B] — The Charge at Beersheba. The Australian Light Horsemen used their bayonets as swords because they were not equipped with traditional cavalry sabres or lances, helping them overwhelm Ottoman defenses and secure the town's vital wells.

text:
EDWARD R. MURROW WOULD BE A PARIAH IN TODAY’S MAINSTREAM MEDIA

The Industry Honors His Name. Would It Tolerate His Standards?

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

Edward R. Murrow would make an excellent guest at a journalism awards ceremony—provided he remained dead. His photograph could appear behind the podium, his courage could be celebrated, and everyone could applaud the importance of speaking truth to power. The trouble would begin if he walked into the newsroom the following morning and applied those principles to the people who had just finished applauding.

That is an argument, not a provable prediction. Nobody can establish which network would hire him today or which controversies he would pursue. But his documented criticism of broadcasting provides a strong basis for believing he would make media executives deeply uncomfortable. He challenged the commercial and institutional habits of his own profession, including the organization signing his paycheck.

On March 9, 1954, Murrow’s See It Now broadcast examined Senator Joseph McCarthy’s methods. Working with producer Fred Friendly and their colleagues, Murrow used recorded statements to scrutinize the senator’s accusations and conduct. McCarthy subsequently received airtime to respond. The approach put material before viewers, drew conclusions, and allowed the subject to answer. That is a more demanding exercise than assembling agreeable commentators to discuss why everyone outside the studio is dangerous.

The consequences also complicate the comforting legend. According to the Television Academy’s historical account, the McCarthy broadcast strained Murrow’s relationship with CBS, where executives questioned whether he had crossed the boundaries of editorial objectivity. Later, Alcoa withdrew its sponsorship after the program investigated a Texas land scandal involving an area where the company was expanding. CBS moved the series out of its regular weekly slot, making it a series of specials. Prestige did not eliminate the conflict between reporting and business interests.

This is why the familiar story of a courageous journalist confronting a powerful politician is incomplete. Murrow also exposed the difficulty of practicing independent journalism inside a business that must sell advertising, protect relationships, and answer to management. The person challenging power may eventually discover that power has an office upstairs.

His October 15, 1958, address to the Radio-Television News Directors Association confronted that problem directly. He criticized television’s retreat into diversion, broadcasters’ submission to political pressure, and management structures that placed crucial editorial decisions in the hands of executives whose experience lay elsewhere. He warned that commercial success offered no guarantee of public service. His concluding description of television without a higher purpose remains devastating: “merely wires and lights in a box.”

Apply that criticism today and the questions become uncomfortable. Does a story receive attention because it matters, because it attracts an audience, or because it flatters the audience already watching? Does an interview challenge a source’s assertions, or preserve access to the next interview? When evidence disrupts an outlet’s favored interpretation, does the reporting change—or does the evidence become an inconvenience?

Those questions apply across the political spectrum. A conservative outlet protecting a Republican administration fails the same test as a liberal outlet protecting a Democratic one. An independent broadcaster who substitutes suspicion for verification gains no exemption by operating outside a major network. Independence must be demonstrated in the work, especially when the findings disappoint the people paying attention.

There is counterevidence to any sweeping indictment. CBS actually broadcast Murrow’s work. His reporting required producers, correspondents, technicians, airtime, and institutional resources. The same industry that constrained him also made his journalism possible. His career therefore cannot honestly support the claim that every major newsroom is incapable of courage. It demonstrates how courage and institutional resistance can exist under the same roof.

Nor should Murrow become an imaginary spokesman for whatever position we happen to hold. We cannot recruit a dead journalist to endorse our entire worldview. We can, however, examine whether we would accept his methods when they exposed weaknesses in our own arguments. Anyone demanding fearless journalism should be prepared to become its subject.

The strongest case that Murrow would be a pariah today rests on that willingness to turn scrutiny inward. Condemning somebody else’s bias is easy. Questioning your employer’s judgment, your sponsor’s interests, your audience’s assumptions, and your profession’s self-congratulation carries a different price.

My verdict: Murrow would probably find admirers throughout today’s media—and encounter serious resistance wherever his reporting threatened revenue, access, or institutional loyalties. The historical evidence supports that tension more firmly than it supports universal rejection. But the central challenge stands: honoring his legacy requires tolerating the discomfort his journalism produced.

A Murrow award can sit quietly on a shelf. A reporter applying Murrow’s standards will eventually ask a question the owner of that shelf would rather leave unanswered.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

Trump Revives Canceled Campaign Rallies.

Canceled campaign rallies in Kansas and Iowa are back on the schedule, the White House said Friday, putting President Trump in both states Sunday for a final in-person campaign push two days before the midterm elections.  

The campaign offered no reason for the switch.  The stops were originally scrapped Thursday, when the Republican National Committee said Republicans were in a strong position in both states and that a “72-hour sprint” of phone rallies would reach more voters.  

The Kansas rally had been set for Saturday and Iowa for Sunday.  

Both will now be held Sunday, rearranged for scheduling to accommodate nearly 20 tele-rallies added to Trump’s schedule.  

In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall faces an unexpectedly close race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. “He is doing very well.  We are going to have a strong Tuesday night,” Trump said.

text:
In “White Gold” author Giles Milton gives a vivid account of the white slave trade, based on letters and manuscripts that survived from the time, several written by slaves. In one account Milton describes how in July 1625 a fleet of over twenty ships manned with Barbary pirates arrived in the thick sea mist and headed up the coast of Cornwall. Many coastal communities were completely destroyed. In 1625 the mayor of Plymouth estimated that the pirates destroyed 1000 fishing boats and a similar number of villagers were carried off into slavery in one summer alone.

Amongst the most notorious slave markets at the time was the souk in the walled city of Sale in Morocco. Milton visited Sale, walking the same path “trodden by wretched European slaves – men, women and children whose steps were slowed by the weight of their iron chains and shackles”. Once sold, most disappeared without trace, subjected to a living hell, as described by slave Robert Adams who was captured in 1620. 

The manuscript of a Cornish boy from Penryn named Thomas Pellow who was captured at sea in 1715 at the age of 11, which Milton quotes in his book, offers valuable insight into the persecution of the white slaves. He became a personal slave to the Sultan of Morocco, Moulay Ismail, in the imperial capital of Meknes. Despite being subjected to a botched circumcision operation after he was forced to convert to Islam (known as ‘turning Moor’) and thrashed senseless on many occasion, he survived to tell his tale. In 1737 at the age of 33, after 23 years in captivity Pellow managed a successful escape.

He explained that one of the Sultan’s many perverted pastimes was to marry off his slaves. He was particularly fond of mulattos or mixed race slaves and started his own “breeding programme”, matching white male slaves with black North African women while white women slaves were incarcerated in his harem and forced to breed. He would line up his slaves and citizens and call out “that one, take that one”.

The white slave trade continued well into the 1800s when the United States of America, Britain and several European nations finally came together and fought and won two wars against the Barbary pirates.

The Barbary empires went into decline from then onwards but the white slave trade continued, albeit to a lesser extent, even after France took control of Algeria and Tunisia in 1830 and 1831, and Britain passed the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833. At the same time European governments passed laws granting emancipation to slaves.

As Europe’s power increased it gradually diminished the power of the sultans, North African merchants and slave traders. Italy ultimately took control of Libya (Tripoli) in 1911 and one year later Morocco became a protectorate of France.

The people in the coastal villages of Britain and Europe could finally live in relative peace, but not for long. Within a few years another demon had raised it’s  head that led to another era of mass slaughter and brutality, human against human. We called this World War I.

text:
Sea Harvest: 

Along the coast in China, engineers are testing a system that pulls more than just drinking water from seawater. The facility cleans ocean water for everyday use while also producing hydrogen fuel as a side output. It relies on renewable energy and reuses industrial heat, keeping the process efficient without heavy fuel demands.

Leftover brine isn't dumped back into the sea but collected for other industrial uses. This approach cuts costs, reduces increasing the salinity of the water and creates less waste than older desalination systems. 

If it scales well, it could change how coastal cities think about water and energy at the same time. For coastal regions, it offers one way to meet demand without leaning harder on freshwater supplies.

text:
Holy crap, how is this not a bigger story? SpaceX, the company NASA and the Pentagon lean on for almost everything in space, is quietly walking away from new government launch work.

According to Ars Technica, SpaceX has told NASA it will stop flying Crew Dragon, the agency’s only reliable ride to the International Space Station, by or before 2030, and it has stopped selling commercial Falcon 9 launches for missions after 2028. The Wall Street Journal reports SpaceX also stopped selling shared rideshare missions on Falcon 9. Politico reported Oct. 22 that SpaceX declined to offer rides for three future Space Force satellite missions, and no other company bid on them either. Ars also reports, citing three sources, that SpaceX told companies building small Moon landers for NASA that it will not launch them.

“I do not think it’s a secret that SpaceX intends to sunset older platforms like Falcon and Dragon as they concentrate on ... Starship,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in September, according to Ars. SpaceX is still flying the government contracts it already signed, and Ars notes it does so cheaper and more reliably than almost anyone. SpaceX’s own filings point to Starlink and AI for most of its future revenue, Ars reports, and Ars and Politico say Starship as built today can’t carry many big NASA or military satellites. SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment from Politico or the Journal.

What’s next: NASA is paying Boeing $359 million to get Starliner flying again, with an uncrewed test as early as December, Space Launch Schedule reports. The Space Force is counting on ULA’s Vulcan and Blue Origin’s New Glenn, and both have had setbacks this year.

Bottom line, SpaceX earned its spot by delivering, and nobody can force a private company to take work it doesn’t want. The real failure is Washington letting one company become the only ride in town. Time for Blue Origin, ULA and the rest to step up NOW.

Sources: Ars Technica, Politico, The Wall Street Journal, Space Launch Schedule

text:
America First Is Not a Passing Phase

Prime Minister Mark Carney appears to be betting that America First is a temporary departure from the economic order Canada once knew. I respectfully disagree. The tone in Washington may change under a new administration. Canada should not assume the underlying policies will change with it.

The mistake is to confuse Donald Trump’s political style with the durability of his economic agenda. A successor can reject his rhetoric while retaining the emphasis on domestic production, investment and American economic interests. Canada cannot afford to build its strategy around the expectation that those priorities will disappear when Trump leaves office.

Nor should we confuse a more diplomatic president with a renewed American embrace of globalization. Friendlier language does not necessarily mean more open markets. Washington can be warmer toward its allies while remaining determined to bring investment, manufacturing and supply chains home.

Carney himself has supplied the right warning: “Nostalgia is not a strategy.” Yet treating America First as a passing episode risks precisely the nostalgia he cautions against, the belief that Canada can wait out an uncomfortable administration and then resume business as usual.

John F. Kennedy offered a useful warning in a 1963 speech in Frankfurt: “Change is the law of life. And those who look only to the past or the present are certain to miss the future.” His subject was Atlantic partnership, not economic nationalism, but the warning against looking backward fits Canada’s predicament.

Canada must recognize the structural changes underway in the United States and adjust accordingly. Accepting that reality does not mean endorsing every American policy. It means recognizing that our economic strategy must respond to the America that exists, not the one we would prefer.

Yes, Canada needs access to the American market. That is precisely why we must strengthen our own position: attract investment, expand productive capacity, remove domestic barriers and make ourselves a more competitive and more valuable, economic partner.

The question is not whether the next president will sound like Trump. It is how much of his economic agenda will survive him. Canada should prepare for continuity rather than count on restoration.

Nostalgia is not a strategy. Neither is hope.

text:
@NDFootball s @NavyFB is more than just a rivalry. This is a little long but worth the read.  

The Notre Dame–Navy rivalry is one of college football’s oldest and most distinctive, built less on geographic or conference ties than on mutual respect and a genuine wartime debt.

The teams first met on October 15, 1927, in Baltimore, when Knute Rockne’s Notre Dame defeated the defending national champion Midshipmen 19–6. They have played nearly every year since (the only interruption was 2020 due to COVID-19), making it the longest continuous intersectional rivalry in the sport. Notre Dame holds a lopsided series lead, but the games are played with unusual civility—both teams traditionally stand for each other’s alma maters afterward. 

The World War II Crisis

By the early 1940s, Notre Dame (then an all-male school) was in serious trouble. Most of its students had enlisted or been drafted. Civilian enrollment collapsed toward Depression-era levels—around 2,600 total students in the spring of 1943, with civilian numbers reported as low as roughly 700 in some accounts. As a private university without state funding, Notre Dame faced the real possibility of financial collapse or severe contraction. 
University President Rev. Hugh O’Donnell offered the campus facilities to the military for officer training. The Army declined or did not respond; the Navy accepted. 

Starting around 1942, the Navy established a V-7 Midshipmen’s School (an intensive indoctrination and training program) on campus. It took over several residence halls, built a drill hall and related facilities (on the site of today’s Hesburgh Library), and later expanded into the V-12 Navy College Training Program in 1943. The V-12 was the largest in the country; overall, more than 12,000 officers trained at Notre Dame between roughly 1942 and 1946. The campus earned the nickname “Annapolis West.” 

The financial support was decisive. A contract provided roughly $487,000–$488,000 for infrastructure, equipment, alterations, and administrative costs, plus ongoing monthly payments for utilities, maintenance, and per-trainee stipends. This infusion kept the university operating, roughly doubled its wartime population with the naval trainees, and stabilized its finances. Longtime president Rev. Theodore Hesburgh later put it bluntly: without the Navy, Notre Dame would have dropped to a few hundred students; instead, it stayed roughly twice normal size and contributed to the war effort. He also said the university was effectively “out of business” during the war until the Navy kept it afloat. 

The arrangement even strengthened the football program. The 1943 national championship team included numerous V-12 participants, among them future Heisman winners Angelo Bertelli and Johnny Lujack (as Navy or Marine trainees). After the 1943 season, coach Frank Leahy and much of his staff entered naval service. 

The Lasting “Debt of Honor”

In gratitude, Notre Dame has treated the annual game as repayment of a debt of honor. Hesburgh is widely credited with the commitment that Navy would remain on the schedule as long as it wished. The series has continued for nearly a century as a formal recognition of that wartime partnership, not merely a scheduling convenience. The bond also includes the continued presence of Naval ROTC on campus—something Notre Dame maintained even when other schools scaled back or ended such programs. 
In short, the rivalry is historic and continuous from the Rockne era, but its special status and endurance rest heavily on the Navy’s wartime use of the South Bend campus, which supplied both the personnel and the money that helped Notre Dame survive as an institution.

​🇮🇪  THE FRACTURED GAELIC KINGDOMS (TOP LEFT)
Ancient Ireland was a patchwork of rival chieftains and shifting territories. Sharing Brehon law and culture, they never united under one sovereign flag.

​🪕 THE NORMAN INVASION (TOP CENTER)
In the twelfth century, armored Norman knights arrived, and built stone castles to project feudal dominance. This began centuries of foreign military, and territorial entanglement.

Tudor forces executed brutal campaigns, systematically felling Ireland's ancient oak forests. This environmental purge stripped native rebels of cover, and cleared lands for foreign plantations.

​☘️ THE 1642 UPRISING AND CROMWELLIAN GENOCIDE (UPPER MIDDLE LEFT)
The 1642 Confederate uprising met Oliver Cromwell's brutal 1649–1652 campaign. New Model Army forces burnt towns, massacred defenders, and drove native families into exile, and starvation.

​🪉 THE 1798 REBELLION AND 1801 ACT OF UNION (UPPER MIDDLE CENTER)
Pikes clashed in 1798 to unite all Irishmen before defeat ushered in the 1801 Act of Union. In a bought parliament, wealthy elites traded independence for British favor, leaving the Catholic majority disenfranchised, and barred from office.

​🇮🇪 ROBERT EMMET'S REBELLION (UPPER MIDDLE RIGHT)
In 1803, Robert Emmet led a defiant but brief rebellion in Dublin's streets. His sacrifice proved the corrupt Act of Union could not extinguish the Irish push for self-determination.

​☘️ MALTHUSIAN CLEARANCES AND THE GREAT FAMINE (CENTER LEFT)
Between 1845 and 1852, potato blight and Malthusian neglect drove clearances, evictions, and catastrophic starvation. As millions suffered or fled on "coffin ships", food was exported under armed guard.

​🪕 THE YOUNG IRELANDERS AND FENIANS (CENTER)
Despite famine and demographic collapse, the 1848 Young Irelander rebellion, and 1867 Fenian uprising kept the physical force tradition alive.

​🪉 THE FAILED ATTEMPTS AT HOME RULE (CENTER RIGHT)
Late nineteenth-century leaders fought for self-governance through constitutional politics in London. Their persistent efforts were repeatedly blocked, diluted, and betrayed by Westminster opposition.

​🎻 THE 1916 EASTER RISING (LOWER MIDDLE LEFT)
The Dublin GPO burned during Easter Week of 1916 as armed volunteers made their stand. Their defeat, and subsequent execution transformed public sentiment, reigniting the struggle for a Republic.

 🇮🇪 THE WAR OF INDEPENDENCE (LOWER MIDDLE CENTER)
From 1919 to 1921, guerrilla "flying columns" waged war against British forces. Supported by local communities, they rendered Ireland ungovernable, forcing the empire to the negotiating table.

​🪕 THE PARTITION OF IRELAND (LOWER MIDDLE RIGHT)
A 1921 treaty created fortified border checkpoints, carving the island into two jurisdictions instead of a united republic. This partition left a lasting legacy of division, and unfinished business.

​🪉 MODERN RESILIENCE (BOTTOM FOREGROUND)
Today, a resilient crowd of modern Irish people stands shoulder to shoulder, looking forward. Having outlasted centuries of conflict, and elite deals, they embody the hope for a truly united, sovereign future.

text:
Samhain in Irish mythology

Samhain appears in several important medieval Irish mythological narratives.

Some particularly interesting examples include:

The Wooing of Étaín (Tochmarc Étaíne)

This story concerns Étaín, Midir, and the supernatural world of the Aos Sí. It explores transformation, love, time, and the relationship between human and supernatural existence.

The Adventure of Nera (Echtra Nerai)

This is particularly relevant to Samhain.

Nera undertakes a challenge on Samhain night and encounters supernatural beings. He follows them into their otherworldly dwelling and witnesses events that reveal the extraordinary relationship between the human world and the Otherworld.

The Intoxication of the Ulstermen (Mesca Ulad)

This narrative involves the Ulstermen travelling through a series of extraordinary events, with Samhain providing an important mythological setting.

The Boyhood Deeds of Finn (Macgnímartha Finn)

The early life of Finn mac Cumhaill is connected with the seasonal and supernatural world of early Irish heroic literature.

These stories are valuable because they show that Samhain was not simply an agricultural holiday. It was also an important literary and mythological setting in which extraordinary encounters, transformations, and challenges could occur. 

What happened during Samhain?

Communal feasting and assemblies

Samhain was a major opportunity for people to gather.

Local rulers, warriors, and communities assembled for feasts and celebrations.

These gatherings also had political significance. They reinforced relationships between rulers and their people, and provided opportunities for agreements and exchanges.

Livestock and agricultural practices

The changing season affected livestock management.

Animals were brought in from summer pastures, and some were slaughtered to reduce the number that needed winter feeding.

This connected Samhain to food, survival, and the redistribution of resources.

Bonfires

Bonfires are strongly associated with later Samhain and Halloween traditions.

However, we should be careful about claiming that every familiar bonfire custom was already practiced in exactly the same form in pre Christian Ireland.

There is clearer early Irish textual evidence for ritual fires at Bealtaine, particularly the driving of cattle between fires for protection.

Divination

Later Irish and Scottish Halloween traditions included attempts to discover future events, especially marriage and romantic relationships.

Apple games, nuts, and other household customs became associated with fortune-telling.

These practices reflect the idea that a seasonal transition could provide unusual opportunities to gain knowledge about the future.

The mystery of the name Samhain

There is actually a fascinating linguistic question here.

Samhain is traditionally explained as meaning something like summer's end.

This explanation is associated with the Irish elements sam (summer) and fuin (end)

However, Celtic linguistics offers a more complicated picture.

University College Cork's Department of Early and Medieval Irish discusses an intriguing connection with the ancient Coligny Calendar discovered in France.

This calendar contains two month names:

•SAMON
•GIAMON

The second is associated with the Celtic word for winter, while the first is associated with summer.

This raises an interesting possibility: Samhain's name may preserve a much older relationship with the summer season than its modern position at the beginning of winter suggests.

There is even a fascinating passage in The Adventure of Nera in which a supernatural woman tells Nera to bring back the fruits of summer from the Otherworld.

He returns with summer flowers and plants even though it is Samhain.

The story suggests that the Otherworld operates with a different relationship with time and the seasons.

Summer, growth, and abundance have not disappeared completely when winter begins.
They exist somewhere beyond the human world.

text:
Trick-or-treating didn’t start with candy companies.

It started more than 2,000 years ago, with bonfires, masks, and a night when the dead were believed to walk the Earth. 🎃

Here’s how a Celtic festival became the night your doorbell never stops ringing 👇

𝐒𝐚𝐦𝐡𝐚𝐢𝐧: 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐯𝐞𝐢𝐥 𝐠𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧

The ancient Celts celebrated Samhain from sunset on October 31 to sunset on November 1. It marked their New Year: the end of the harvest and the start of the long, dark winter.

The Celts believed that the boundary between the living world and the spirit world became blurred during this transition. Spirits, ancestors, and mischievous creatures like the shape-shifting púca, were thought to walk the Earth.

To protect themselves, people lit massive bonfires and wore disguises made of animal skins and masks so roaming spirits wouldn't recognize them. Many also left out food and drink to keep the spirits happy.

𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠

By the Middle Ages, the poor went “souling.” They knocked on doors and offered to pray for a household’s dead in exchange for “soul cakes,” small spiced buns.

In Scotland and Ireland, kids went “guising” short for “disguise”. They went house to house in costume performing either a song, poem or trick for food and drink—an early forerunner to modern trick-or-treating.

No act, no snack. 🎭

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐩 𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧

Irish folklore tells of Stingy Jack, a man who tricked the Devil so many times that when he died, neither heaven nor hell would take him. He was left to wander the dark with only a burning coal in a carved turnip to light his way.

People carved scary faces into turnips and potatoes to scare off Jack and other wandering spirits. These became “Jack of the lantern.”

𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚

In the 1800s, millions of Irish and Scottish immigrants crossed the Atlantic, many escaping the Great Famine. They brought Halloween with them.

They also found pumpkins: bigger, softer, and much easier to carve than a turnip. 🎃

Bonfires became porch lights. Animal skins became superhero costumes. Soul cakes became fun-size Snickers.

𝐒𝐨, 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧…

When a tiny vampire rings your doorbell this Halloween, they’re keeping up a 2,000-year-old tradition. Have the good candy ready. 🍬

Synopsis
Global traditions and creative local alternatives offer many ways to celebrate the spirit of the season beyond traditional trick-or-treating—which historically evolved from Celtic Samhain-inspired guising and later included rowdy youth mischief that sometimes escalated into urban hooliganism with pranks, property damage, and chaos in 19th–20th century cities. The provided resources emphasize safer, structured, spiritual, and inclusive options that reclaim the liminal, ancestral, and harvest-honoring essence of the season while moving past chaotic elements.
Alternative Halloween Activities (At Home or Locally) • Outdoor Parades & Scavenger Hunts: Organize a neighborhood bike and wagon parade in costume, or set up a yard-to-yard themed scavenger hunt with clue sheets. • Backyard or Drive-In Movies: Set up an outdoor projector with pre-made popcorn or host a cozy “Ultimate Night In” with jack-o’-lanterns and pillow forts. • No-Carve Pumpkin Decorating: Use paint, fabric markers, stickers, or stencils on outdoor tables instead of carving. • Mask and Craft Decorating: Use plain cotton masks, sequins, and fabric markers, or craft autumn paper plate designs. • Community Sharing Boxes: Create a charity food or book donation box to share love with the local community.
Supporting the Autism Learning Partners page (“20 Alternative Activities To Do On Halloween”) adds sensory-friendly and lower-crowd ideas suited to neurodiverse individuals, such as cozy movie nights, indoor trick-or-treat stations, backyard carnival games, pumpkin-patch visits, craft/baking parties, photo booths, neighborhood decoration tours, karaoke, storytelling, escape-room challenges, and puzzle nights—emphasizing control over environment, reduced sensory overload, and flexible participation.
International Halloween-Like Traditions Explore how other cultures honor ancestors, harvest seasons, and spirits around the world: • Día de los Muertos (Mexico): Observed from November 1 to 2, this UNESCO-recognized tradition honors deceased family members with colorful ofrendas (altars) of food, marigolds, and pan de muerto, alongside street processions and skull makeup. • Samhain (Ireland & Scotland): Celebrated on October 31, this 2,000-year-old Celtic festival marks the boundary between worlds. In Scotland, the Samhuinn Fire Festival features fire-dancing, wild drumming, and costumed parades, while in Ireland people eat fruit cake called barmbrack to discover future fortunes. • Fastelavn (Denmark): Celebrated every February as a carnival-like children’s holiday where kids wear costumes, eat cream-filled fastelavnsboller, and play slå katten af tønden (whacking a decorated barrel full of candy). • Hungry Ghost Festival (Hong Kong): Held during the seventh lunar month, communities burn “hell money” and paper goods, light candles and lanterns, and leave food offerings to appease roaming spirits. • Seleenwoche (Austria): During All Souls’ Week, families place bread, water, and a lighted lamp on a table before bed to welcome the souls of the dead. • Correfocs (Spain): A high-energy Catalan tradition featuring pyrotechnics, fire-runners, and festive street parades. • Walpurgis Night (Germany): Held on April 30 across the Harz Mountains, this family-friendly festival features bonfires, folk music, and witch-themed costume parades.

The Walk Away option:

The President can avoid another round of diplomatic frustrations and dangerous escalation by simply declaring victory and walking away. President Trump has already laid the groundwork for this scenario; each time he’s discussed the war and listed off the number of Iranian capabilities we’ve destroyed, he’s messaging a win. 

Per his own statements, the war ends when Trump says it’s over. 

Now is the perfect time for him to say it’s over.  
 
By pulling our blockade from the Gulf & our troops out of our remaining bases in the region,  we end the conflict kinetically while simultaneously (finally) depriving Iran a key point of leverage: actionable military targets to strike. We essentially force Iran to reopen the SOH because they can no longer reasonably justify attacking ships without an active aggressor to blame.  

The Iranians have demonstrated that they care deeply about public opinion—therefore, once we lift the blockade, they’re likely to engage in serious talks with the Gulf states to come up with an arrangement that quickly opens the SOH. 

We then use economic leverage to our advantage: we offer incremental sanctions relief on Iranian oil to make opening SOH a non-negotiable for the Iranians. While President Trump takes a victory lap about having ended the war & ensuring that Iran won’t have a nuclear weapon, our diplomats can quietly work with our Gulf allies and the Iranians to negotiate a workable peace plan that ensures the SOH stays open.  
 
Right now Iranian leaders are unable to make many concessions with the U.S. threatening another round of strikes. 

The Iranian people rallied around the hardliners in their government after we killed the former supreme leader & members of his family including children, and the tragic bombing of a girl’s school. If you understand basic human nature, you’ll understand why all of this has had a radicalizing effect on their population. Now,  many Iranians believe that the only acceptable path forward, for the sake of their national pride and to deter future attacks, is by forcing a badly blooded U.S. retreat from the region. 

Our walking away from the conflict will provide Iranian leadership a symbolic victory they can tout to their now-galvanized people, allowing more latitude for them to eventually reach a compromise with us on bigger items, like the nuclear issue. By walking away, we buy more trade space for compromise in future negotiations that won’t be possible if we remain poised to strike Iran.  
 
At the moment, Trump has the political power in the U.S. to sell walking away as a victory to his base. Of course, the same neocons who talked him into this war will complain and attack him, but they don’t represent a legitimate constituency. 

This war is widely unpopular—ending it will be widely popular. In the long run, history will commend Trump for choosing this option. 

In recognizing that the war was a mistake, and by leaving quickly before getting bogged down in a quagmire, he avoids falling into the gambler’s fallacy that ensnared many of his predecessors and got thousands of Americans killed.

We’re already unable to help the Saudis deter the Houthis—if we engage in kinetic combat against Iran, we’ll be even more  incapable of assisting our already-weakened allies.

More strikes won’t change the game. Walking away & declaring victory before Tuesday sets a positive tone for the elections & resets the parameters for negotiations with Iran.

President Trump can avoid the escalation trap by walking away now, before the fog of war envelops the rest of his presidency.
