text:
Are car buyers turning away from electric vehicles, or back toward them? The answer depends a lot on which survey you read, and when it was taken.

Last December, EY’s global survey found 50% of car shoppers planned to buy a gas-powered vehicle in the next two years, up 13 points. Interest in fully electric vehicles dropped 10 points, to 14%. The federal EV tax credits had just ended, and Ford, GM and other automakers were scaling back their EV plans.

Then gas prices took off. Since the conflict with Iran began in late February, gasoline prices are up about 34% over the past year, according to the government’s inflation data. A survey released in September by HERE Technologies and SBD Automotive found that more than half of U.S. drivers say high gas prices have made them more interested in going electric. The share who think there are enough public chargers jumped from 28% to 47%.

Still, about two in five drivers say EVs cost too much, and that’s the real sticking point. The average new car payment is already about $787 a month, according to Edmunds. Most families can’t stretch further for a pricier car, no matter what’s under the hood.

My take: this isn’t a culture war. It’s a math problem, and the math keeps changing. When gas is cheap, a gas car wins on price. When gas spikes, an EV or a hybrid starts to look a lot better, especially if you can charge at home.

If you’re car shopping, run your own numbers:
~Compare the total cost, not just the sticker price. Include fuel, insurance, maintenance and how long you plan to keep the car.
~Look at hybrids. They often split the difference on price and fuel savings.
~Consider used. EVs lose value quickly, so a three-year-old one can be a bargain.
~Check for state incentives. Colorado has offered its own EV tax credit, so see what’s available now.

Buy the car that fits your budget and your driving, not the one that fits a headline.

I’m not a financial advisor.

Sources: EY Mobility Consumer Index, HERE Technologies and SBD Automotive EV Index, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Edmunds, Autoblog

text:
All 13 offensive snaps from Marvin Harrison Jr. vs. NYG.

DeMeco Ryans said he'd see more playing time, and Ryans, Nick Caley and C.J. Stroud have all praised his intelligence and how quickly he's picked up the offense. Yet he played just ONE more snap than last week.

Stats:
• 13 snaps (9 pass, 4 run)
• 3 slot snaps (33.3% of passing snaps)
• 1 reception, 6 yards, 1 TD
• 68.6 PFF offensive grade
• 67.7 PFF receiving grade

My observations:
• His first two snaps were essentially clear-out assignments, one on a run play (called back by penalty, which could have been on him or Braden Smith, I suspect on Marv looking at another play in same formation where MHJ was off) and another on a screen.
• Drew a defensive holding penalty on another rep.
• Nice red-zone TD on a fake drag into a seam route. Good catch.
• Had a chance on the deep over with Stroud under pressure. Tough catch, and PFF didn't charge him with a drop. I thought he could've gotten more extension by going with one hand (he said the same post game), but I don't criticize him much here. Looked worse on TV than it actually was.
• On the very next play, Stroud overshot him on a deep post. Really liked Harrison's release and how he stemmed back outside after initially releasing inside to create additional space. Expect that connection to improve as they build chemistry.
• Two encouraging blocking reps on tosses to Woody Marks. Willing blocker who showed good awareness, including identifying the safety as the most dangerous defender with the corner playing off.

Overall, some encouraging flashes in a VERY limited sample. The route-running ability is evident, he's willing to block, and the TD showed what he can offer in the red zone.

Now I'd like to actually see the increased playing time we've heard about. Hard to build chemistry and make a meaningful impact playing just 13 snaps a game.

EQUIGAS Announces New Authorized Distributor Partnerships

At EQUIGAS, we are always looking for ways to improve our services and better support our customers. Our goal is to offer a complete line of products for the gas industry and be a true One-Stop Shop: ONE company serving customers from three locations across the United States.

Today we are excited to announce not ONE but TWO New Partnerships. EQUIGAS is proud to be the Authorized Distributor for Norris Cylinder, a TriMas Company and Premier Cryogenic Services. Both are American manufacturers known for the quality of their products and the strength of their people.

Norris Cylinder Company
Was founded by Kenneth T. Norris in 1930 to make fabricated metal products. In 1940, the company started its Compressed Gas Cylinder Division. Today, Norris Cylinder is the only US manufacturer of Steel High-Pressure Cylinders for Industrial Gases. It is also one of the world's largest manufacturers of high and low-pressure cylinders, with plants in Longview, TX, and Huntsville, AL.

Norris Cylinder makes a wide range of seamless and welded steel cylinders in the United States and sells them in more than 80 countries. They are used in welding, medical, laboratory, food and beverage, breathing air, fire protection, aviation and many other applications.

Premier Cryogenic Services, LLC, (PCS)
Joe and Mark the Morreale Brothers, founded PCS in July 2019. The company is headquartered at 615 North 6th Street in La Porte (Houston), Texas, with additional locations in Slidell, Louisiana, and Delphi, Indiana.

PCS's mission is to deliver the same high-quality cryogenic equipment service that the Morreale family has been known for over decades. PCS is a DOT-Registered, ASME R-Stamp facility. It specializes in inspecting, retesting, repairing and rehabilitating cryogenic containers and transport trailers, including LIN, LOX, LAR, LNG and LH2 equipment.

PCS recently acquired Elite Cryogenics LLC of Slidell, Louisiana, Elite is an industry leader in retesting, repairing and rehabilitating Liquid Hydrogen Transport Trailers, and it now operates as part of Premier Cryogenic Services.

PCS also plans to begin manufacturing Cryogenic Bulk Tanks, Microbulk Tanks and Liquid Cylinders in the USA very soon.

Our sister company, Correct Cryogenics, has facilities in Fontana, CA and Greensboro, NC. Those facilities can serve as satellite locations where PCS customers can get minor repairs and 1-year and 5-year trailer inspections.

text:
My Soul Is Not Theirs to Command: A Magical Vision of Freedom, Solidarity and Becoming: The past few months have been a journey back towards myself; a gradual unlearning of hesitation and self-denial, until I am finally starting to find the courage to give the fullest expression of my soul permission to exist, darlings. As I continue to write book 1 of my new magical world, something is shifting inside of me. That's hot! I am starting to embrace my soul and the great light that is within me. Claps for me! I no longer wish to negotiate with, suppress or apologise for the parts of my soul that are simply asking to be embraced and loved in this world in which we all have to live. F U to this idea. There are some in society who think they control people like me and dictate who our soul is. They can AVADA KEDAVRA away, dears. These people do not possess jurisdiction over my soul or indeed the souls of my transgender brothers and sisters. So Ta-ta to them and their way of doing things. The soul's autonomy is a divine right. Yes, amen to this! I absolutely refuse to surrender the keys to my own soul's identity to mere mortals who have appointed themselves its gatekeepers. How innovative of me, darlings. My soul is not a territory over which other people have been granted sovereignty. The sooner people realise this glorious divine fact, the better. My soul does not require permission to transform. People may attempt to define me, diminish me or dictate the parameters of my existence, but they will never be the custodians of my becoming, dears. Nor shall they ever command the transformation, dictate the becoming or presume supreme dominion over the precious souls of my fellow transgender witches and wizards!

I do not regard the identities of transgender people as Hogwarts letters inviting debate, darling. I have come to accept that I am a true creative. I have always felt that my purpose in this world is to make things: to write, to perform, to imagine, to dream, to construct and to contribute something meaningful to this world. I regard myself as a humanity raiser and someone who values innovation in creative thinking. After all, Paris Hilton taught me that my ADHD is a superpower! That's hot! However, when it comes to this particular issue, my ambition is not only artistic. Ah, I have bigger dreams, darling. I have come to the realisation that I do not want my art to exist in a moral vacuum. That would be so 2K era coded. If I have been given an aptitude for language, storytelling and connecting with fellow beings, I want to put those gifts towards something that truly matters, darling. There is something deeply meaningful to me about the prospect of turning my own personal talent into a collective resource to come to the aid of transgender people. I would love women and transgender women to stand together for the good of all womanhood! Although I have a strong desire to defend my community, I am also interested in building bridges between artistic ambition and practical solidarity. My ultimate ambition is to turn my imagination into practical infrastructure and solidarity into something people can actually access in the real world, darling. Something meaningful that can really help them to live better lives. I wish to create wealth through my writing that can lead to the creation of opportunities that do not merely sound compassionate in a statement but become genuinely useful in somebody's everyday life. I wish for my ideas to acquire safe walls, foundations, doors of hope and windows of light. I want them to become places where people can actually live their lives without fear. I desire them to become places where people can actually live their lives in a state of happiness, inner acceptance, and love. Essentially, I do not want to spend my life drawing maps towards a better magical world. I want to help the magic to leap off of the pages and build the places those maps promise. I am someone who knows what it means to struggle, and who is trying to create a future in which my own possibilities are not dictated by the limitations of my present dire circumstances, darling.

Darlings, I know what it means to have ambitions that exceed the resources currently available to pursue them. I lay awake at night dreaming of ways in which I can create a life in which I can afford to become more fully myself, while also helping to create a world in which other transgender people have greater opportunities to do the same. I am trying to build a stable future for myself in which my soul can be free. In an ideal world I would like financial independence in order to pursue my artistic fulfilment and the freedom to pursue my own transition. I have come to realise that there is no contradiction between wanting to save yourself and wanting to help others find safety. Both can coexist. My intentions are to save lives, including my own. I want to build a life in which I can flourish. This flourishing shall never come at the expense of my community, but with the knowledge that my own flourishing shall help make room for theirs. You could place a billion pounds on the magical table, and it would still not purchase the right to ask me to abandon my principles, darling. I am not prepared to exchange the people I stand beside for the people who might offer me a seat at their table. There have been some Muggles who have tried to tell me that Harry Potter is not for people like me. These people did not write Harry Potter. They did not create the magic. Yet, they are telling me, a fan, that the world is not for someone like me. Let me be very clear to those people: if the price of admission to somebody else's establishment is silence about the mistreatment of my community, I would rather remain outside, darling.

There are those who have suggested I try to work with Ms Rowling to help transgender people. I find this idea rather amusing. As if she would ever work with somebody like me! Trust me, darlings, I have dreamed of this possibility myself. In my wildest dreams I dreamed of somehow getting an audition for Harry Potter and representing my community. I guess I dreamed of trying to bring people together, soften hearts, change minds and show the world that magic is for everyone. However, I am now putting my efforts into building my own magical world. I am trying to build a place where people like me can belong. I shall never presume that anybody would ever see my X posts or that anyone would ever consider funding somebody like me. After all, I am a mere Muggle from Scotland. However, I would like to note for anyone who may ever see this that I would rather be a one-woman undertaking than become a well-funded accomplice to the abandonment of my own community. And to the trolls who like to say the most horrific things to me: I am not looking for permission to care about the people I care about. I am building a world to generate outcomes in which transgender people can encounter a world in which their safety is not an afterthought and their dignity is not a matter of public convenience. I understand not everyone shall agree with me. That is a choice for YOU to make. I am currently looking for funders to help me in my quest to save myself and all other transgender souls. I know where I stand. The question is, do you?✨

text:
An Inspirational Leadership Journey at Sri Lanka’s Largest Bank

The journey of Y. A. Jayathilaka — shaped by education, perseverance, and a belief in purposeful transformation.

There are journeys that are measured by positions held and milestones achieved. And then there are journeys that carry a deeper meaning, journeys that demonstrate what education, opportunity, and perseverance can make possible.

The journey of Y. A. Jayathilaka, Chief Executive Officer/General Manager, Bank of Ceylon, belongs to the latter.

From a modest classroom in Embilipitiya to the leadership of Sri Lanka’s largest bank, his story is not simply one of professional advancement. It is a reflection of the possibilities created by Sri Lanka’s free education system, the value of determined effort, and the importance of remembering the communities and people who shape us along the way.

His recent return to the two schools that played a defining role in his early life, Moraketiya Maha Vidyalaya, where he completed his formative schooling, and Embilipitiya Central College, where he pursued his Advanced Level studies, brought that journey into particularly sharp focus.

The Upahara ceremonies held in his honor were more than occasions of recognition. They were moments of reconnection with former teachers, classmates, friends, and communities, and with the beginnings of a journey that eventually led him to the helm of one of the country’s most important institutions.

Returning to those classrooms as the CEO of the Bank of Ceylon, however, was not simply a return as a senior corporate leader. It was a return as a former student, one who had once shared the same aspirations, uncertainties, and hopes as countless young Sri Lankans.

One of the most poignant moments was his tribute to Piyadasa Kapuge, his former Head of the Commerce Section. In presenting an Upahara plaque to his former teacher, Jayathilaka acknowledged the guidance and encouragement that had helped him recognize the possibilities that education could offer.

That moment captured something fundamental about his journey: success is rarely achieved alone.

Education is the foundation

He began his education at Moraketiya Maha Vidyalaya before continuing at Embilipitiya Central College. His academic performance, including achieving the second-highest in the district, opened the way to university education at the University of Sri Jayewardenepura.

He subsequently obtained a Bachelor of Science (Special) in Business Administration from the University of Sri Jayewardenepura and a Master of Business (Finance) from the University of Kelaniya. His professional education was further strengthened through a Diploma in Banking and Finance, Associate Membership of the Institute of Bankers of Sri Lanka, and executive and professional programs at the Postgraduate Institute of Management, University of Sri Jayewardenepura, and the Advanced Management Program at INSEAD, France.

For him, education was never merely a pathway to a qualification. It was an opportunity to broaden horizons.

That perspective has remained visible throughout his career, particularly in his emphasis on developing people, sharing knowledge, and ensuring that technology and innovation create opportunities rather than barriers.

A career built from the ground up

Before entering banking, Jayathilaka gained corporate experience at John Keells Holdings and Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation. In 1997, he joined the Bank of Ceylon as a Management Trainee.

His early banking experience included service at a rural branch in Bibile, providing first-hand exposure to the realities of grassroots banking and the financial needs of communities outside the major commercial centers.

His career subsequently expanded across a remarkably broad range of banking functions.

He gained experience in branch banking, Treasury, and Treasury Back Office operations, international banking, and exposure to BOC UK. Along the way, his responsibilities expanded to include project management, credit and recovery, product development, process automation, and digital banking.

This breadth of experience became one of the defining characteristics of his leadership.

Rather than developing within a single specialist discipline, he accumulated an understanding of banking from multiple perspectives: the customer at the branch, the treasury dealing room, the credit function, the technology platform, and the international banking environment.

His progression through the Bank’s leadership structure was equally gradual. He entered Executive Management in 2015 through key Assistant General Manager responsibilities and moved into Corporate Management in February 2020, taking on a broader strategic role in the institution. In August 2025, he assumed duties as Acting General Manager/Chief Executive Officer of the Bank of Ceylon. His appointment was formally confirmed on February 27, 2026 as the Bank’s 24th General Manager/Chief Executive Officer.

Innovation with a purpose

Modern banking is increasingly defined by technology. But technology alone does not constitute transformation.

Throughout his career, Jayathilaka has maintained a practical view of innovation: technology must ultimately make banking simpler, more accessible, and more useful to people.

His experience in major technology and transformation initiatives has included core banking systems, trade finance platforms, workflow automation, and digital banking solutions. His Project Management experience at BOC UK Limited also provided exposure to large-scale system implementations and international banking practices.

At the Bank of Ceylon, this philosophy was reflected in initiatives such as BOC Digi Branches, Branch on Wheels, Smart Passbooks, and Cardless Withdrawals efforts aimed at taking banking beyond conventional boundaries and making services more convenient for customers.

His focus on innovation also extended to the Bank’s employees.

Initiatives such as BOC Meta Banking, BOC e-Learning, and BOC Bankpedia were designed to improve access to information and knowledge within the institution. TV BOC (Sri Lanka’s first dedicated television channel managed by banking staff) provided another platform for communication, learning, and staff engagement.

Perhaps more importantly, his approach has consistently linked technology with inclusion.

BOC Connect, the Agent Banking Service launched in 2021, sought to take banking services closer to communities that traditionally had limited access to conventional banking facilities. Its expansion through the postal network represented another step towards bringing financial services closer to the people. Furthermore, the expansion of agent banking services in partnership with the Sri Lanka Post Department was another important step towards bringing financial services closer to the people. Today, BOC Connect has expanded across all 25 districts, covering 331 Divisional Secretariat Divisions. Through such innovative initiatives, he has been able to respond to the real needs of the people and make banking services more accessible, convenient, and inclusive.

These initiatives reflect a broader philosophy: innovation is most valuable when it addresses a real need.

Leadership beyond the balance sheet

Jayathilaka’s leadership philosophy has also been shaped by the belief that a bank’s responsibilities extend beyond financial performance.

His interest in developing communities was equally evident through initiatives such as “Ran Kekulu Chaarika”, which provided children from rural areas with opportunities to visit Colombo and experience educational and cultural landmarks, including the BOC Currency Museum fully sponsored by the Bank.

The creation of Sri Lanka’s first dedicated agricultural banking arm was another expression of this approach. By developing financial solutions specifically for farmers and agri-businesses, the initiative sought to connect banking with one of the fundamental sectors of the national economy.

For a state-owned institution with a nationwide presence, such initiatives carry significance beyond commercial returns. They speak to the role of banking in enabling opportunity, supporting enterprise, and contributing to inclusive economic development.

Leading BOC into a digital future

Today, as CEO of the Bank of Ceylon, Jayathilaka leads the institution at a time when the banking industry is undergoing perhaps its most profound transformation in generations.

Customers increasingly expect banking to be instantaneous, intuitive, and available wherever they are.

Against this backdrop, the launch of BOC Flex- the Bank’s Internet and Mobile Banking solution marked an important milestone in BOC’s digital journey. Launched on March 21, 2025, Flex has rapidly expanded its customer base and transaction volumes. According to the figures cited in the Bank’s profile, the platform has reached approximately 2.5 million registered users, facilitating around 300 billion rupees in monthly transactions and approximately 400,000 transactions a day.

Yet the significance of Flex is not simply measured by transaction volumes.

For Jayathilaka, digital transformation represents a fundamental change in how a bank relates to its customers. The objective is not to digitize existing processes for their own sake, but to understand how people live and manage their finances and then redesign banking around those realities.

That philosophy is increasingly shaping BOC’s future direction, with the Bank seeking to combine its traditional strength of trust and accessibility with technology, innovation and a more seamless digital customer experience.

Beyond the boardroom

Jayathilaka’s contribution to the financial sector extends beyond his executive responsibilities at BOC.

Over the years, he has served on the boards of institutions connected with banking, finance, technology, and the wider economy, including BOC Property Development and Management, Ceybank Holiday Homes, BOC IT Solutions, LankaPay, BOC London Board, and the Credit Information Bureau of Sri Lanka.

His association with BOC UK Limited has provided additional international exposure, while his involvement with LankaPay and CRIB has connected his experience with two important components of Sri Lanka’s financial infrastructure digital payments and credit information.

He has also contributed to the development of the banking profession through his role on the Governing Board of the Institute of Bankers of Sri Lanka, supporting professional development and the strengthening of banking capabilities.

These responsibilities illustrate the breadth of his professional journey, spanning rural branch banking to international finance, customer service to technology, and operational management to institutional governance.

Looking back on Jayathilaka’s journey, perhaps the most enduring lesson is that the greatest measure of success is not simply how far one travels, but how much one can contribute along the way.

text:
The Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna campaigned for decades against the Prevention of Terrorism Act. It called the PTA a tool of state oppression: a law so fundamentally incompatible with democratic governance that it could not be reformed, only repealed. "Repeal the PTA" was not a footnote in the NPP's 2024 platform. It was a headline, a moral commitment offered to the electorate as proof that this government, unlike every government before it, would not use the architecture of counterterrorism to silence the citizens it was elected to serve. The electorate believed them. The electorate was wrong.

The Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill is not the repeal of the PTA. It is the PTA's resurrection in a body that is, by every meaningful legal measure, stronger, broader, and more dangerous than the law it claims to replace. The PSTA does not narrow the state's power to detain, surveil, restrict, and punish. It expands that power, extends it into territories the PTA never reached, and does so under a title carefully chosen to make opposition sound like sympathy for terrorism. This is the oldest trick in the authoritarian playbook, and the one the JVP spent thirty years denouncing when it was deployed by others.

Begin with the definition of terrorism, because the definition is where the danger lives. The PSTA's definition is not precise; it is panoramic. Damage to property. Disruption of essential services. Actions intended to intimidate a section of the public. Actions intended to compel the government to do or abstain from doing any act. Read those phrases as a lawyer, not as a citizen who trusts the government's assurances. A hartal that disrupts essential services is terrorism. A protest that damages public property is terrorism. A trade union action intended to compel the government to raise wages is, on the plain text of the statute, terrorism. The JVP (the party that enforced hartals through assassination during the 1987–1989 insurrection, and killed bus drivers who defied its strike orders) has drafted a law under which its own historical conduct would constitute terrorism of the most unambiguous kind. The party that would have been proscribed and dismantled under the very statute it now proposes has decided that such a statute is, after all, necessary. The only thing that has changed is who holds the pen.

The detention provisions are the heart of the matter. The PSTA permits extended detention on the authority of a ministerial order. Not a judicial order. A ministerial order. The minister, a political appointee answerable to the party leadership and in the final analysis to Tilvin Silva and the JVP Politburo, is empowered to authorise the detention of any person suspected of involvement in terrorism, as defined by a statute whose reach encompasses virtually every form of forceful dissent. A judicial warrant requires a judge to be persuaded, before detention occurs, that there are legal grounds for it. A ministerial order requires only that the minister sign a form. The safeguard is not the law; the safeguard is the minister's restraint. And the restraint of a minister operating within a party whose institutional culture treats criticism as sabotage and dissent as betrayal is not a safeguard any serious legal analyst would rely upon.

The admissibility of confessions is where the Bill reveals its true inheritance. The PTA was internationally condemned for permitting confessions obtained during police custody to be admitted as evidence. A suspect detained without charge, held for weeks or months, isolated from legal counsel, and subjected to the pressures that attend prolonged detention produces a confession. The confession is admitted. The conviction follows. The detention produces the evidence that justifies the detention, and the circle closes. The PSTA does not break this circle; it draws it in slightly different ink. The provisions governing the admissibility of statements made during detention are insufficient by every standard articulated by international human rights law, by the UN Human Rights Committee, by the International Commission of Jurists, and by the very civil society organisations the JVP courted as allies in opposition and now dismisses as obstacles in government.

The proscription power is perhaps the most dangerous provision and the one that has received the least scrutiny. The PSTA empowers the government to declare organisations terrorist by executive order, rendering membership, support, and association criminal offences. This is the power to criminalise a political party, a trade union, a student federation, or a media outlet by ministerial decree. The JVP knows, from direct and bitter experience, what proscription means. It knows that the power to declare an organisation terrorist is the power to destroy it without proving, in a court of law, that it has committed a terrorist act. It knows this because it lived it. And it has chosen, with the full weight of that historical knowledge, to claim the same power for itself.

The JVP used the PTA before it even had the chance to replace it. Suresh Sallay was detained under the PTA by the very government that had promised to repeal it. The PTA was necessary in this case, they said. The threat was real. The detention was warranted. These are the same arguments made by every previous government, the same arguments the JVP spent decades condemning as authoritarian pretexts, and the same arguments that are now apparently valid when the JVP is the one making them. The Sallay detention was not an anomaly; it was a preview. It demonstrated that the JVP's objection to the PTA was never principled. It was positional. The JVP did not oppose the PTA because it was a bad law; it opposed the PTA because the JVP was not the government.

The international community has noticed. The United Nations, the International Commission of Jurists, Amnesty International, the Bar Association of Sri Lanka, and legal scholars and constitutional experts across the country and around the world have examined the PSTA and concluded that it fails to meet the minimum standards required by international human rights law, by the ICCPR to which Sri Lanka is a state party, and by the basic principles of due process that distinguish a democracy from a state that merely holds elections. The JVP's response follows a pattern by now familiar: the critics are misinformed, politically motivated, and aligned with the forces the state must protect itself against. This is the same reflex exhibited by the Rajapaksa government when criticised for the PTA, the same reflex exhibited by every government that has ever used national security to justify the erosion of civil liberties, and the JVP,having built its identity on opposing this exact reflex, now exhibits it with the fluency of long practice.

There is a test every terrorism statute must pass: would you be comfortable with this law if your worst political enemy were the one enforcing it? Would you trust the Rajapaksas with this proscription power? Would you trust Gotabaya with this surveillance authority? Would you trust Mahinda with this detention provision? If the answer is no, then the law is not safe, because the law will outlast the government. The PSTA, once enacted, will remain on the statute books for the next government, and the one after that. The proscription power the JVP assures the public it will use responsibly will be available to every future president, every future minister, and governments the JVP would consider authoritarian and corrupt. The JVP is not drafting a law for itself. It is drafting a law for every government that will ever follow it, with powers it would never have trusted its predecessors to wield.

The JVP knows what these laws do to people. Its members were detained without charge. Its leaders were tortured in custody. Its cadres were killed under the cover of emergency regulations and terrorism statutes that gave the state power to act without judicial oversight. The party carries this history as its founding wound, invokes it as the moral basis of its political existence, and uses it still to explain why it, unlike every other party, understands the danger of unchecked state power. And then, having stood before the electorate as the party that suffered under unjust laws and therefore would never impose them, it drafts a law that gives the state every power it once condemned, and asks the public to trust that this time,under this government, the power will be used wisely. Every government says this. Every government that has ever enacted a terrorism statute has said this: "Trust us." The JVP said, for thirty years, that this assurance was worthless when offered by others. It was right. It is no less worthless now that the JVP is the one offering it.

text:
They told me the football game started at one in the afternoon, so I arrived at the stadium parking lot at eight in the morning to avoid traffic.

I was three hours late.

Ten thousand pickup trucks and vans were already parked in formation across the asphalt. It did not look like a parking lot. It looked like a sixteenth-century warlord's army camp before a siege.

It was twenty-eight degrees outside. Smoke rose from a thousand steel offset smokers. Men had wired sixty-five-inch flat-screen televisions to portable generators in the backs of their trucks just to watch pre-game commentary about the game they were already attending.

I walked past a truck with a smoker the size of a cannon. A man in a team jersey and face paint saw me looking at the ribs.

"Where you from, brother?" he asked.

"Japan," I said.

He yelled to four men in folding chairs: "Boys! Get this man a plate!"

By 8:20 AM I was holding half a rack of smoked pork ribs, a bratwurst, and a cold beer I did not pay for.

I tried to offer him twenty dollars. He looked offended.

"Your money is no good in Lot C," he said, pointing his tongs at me. "Just promise me you hate their quarterback for the next four hours."

I promised. A samurai pays his debts.

text:
SANKEN GEN: A New Chapter in Global Expansion

With nearly five decades of experience in the construction industry, Ranjith Gunatilleke, Chairman of SANKEN GEN, has witnessed the evolution of Sri Lanka’s construction sector. Rooted in the discipline and technical expertise of Japanese construction practices, the Group has evolved into an international enterprise, executing projects across diverse markets.

The establishment of SANKEN GEN as an independent international group marks a new chapter, strengthening overseas operations and empowering the next generation of leadership.

Speaking with Business Today, Ranjith Gunatilleke shares his perspectives on diverse areas connected to the construction industry. A career in the military and working with Japanese management has ingrained in him the importance of discipline, integrity, and sound leadership.

Words: Jennifer Paldano Goonewardane.

Photography: Rasanga Dissanayake and Dinesh Fernando.

SANKEN GEN has evolved from a Sri Lankan operation established under Japan’s Mitsui Construction Company into an international group with a presence across multiple regions. Looking back, what were the defining decisions that shaped this transformation, and which proved most consequential to its long-term success?

Although Japan’s Mitsui Construction commenced operations in Sri Lanka in 1977, my direct involvement began in 1979, when the company was contracted to construct the new Parliament complex. That project marked an important beginning for me and laid the foundation for my subsequent growth.

Over the years, the company underwent several transitions, beginning as Sanken Mitsui Construction Lanka, then Sanken Lanka, and finally Sanken Construction, before evolving into what is now SANKEN GEN.

However, beyond these changes in identity and the expansion of our operations, the foundation of our success has remained unchanged. It is the discipline we inherited from the Japanese, which became deeply embedded in our working culture. That discipline, reflected in everything we do, has been fundamental to our growth and long-term success.

What did the transition to full Sri Lankan ownership and leadership require in terms of institutional capability, management culture, technical expertise, and financial independence? How did you ensure that the standards and discipline associated with the company’s Japanese origins were retained?

I joined Mitsui Construction in 1979 as Chief Engineer. From the beginning, I had the opportunity to work closely with the Japanese management team and experience firsthand their approach to business and engineering.

The Japanese maintained exceptionally high standards, whether in technical matters, commercial dealings, or the overall management of the organization. Beyond contractual obligations and formal agreements, they placed tremendous importance on trust, integrity, and discipline. These were principles that shaped the company from its earliest days and continue to guide us.

When Sanken Lanka was established in 1984, the Japanese remained directly involved in its management. Until 2002, the Managing Director and the Board were led by Japanese representatives, while I served as a Director. I assumed the position of Managing Director in 2002. Even after that transition, we continued to have a Japanese Director on the Board, although not from Mitsui Construction, to preserve the management philosophy and values that had become integral to the organization.

I have enormous respect for the Japanese approach to management. Their commitment to discipline, responsibility, and maintaining high standards is quite remarkable. I believe that retaining these values throughout our transition to Sri Lankan leadership has been one of the most important reasons for our success.

Before joining Mitsui Construction, I served in the Army as a professionally qualified engineer. The discipline I experienced in the Army during the 1970s was very similar to what I encountered in Japanese management. Therefore, adapting to that working culture came naturally to me.

Punctuality, loyalty, commitment, and accountability were not considered additional expectations. They were fundamental responsibilities of the job. That was the culture we established and continued to uphold.

Our Sri Lankan engineers joined the company with strong academic qualifications and technical knowledge acquired through our universities. Working within Sanken gave them the opportunity to combine that knowledge with the discipline and professional standards of the Japanese system. Over time, these principles became part of the organization’s culture, which continues to define how we operate today.

The establishment of SANKEN GEN as an independent international group represents a significant structural change. What prompted this transition, and how will the new structure strengthen the Group’s international operations while creating opportunities for the next generation of leadership?

The fundamental principles of our organization, particularly discipline, commitment, and our approach to business, have not changed. I remain a shareholder of Sanken Construction while serving as Chairman of SANKEN GEN. What has changed is the structure through which we intend to pursue future growth.

As Sanken Construction expanded, we recognized that success depended on financial strength and technical expertise. I have always believed in specialization, whether in infrastructure development, piling, or other construction activities. Specialized work must be undertaken by people with the necessary expertise, rather than by a jack-of-all-trades.

The period from 2019 to 2026 has been particularly challenging for Sri Lanka’s construction industry, with financial difficulties compounded by the pandemic and economic crisis. Although we began expanding overseas in 2003, there was less urgency then because the domestic industry was performing well. The challenges of recent years reinforced the importance of international expansion.

However, operating internationally requires greater independence in decision-making. Those managing overseas projects must have the authority to act promptly because delays can have serious financial and operational consequences.

This was a principal reason for restructuring. We wanted to empower the next generation of leadership, giving my son and his team the independence and responsibility to take the business forward.

My son, Mevan Gunatilleke, is professionally well qualified, perhaps even more so than I am, although experience naturally comes with time. Leadership transitions are inevitable, but succession is not merely about passing responsibility from one generation to another. It is about building confidence among younger professionals and providing them with capable, disciplined leadership. I believe my son is ready to take on that responsibility.

SANKEN GEN’s new structure brings together operating companies within a wider network, allowing them to draw on shared financial resources, technical expertise, and operational capabilities. How will this collaborative model strengthen the Group’s competitiveness and support its international expansion?

In the construction industry, growth can take place both vertically and horizontally. However, expansion in either direction requires substantial financial resources and technical capabilities.

In Sri Lanka, companies generally depend on banks and other financial institutions to support their expansion. At the same time, they must invest in technology, research, and specialized expertise to remain competitive. Developing all these capabilities independently is not always practical, particularly when several companies are operating in different areas of construction.

Consider a group of five companies. They will not necessarily grow at the same pace or achieve the same level of success at any given time. One company may be performing exceptionally well, while another may require additional financial assistance, technical support, or management expertise. The strength of a group structure is that these companies can support one another rather than operate entirely independently. That is the thinking behind our approach. We want the companies within the Group to benefit from each other’s strengths. The company with the greater resources or capabilities at a particular time can provide support to others, enabling the entire network to grow.

As SANKEN GEN expands its international operations, it will also be in a stronger position to provide financial and technical support to other companies within the Group. Sanken Construction, for instance, is primarily engaged in domestic construction, whereas SANKEN GEN is focused on opportunities beyond Sri Lanka.

The scale of international operations can create significant advantages. If our domestic operations can employ 5,000 people, while our international operations create opportunities for 10,000 people with better remuneration and greater exposure, naturally, the international business will become an increasingly important source of strength for the Group.

What additional capabilities must Sri Lankan contractors develop to compete successfully in overseas markets, particularly in managing financial, regulatory, and contractual complexities?

International construction is a complicated business because you must manage challenges both within the organization and in the external environment. There is a Sinhala expression, “Anto Jata, Bahi Jata,” which refers to internal and external complexities. The challenge is knowing how to manage both successfully.

When Sri Lankan companies venture overseas, they must navigate different financial and regulatory environments. We must comply with Sri Lanka’s Central Bank regulations while understanding the laws and financial systems of the countries in which we operate. For instance, companies in financially stronger economies such as Japan may enjoy greater flexibility in transferring funds internationally, whereas Sri Lankan companies face restrictions shaped by our economic circumstances.

Beyond finance, technical specifications, safety standards, and contractual obligations differ across markets. In Sri Lanka, we are familiar with the regulatory framework of the Construction Industry Development Authority (CIDA). Internationally, however, we must understand frameworks such as the FIDIC conditions of contract, including performance bonds, guarantees, warranties, and retention payments. These directly affect a project’s financial viability and successful execution.

We cannot approach international business with a limited understanding of how the industry operates beyond Sri Lanka. We must be familiar with international standards, practices, and expectations.

This also highlights the importance of developing our professionals. A young engineer may graduate with excellent technical knowledge, but a university degree alone cannot provide the practical experience required to manage complex international projects. Overseas, professional credibility depends on knowledge, experience, and the ability to deliver.

Sri Lankan engineering graduates are highly capable, and I believe their technical knowledge compares favorably with international standards. However, technical competence must be complemented by discipline, loyalty, commitment, and professional responsibility. These are qualities we have consistently sought to instill within our organization through training, mentoring, and experience. Our responsibility is to continue developing professionals who can meet the demands of international construction.

Over the past five years, the Group has executed a project portfolio valued at approximately USD 900 million across seven countries. What does this experience reveal about the competitive strengths Sri Lankan construction companies can bring to international markets, and what challenges must they overcome to compete with larger global players?

One of our biggest challenges is access to finance. Sri Lanka’s limited foreign exchange reserves and restrictions on overseas investment place local companies at a disadvantage relative to international competitors with greater financial capacity.

However, the Government has introduced some flexibility, considering certain investments on a case-by-case basis. I believe this is necessary because when a company can demonstrate that an overseas investment will generate returns and bring foreign exchange into the country, it should be encouraged. For instance, investing USD 100 million to generate USD 120 million is a commercially sound proposition. Of course, such flexibility must be accompanied by accountability to prevent misuse.

Despite these financial constraints, Sri Lanka has a significant competitive advantage in its human resources. We have highly qualified engineers, quantity surveyors, lawyers, and other professionals whose expertise is available at competitive costs. This does not mean we undervalue them. Our free education system has produced a technically competent workforce, and that is a national investment whose value we must recognize. I believe our professionals can compete with, and in many instances surpass, their international counterparts.

However, we must understand the realities of different markets. The opportunities, working environments, and acceptance of professionals from our region vary considerably between countries such as India and the United States. We must identify where our capabilities can be most effectively utilized.

Our strength is combining technical expertise with competitive costs, enabling us to undertake international projects and generate foreign exchange. But we need the financial capacity to invest overseas before we can earn those returns.

We must also broaden our understanding of the scale of international business. In Sri Lanka, billions of dollars seem enormous, particularly when discussing our national debt. Yet, in larger economies, such sums are relatively modest. For instance, the value of Saudi Arabia’s daily oil production can exceed one billion dollars.

Sri Lankan companies have the professional capabilities to compete globally. What we need is greater financial flexibility, a broader international outlook, and the confidence to operate on a larger scale. Addressing these limitations will enable our construction industry to expand internationally and contribute more significantly to the country’s foreign exchange earnings.

Sri Lanka’s construction industry has faced considerable volatility in exchange rates, material prices, and operating costs. How have these challenges affected the industry’s competitiveness, and how can greater international exposure help companies such as SANKEN GEN adopt technology and manage costs more effectively?

One of the biggest challenges facing Sri Lanka’s construction industry is currency volatility and the resulting fluctuations in construction costs. These changes are often driven by the country’s broader economic circumstances rather than developments within the industry itself.

We experienced this when the exchange rate moved from approximately 180 to 360 rupees against the US dollar within a relatively short period. The impact was enormous because, apart from locally sourced materials such as sand and aggregates, a substantial proportion of construction materials and equipment is imported. Consequently, currency depreciation can cause costs to increase almost immediately, creating considerable uncertainty for contractors and developers.

Another concern is the efficiency of public sector administration and procurement practices. Weaknesses in these areas have contributed to inefficiencies and price distortions. Consider steel reinforcement bars, which once cost approximately 514,000 per metric ton, compared with around 230,000 rupees today. Yet, despite reductions in certain material prices, the overall cost of constructing a house has increased considerably. This raises questions about how construction costs are determined.

In countries such as Singapore, price movements tend to be more predictable. In Sri Lanka, however, our dependence on imported materials, machinery, fuel, and technology makes us particularly vulnerable to external economic conditions.

We must also be selective in adopting technology. While technological advancements improve convenience and efficiency, we must consider their economic value. In construction, for instance, manual labor using traditional tools has increasingly been replaced by mechanized equipment. This improves productivity, but the machinery, spare parts, and fuel are largely imported, increasing our dependence on foreign exchange.

Therefore, we must strike a balance between technological advancement and economic sustainability. We cannot simply invest in every new technology without assessing its necessity, cost, and long-term benefits.

This is where SANKEN GEN’s international expansion becomes important. Operating in different markets exposes us to advanced construction methods, equipment, and technologies, enabling us to identify what is commercially viable and appropriate for our operations. International projects also generate foreign exchange, strengthening our capacity to invest in the right equipment and expertise.

We cannot remain like a frog in a well, unaware of developments beyond our borders. We must understand how the global construction industry is evolving and adopt the technologies and practices that will improve our efficiency and competitiveness.

Governments across emerging markets continue to invest in infrastructure, urban development, and tourism. However, financial constraints and weaknesses in project implementation can undermine the returns on these investments. In your view, what should determine investment priorities, and how important are sound planning and efficient public sector execution?

Every investment must generate a reasonable return. Otherwise, why would an investor take the risk of entering a business when they could earn a return by placing their money in a fixed deposit? Unfortunately, Sri Lanka has relatively few sectors where investors can confidently expect returns that justify the risks.

Take tourism, for example. Despite substantial investment in hotels and infrastructure, we must examine the returns being generated. Tourist arrivals have improved, but attracting high-spending visitors remains a challenge. A hotel room in Colombo that once commanded around USD 125 per night may now fetch approximately USD 60 per night. Compare that with Singapore or the Maldives, where room rates can be considerably higher. If we invest in facilities of comparable standards, we must be able to generate sufficient revenue to justify the expenditure.

Sri Lanka must therefore identify sectors with genuine growth potential. Education is one such opportunity. We have excellent human resources, and countries such as Australia and Malaysia have demonstrated how education can become a significant industry. Agriculture and healthcare also offer opportunities, including attracting patients from regional markets such as India and the Maldives.

However, identifying opportunities is only part of the challenge. Equally important is the Government’s ability to implement projects efficiently. We have seen substantial budget allocations remain unutilized because institutions lack the capacity to execute planned projects.

Public procurement must function effectively, supported by competent professionals at every level. Unfortunately, the migration of skilled personnel has weakened institutional capacity. Unless we address these inefficiencies, even well-funded projects will struggle to deliver the economic returns the country needs.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns a Russian victory in Ukraine could shatter global alliances, reshape the world economy, and force nations to question whether they can still rely on America. 🇺🇸

Asked what a Russian victory in Ukraine would mean for the global economy, Dimon responded:

“It could be a potential disaster.

This is the first war in Europe where a free, democratic nation was invaded by 200,000 or 300,000 Russian soldiers under the threat of nuclear blackmail.

We’ve never had nuclear blackmail before.

You’re also teaching the whole world that maybe having nuclear weapons is a pretty good thing, because people will be afraid of you, and you can abuse a neighbor if you feel like it.

Russia would be on the border of NATO. Obviously, NATO is rearming right now.

But the other thing is, it’s affecting all alliances, military alliances and global economic alliances.

And the nexus of Iran, North Korea, and China makes it very hard, in my view, for the Chinese-American relationship.

China says they’re neutral, but they’re helping. We are clearly not neutral.

If Russia wins, you might see a lot of people deciding: Will America stand up for Europe? Can you rely on them? And if you can’t rely on them, what are you going to do?

That includes economically.

Every nation is going to say, what makes me secure? Energy, food, all the things I need.

I’m worried that if Russia wins, you could see the world enter a little bit of chaos as people realign alliances and economic relationships.”

text:
Artist, Block Carver, Applying Sizing (Eshi, hangashi, dosa-biki), from the series The Cultivation of Brocade Prints, a Famous Product of Edo (Edo meibutsu nishiki-e kosaku)
Kitagawa Utamaro 喜多川 歌麿 · Art Institute of Chicago
Artist, Block-carver, Applying Sizing (Eshi, hangashi, dosa-biki), from the series Edo meibutsu nishiki-e kosaku (江戸名物錦絵耕作, “Cultivation of Brocade Prints, a Famous Product of Edo”), c. 1803, by Kitagawa Utamaro.

Vertical ōban nishiki-e triptych (combined dimensions approximately 38.5 × 74.4 cm). Each sheet signed “Utamaro hitsu.” Published by Tsuruya Kiemon (Sōkakudō). An impression of the complete triptych is held by the Art Institute of Chicago (Clarence Buckingham Collection, 1939.2141). Related sheets are also in the British Museum.

The three sheets form a continuous scene of the production of color woodblock prints (nishiki-e), with women performing every stage. Visible activities include:

Applying sizing (dosa)—a mixture of animal glue and alum—to sheets of handmade paper so that pigments will not bleed.

Carving the key block (omo-han) and clearing large areas of wood.

Drawing or pasting the design onto the block.

Other preparatory and finishing tasks, with stacks of paper, tools, and blocks throughout.

Inscriptions on the sheets explicitly equate each stage of print production with a stage in rice cultivation (seedling bed, transplanting, harvest, etc.), turning the making of a “famous product of Edo” into an agricultural metaphor.

Subject and Style

In reality, most of these craft roles (especially block-carving and printing) were performed by men. Utamaro substitutes elegant women, converting the workshop into a world of beautiful figures, patterned robes, and graceful gestures. The result is a characteristic late Utamaro bijin-ga treatment of an occupational theme: intimate, detailed observation of work combined with the refined, elongated female ideal he had perfected in the 1790s.

Context within Utamaro’s Career and the Regulatory Environment

Dated circa 1803, this is a late work, produced after the main wave of Kansei restrictions (naming bans on non-courtesans ~1793, suppression of hanji-e rebuses in 1796, and tighter controls on certain formats and content). By this point Utamaro had largely moved away from named Yoshiwara celebrities. Occupational and domestic scenes—women engaged in silk production, needlework, or, here, the print trade itself—offered a relatively safe vehicle. The subject is the craft process rather than contemporary scandal, named individuals, or prohibited historical figures. The agricultural metaphor further frames the activity as productive and wholesome.

At the same time, the print remains thoroughly in the floating-world idiom: the women are idealized beauties, and the scene retains a mild, observational sensuality in the fall of robes, the play of hands, and the close physical proximity of the figures. It is also mildly meta—an image about the making of images—produced at a moment when the industry itself was operating under increasing official scrutiny.

This work sits immediately before the 1804 incident in which Utamaro (along with other artists) was imprisoned and then manacled for fifty days for prints depicting Toyotomi Hideyoshi in ways the shogunate found disrespectful. Those political offenses, rather than any erotic content, effectively ended his most productive period; he died in 1806.

In the broader arc of his response to censorship, the Edo meibutsu nishiki-e kosaku triptych exemplifies the late adaptation: relocating the intimate, beautiful depiction of women from the pleasure quarters into the sphere of everyday skilled labor. The print industry becomes both subject and, through the beauty of the women who “cultivate” it, a vehicle that could still be published. It is one of the clearest statements of Utamaro’s continuing interest in the material and human processes that produced the floating world, rendered with the same psychological and aesthetic care he had earlier applied to courtesans and mothers.

*ROOTED IN GRACE*

*Why Trees Are Earth’s True VIPs and We Just Live in Their Shade*

Human beings are rather pleased with themselves. We built the internet, sent rovers to Mars, and invented cheese-burst pizza. Yet for staying alive, our entire civilization depends on a quiet collective of leafy organisms standing outside in the rain. Trees are the original *VIPs—_Very Important Plants_*. They produce oxygen, clean our air, and cool our boiling streets, without issuing invoices or updating LinkedIn.

Human society, by comparison, is exhausting. We nurse rivalries, argue over imaginary problems, doomscroll till our eyes burn, then complain about stress. Plants do none of this nonsense.

*The Ultimate Houseguests*

No major Indian celebration dares proceed without a plant. During _Ugadi_ or housewarmings, doorways are framed with fresh mango leaves *(Mamidi Aakulu)* — natural green bouncers who say welcome, provided you remove footwear. Festivals come alive with *marigold* _(Banthipoolu)_ and *jasmine* _(Malle)_. In the courtyard, the *Tulasi Kota* gets more daily devotion than most family members — and crucially, nobody asks _Tulasi_ about its salary or retirement plan. Down the street, the *Banyan* _(Marri Chettu)_ offers free shade without asking for an entry pass.

Without plants, civilization grinds to a halt. In proper Hyderabadi terms: *without paddy fields, no rice; without rice, no biryani; and without biryani, what would Hyderabad discuss at dinner?* Yet we fell fifty-year-old trees to widen a road by three yards, pave it in tar, and then act shocked that May feels like a furnace. Replacing a mature canopy with two plastic-potted saplings is not an equal trade. A tree is not an obstacle to development; it is the infrastructure that makes living here possible.

*A Garden Guide to Difficult People*

Garden pests look suspiciously like people in our office and WhatsApp groups:

- *The Ghoster _(Root Rot)_:* Lush on top, rotted underground. The friend who vanishes for eight months and messages, _"Hey! Quick favor—are you free this weekend?"_
- *The Micromanager _(Spider Mites)_:* Invisible pests that suffocate leaves in fine webs. The boss who approves font sizes and needs a PowerPoint before you take tea.
- *The Chronic Complainer _(Powdery Mildew)_:* A grey film over everything. The colleague for whom tea is lukewarm, monsoon is mistimed, and the peacock at KBR Park is showboating. Ten minutes with them and even a cactus feels depressed.
- *The Emotional Parasite _(Dodder Vine)_:* A leafless vine that drains its host. One gives endlessly, the other takes relentlessly.
- *The Fragile Egoist _(Fiddle-Leaf Fig)_:* Drops leaves if temperature shifts two degrees. The coworker who needs three alignment meetings to sign a routing slip.

*The Executive Botanical Gift Guide*

- *Veteran Statesperson — Banyan Sapling _(Marri Chettu)_:* Wide-canopied, anchored by roots that outlast political seasons.
- *Opposition Leader — Bougainvillea _(Kagitha Puvvu)_:* Thrives in heat, brilliant color, armed with sharp thorns.
- *IT Manager — Snake Plant:* Indestructible. Survives low light, no water — ideal when engineers vanish during midnight crashes.
- *Legal Counsel — Euphorbia Trigona:* Heavily spined. For someone who thinks every handshake needs a five-page disclaimer.
- *Chartered Accountant — Jade Plant:* Compact, steady growth. A tribute to disciplined compounding.

*Rooted in Grace*

My affection for trees began with my late father, who taught me to notice their silent dignity. Over 53 years, my wife has shared and nurtured this fascination — my father planted the first seeds; my wife helped them flourish.

In a world of digital noise and inflated egos, trees offer something simple: *stay deeply rooted, grow with patience, and offer shade to everyone without asking who sits beneath it*.

text:
There appears to be a growing atmosphere of scaremongering, with several European countries and Japan repeatedly advising their citizens to stock up on essential supplies and prepare for potential emergencies. 

What is particularly concerning is that nobody seems to have a clear understanding of the nature, scale or likelihood of the threat. Is it the possibility of war, disruption to energy supplies, cyberattacks, breakdown of critical infrastructure or another global crisis?

 Repeated warnings without sufficient explanation inevitably create anxiety and uncertainty among ordinary people.

This situation reminds me very much of the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic and how much of the Western world reacted to the prospect of a lockdown. 

I vividly remember one Friday afternoon when strong rumours began circulating that a lockdown was about to be announced. I had gone to a nearby Desi grocery shop to purchase something, completely unaware of what I was about to witness. The scene inside was genuinely shocking. People were arriving with enormous shopping trolleys, buying 50–100 kg bags of chapati flour, rice and virtually anything else they could get their hands on. The shopkeeper himself warned me that severe shortages were imminent and advised me to purchase whatever was still available.

I initially refused to participate in this sudden panic buying, but subsequently realised that my decision had been rather naive. 

Within a remarkably short period, everyday essentials disappeared from supermarket shelves. From handwashing liquids and sanitising products to toilet rolls, kitchen rolls, flour and other basic necessities, there was widespread scarcity almost overnight. It was a striking demonstration of how quickly apparently well-functioning societies can become vulnerable when normal supply chains are disrupted and public anxiety takes over.

One of the biggest weaknesses exposed during the pandemic was the limited physical and psychological preparedness of many Western societies for prolonged disruption. 

Modern Western economies have become heavily dependent on just-in-time supply chains, centralised distribution systems and the assumption that supermarkets, pharmacies, electricity networks and other essential services will always function normally. 

While this system is highly efficient during stable times, it can become a significant vulnerability during a major crisis. 

Many people belonging to the present generation have never experienced prolonged shortages of food, drinking water, electricity or other basic necessities. Consequently, even a relatively short disruption can create considerable anxiety and social instability.

By contrast, Indian society has historically developed a different kind of resilience. Despite its many economic and infrastructural challenges, India has a deeply embedded culture of family support, community networks, resourcefulness and collective responsibility.

 Extended families, neighbourhood relationships, local food networks and informal support systems often become particularly important during difficult circumstances. 

People are accustomed to adapting, making limited resources stretch further and finding alternative solutions when formal systems fail. This does not mean that India is immune to shortages or that its infrastructure is without weaknesses, but its social fabric provides an additional layer of resilience that is often underestimated.

The COVID-19 pandemic offered an interesting illustration of these differences. At the beginning of the crisis, sections of the Western media published alarming predictions about India's impending collapse, anticipating catastrophic food shortages, a breakdown of healthcare services and an inability to provide essential medicines to its enormous population. 

India undoubtedly faced immense challenges, including a devastating second wave, pressure on hospitals, oxygen shortages and considerable human suffering. It would be wrong to overlook these realities. However, the country also demonstrated remarkable mobilisation and adaptability. Government agencies, healthcare workers, pharmaceutical manufacturers, voluntary organisations, religious institutions and ordinary citizens contributed to the response. 

India developed and manufactured vaccines, expanded its pharmaceutical and medical supply capacity and, through its Vaccine Maitri initiative, supplied vaccines to numerous other countries. It also provided medicines and humanitarian assistance internationally during the pandemic.

What this demonstrated was that national resilience cannot be measured purely by GDP, per-capita income, modern infrastructure or the appearance of well-stocked supermarkets. 

The ability of a society to withstand adversity also depends on its people, community relationships, cultural adaptability, domestic manufacturing capabilities and willingness to support one another.

Of course, India has its own vulnerabilities, particularly its enormous population, dependence on imported energy, regional inequalities and the pressure that a prolonged disruption could place on its infrastructure. 

No country can claim complete protection against a major global catastrophe. 

Nevertheless, India's combination of domestic agricultural production, pharmaceutical manufacturing, established community networks and an adaptable population gives it certain advantages that should not be underestimated.

Without hesitation, I would argue that, in the unfortunate event of a major global catastrophe, India could prove to be one of the more resilient and potentially safer places to be. 

The modern world has become so accustomed to convenience, uninterrupted supply chains and instant availability of everything that it may have forgotten an important lesson: when systems fail, it is not necessarily the wealthiest societies that cope best, but those whose people know how to adapt, share resources and stand together.

text:
Acoustic therapy for muscle recovery primarily involves therapeutic ultrasound and related acoustic/vibration modalities that use sound waves to promote tissue healing, reduce pain and inflammation, improve circulation, and support regeneration in muscles and soft tissues.

The most evidence-backed clinical form is Sustained Acoustic Medicine (SAM), a wearable, low-intensity continuous ultrasound therapy (typically 3 MHz at ~0.132 W/cm²) applied for 1–4 hours daily. It differs from traditional clinic ultrasound by delivering a much higher total energy dose over longer periods via a portable device and coupling patches.⁠

How It Works
SAM and related low-intensity ultrasound therapies act through both thermal and mechanical (mechanotransductive) effects:

Tissue heating (diathermy): Raises intramuscular temperature (reported increases of several °C), which boosts blood flow, vasodilation, and nutrient delivery.
Acoustic streaming and microstreaming: Creates convective flow deep in tissue (up to ~5 cm), increasing capillary permeability, exchanging nutrients/oxygen, and helping clear waste products.
Cellular stimulation: Activates membrane receptors and pathways (e.g., involving FAK, MAPK) that promote cell proliferation, migration, collagen deposition, and tissue remodeling. It can also influence inflammation and support muscle repair processes.
Specific recovery benefits include improved lactate clearance after intense exercise.⁠
These mechanisms help with muscle strains, contusions, spasms, tendinopathies, and post-exercise recovery. Related approaches include standard/low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS/LITUS), which supports myogenesis, satellite cell activity, angiogenesis, and biomechanical improvements in animal and clinical data, and higher-energy extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT/acoustic wave therapy) for certain muscle injuries and hematomas.

Lower-frequency vibroacoustic stimulation (sound + vibration via chairs, mats, or transducers) has been studied for post-exercise recovery and may support parasympathetic activation (e.g., increased heart-rate variability) and subjective recovery in some athletes, though results are mixed and sometimes consistent with placebo effects for delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS).⁠

Evidence
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies (372 participants) on SAM found clinically meaningful reductions in musculoskeletal pain (roughly 2–4 points on 0–10 scales) and improvements in joint function (20–87%). It was useful as an adjunct when standard physical therapy alone was insufficient, with a favorable safety profile.⁠

One placebo-controlled crossover study in people after high-intensity resistance exercise reported ~20% lower blood lactate with active SAM versus sham, plus gains in peak torque, total work, and power output. Professional sports athletic trainers have reported high satisfaction with SAM for accelerating healing of muscle strains, contusions, spasms, and related soft-tissue issues; many athletes use it at home.⁠Pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih

Broader literature supports low-intensity ultrasound for soft-tissue recovery (tendon, muscle, ligament), though results depend on parameters (intensity, duration, duty cycle). Shockwave therapy shows promising results for pain, function, and return-to-play in some muscle injury studies but needs more high-quality trials. Overall, acoustic approaches are non-invasive and drug-free adjuncts rather than standalone cures.

Practical Use
SAM devices (e.g., sam® Sport/Pro systems) are FDA-cleared for prescription home use. They involve attaching transducers via gel-capture patches over the target area (often with one over the site and another nearby for broader coverage). Treatment is typically daily for multi-hour sessions. Athletic trainers and clinicians use it across healing phases, often alongside RICE, physical therapy, or other modalities.⁠Pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih

Access is usually by prescription; costs can be substantial (thousands of dollars for multi-week kits, sometimes covered in certain injury or workers’ compensation contexts). Traditional ultrasound is available in physical therapy clinics. Always consult a physician or qualified clinician before starting, especially for acute injuries, as it is an adjunct to proper diagnosis, rest, progressive loading, and rehabilitation—not a replacement.

Limitations: Evidence is stronger for pain, function, and soft-tissue support than for dramatic standalone performance recovery in healthy athletes. Individual results vary. Broader “sound healing” or sound-bath approaches are more wellness-oriented with less specific data for muscle repair.

In short, sustained acoustic medicine and related ultrasound therapies offer a mechanobiological way to support muscle and soft-tissue recovery with growing clinical use in sports and musculoskeletal care. Speak with a healthcare provider to see if it fits your situation.

text:
I don't understand why more people don't get this.  In 2016, after seeing an article in the WSJ by Nina Teichholz, I looked into her book about diet and health.  I read the reviews and they said it was basically derivative of an earlier work, Good Calories, Bad Calories by Gary Taubes.  His is the book I bought.

After reading his book, he being a science journalist, I decided I would experiment on myself.  I love hamburgers--pretty much the perfect food.  So I generally would have a burger for lunch three times a week.  It was always had ketchup and was alwasys accompanied by a large order of fries, and a Coke or sweet tea.  
Week 1, I exchanged the Coke or sweet tea for unsweet tea--also, no more ketchup.
Week 2, I cut out the french fries.  
Week 3 and after, I ordered my burger on iceberg lettuce leaves rather than on a bun.  I carried my low carb-high fat diet into dinner as well.  The carbs are usually a discreet portion on the plate--mashed potatoes, a roll, white rice.  Those I would just leave on the plate.  Within a month, if offered anything sweet, I realized it would make me shaky and nauseated if I ate more than a bite. That was my insulin sensitivity returning.  Insulin has just as much capacity to activate the sympathetic nervous system as adrenaline--increasing heart rate, decreasing peripheral circulation, and making you feel shaky.

As a 6' tall man, I weighed 237 pounds when I began my experiment.  That was most definitely NOT all muscle.  Within three months, I had lost thirty pounds.  I lost another twenty by the end of the sixth month.  

Blood pressure, resting heart rate, and particularly cholesterol all came down.  On statins, my LDL dropped 4 points.  Off of the statins, and on low carb-high fat, my cholesterol dropped 40 points, into the reference range.  My doctor kicked me out of his practice after I told him what I had done.  

I never counted a calorie, and I never went hungry.  I wound up eating less during the biggest period of weight loss, because I was dining on my own stored energy--the fat that had been stuck in my fat cells as triglycerides by a constant release of insulin was now free to move about my blood stream as fatty acids.  

There is no such thing as a dietary carbohydrate deficiency.

text:
The Rising Star 🇺🇸

At 16, Marcus Johnson lived with his mother in a small apartment in Detroit, Michigan. His mother worked two jobs to keep food on the table, while Marcus dreamed of becoming a professional basketball player.

Every evening, after finishing his homework, Marcus walked to a public basketball court with a cracked backboard. He practiced until the streetlights came on, even during the cold Michigan winters.

Some boys laughed at his worn out sneakers.

“NBA? You?” one of them joked. “You can barely afford new shoes!”

Marcus smiled and kept playing.

One Friday night, his high school hosted a basketball game against its biggest rival. Sitting in the bleachers was a college scout who had come to watch another player.

But when Marcus stepped onto the court, everything changed.

He scored 28 points, made a game winning shot, and led his team to victory. The crowd erupted, chanting his name.

The scout approached him after the game and offered him an opportunity to attend a prestigious basketball camp.

Marcus ran home to tell his mother. She hugged him tightly, crying with happiness.

Years later, Marcus became a first round NBA draft pick. Cameras flashed as he walked onto the stage wearing his new team's cap.

When a reporter asked what kept him going through the difficult years, Marcus looked straight into the camera.

“My mom worked double shifts so I could chase a dream. Every time I wanted to quit, I remembered who was sacrificing for me.”

With his first major paycheck, Marcus bought his mother a beautiful home not because he wanted to show off, but because he remembered every night she went to bed worried about rent.

On the front porch of their new home, his mother held his face and whispered, “I always knew you were special.”

Marcus smiled.

“No, Mom. You just never let me believe I wasn't.”

And that was how a boy from a small Detroit apartment became a rising star not just because of his talent, but because he never forgot the woman who believed in him before the world knew his name.
